en: The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master Guangfan, Scroll One.
Translated by the Purple-Garbed Śramaṇa and Subject Weijing et al., by Imperial Decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Great Bodhisattva Palace within the Supreme Dharma-Assembly Hall of Great Jewel Adornments, which is the realm of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers. That Dharma-assembly hall was established through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; it was adorned with the accumulation of vast and supreme merit, perfected through the wondrous practices of great merit and wisdom, and manifested as the superior retribution of all Buddha-dharmas. It displayed the power of the Tathāgata’s boundless miraculous transformations and empowerments, and through the great wisdom that skillfully enters the unobstructed realm, it brought immense joy to all who beheld it.
It entered the practice of mindfulness and wisdom, universally operating the immovable, wondrous wisdom that has cultivated and accumulated immeasurable masses of merit over boundless eons.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has realized the path of awakening to the equality of all phenomena and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma; he is able to skillfully discipline boundless assemblies of disciples and has attained great mastery over all phenomena.
He thoroughly knows the mentalities and the various faculties of all sentient beings and has reached the supreme further shore.
Having completely severed all seeds and habitual tendencies, he has attained the unconditioned tranquility of the Buddha-body.

At that time, he was accompanied by a great assembly of six million eight hundred thousand bhikṣus; all were established in the proximity of the mind, having completely severed all seeds and habitual tendencies of affliction, and were all sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King.

They were able to skillfully give rise to the profound practice of the Dharma of non-apprehension; their physical forms were upright and majestic, their deportment was perfectly complete, and they served as great fields of merit, fully endowed with right wisdom.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, incomparable, and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. They had all attained the Bodhisattva’s patience of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-kṣānti*), had already transcended the stage of Bodhisattva consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and were able to sport with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas in the stage of effortless mastery (*anābhoga*). They had attained inexhaustible *dhāraṇīs* and the various *dhāraṇī-gates* of Bodhisattvas;
they attained sovereign mastery within the *Śūraṅgama-rāja-samādhi* of all Bodhisattvas, and were joyfully beheld by all sentient beings.

Having attained the various unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of Bodhisattvas, they gave rise to the unawakened conduct of Bodhisattvas, and their profound minds dwelt securely in sublime adornments.
Their names were:

the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayakośa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amitamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nirālambanadarśin, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vīramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anupacchinnapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Asaṅgābhayaskandha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Atyantārthamati.
In this manner, an assembly of immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, incomparable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered together.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through the stages of the bodhisattva practice, skillfully brought forth the profound, true Dharma of the gate of non-obstruction to adorn the path of all bodhisattvas. He accomplished the true wisdom and practices of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, and entered the gate of the seal of the supreme sovereign dhāraṇī of all phenomena.

Entering the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he decisively gave rise to the wondrous realm of the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and proclaimed the wheel of non-retrogression for all, universally gathering all vehicles within the principle of equality.

Merging with the non-conceptual nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he revealed and expounded [the teaching] in accordance with the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings.
In accordance with the knowledge of reality, one ascertains the true Dharma and shatters all demonic realms;
through the profound and firm principles of the Dharma, one brings to rest all afflictions, views, and the like.
Entering into non-attached wisdom, one proclaims the skillful means of universal, vast, and great dedication.
Entering into the wisdom of the equality of all Buddhas, they proclaim all phenomena with precise certainty through the dharma-gate of unattached empowerment.

They enter into equality regarding both non-discrimination and the absence of non-discrimination; they fully awaken to the profound dharma of dependent origination and accumulate immeasurable sublime practices of merit and wisdom.

The Buddha’s body, speech, and mind are equally adorned; according to his knowledge, he reveals the inexhaustible gateways of wisdom—such as mindfulness, insight, and conduct—to manifest the Śrāvaka vehicle through the principle of the Four Noble Truths;
he manifests the Pratyekabuddha vehicle by awakening to the nature of body, mind, and cognition;
and he manifests the Mahāyāna dharma by attaining the empowerment of omniscience.
Entering into the principle of mastery over all phenomena, one gives rise to the boundless merits of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata reveals, expounds, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, explains, illuminates, and proclaims it.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was about to expound such a vast, profound, and definitive Dharma, suddenly this trichiliocosm became filled with great water, like a vast ocean, extending from the earth realm below up to the most excellent site of enlightenment adorned with great jewels.

Furthermore, just as when the calamity of water at the end of an eon manifests, the entire trichiliocosm is filled with vast waters, merging down to the water-circle into a single ocean; so too is this present great water.

Yet, although this trichiliocosm is thus completely filled with such great waters, the lands, cities, towns, villages, and all the people therein are entirely unharmed and encounter no obstruction; likewise, Jambudvīpa, the four great continents, even the great oceans and Mount Sumeru, as well as all the palaces of the devas of the desire realm, suffer not the slightest damage or hindrance.
After these signs had first appeared, there subsequently emerged within this great body of water hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vast lotus flowers.

Those flowers were lofty and prominent, with stems of lapis lazuli, branches of sapphire, and leaves of Jāmbūnada gold; their filaments were made of the śrīgarbha jewel, their pedestals of agate, and they were interlaced with pearls.
Each flower had countless koṭis of hundreds of thousands of petals, each petal being one krośa in breadth.

These lotuses emerged from the void within the most excellent site of enlightenment, the Great Jewel Adornment, rising to the height of a *tāla* tree. The entire great assembly sat upon the lotuses, and from within each lotus, light was radiated according to its respective color and form; this light universally illumined immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
When these rays of light shone forth extensively, the entire assembly within this gathering marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; with palms joined in reverence, they all spoke thus:
"Now that such a rare and auspicious sign has appeared, will the World-Honored One not preach the sublime Dharma?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having witnessed these vast and great miraculous manifestations, sat upon his lotus pedestal, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, paid respectful homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason has this sign appeared at this time?

Within this great trichiliocosm, vast waters have filled it until it is as one single ocean, and within it there appear hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotus flowers, rising high and manifest.
“World-Honored One!
This vast and rare spiritual transformation is such that we have never heard of it before, nor have we ever seen it before. We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
“Maitreya, you should know!

Below this buddha-field, passing through as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten hundred-thousand koṭi-nayuta unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields, there is a world named Immeasurable Merit Jewel Stainless Exquisite Adornment. In that land there is a Buddha, titled Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.”

In that realm there is a bodhisattva named Sāgaramati, who, together with a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas beyond all calculation, is about to come to this Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to me; furthermore, he intends to inquire about the Dharma I have taught.
For these reasons, these auspicious signs have first appeared.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That Bodhisattva Sāgaramati is very far from here; for what reason does the World-Honored One say that this bodhisattva is able to hear the Dharma preached by the Buddha in this assembly?”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! Just as you now hear the True Dharma spoken before me, so too does the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati hear the Dharma I speak, even though he dwells in that other world.”
Śāriputra! Just as you now behold me and this great assembly before your eyes, so too does the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati see my body and this great assembly.
Śāriputra said:
"It is marvelous, World-Honored One!

The power of the superknowledges and wisdom of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is inconceivable; for that Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, though dwelling in an extremely distant land, is able to see this physical form with unobstructed eyes and hear this sound with unobstructed ears."
World-Honored One!
If there were anyone who heard of these inconceivable merits and majestic spiritual powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken these words, twenty-four thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, together with a multitude of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas beyond calculation, respectfully surrounded him. Having simultaneously gazed upon that Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña, they received his instructions. Relying on the supernatural power of the Tathāgata’s *ṛddhi* and the unconditioned, perfected supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas, in the space of a single thought-moment—the blink of an eye—they vanished from that world and immediately appeared in the sky above this Sahā world, at the most excellent site of adornment known as Mahāratnavyūha. There, at a height of one *tāla* tree, they sat calmly upon lion thrones atop the highest and widest lotus pedestals.
The other bodhisattvas likewise each sat upon lotus-flower pedestals.

Furthermore, from within the immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-fields of the worlds below, there were also immeasurable and innumerable assemblies of bodhisattvas who followed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, within the most excellent site of enlightenment adorned with great jewels, all the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions were seated upon lotus pedestals, filling the space on every side in a manner both exquisite and extraordinary.

All those who had gathered there felt joy in their hearts and attained complete purity; marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, they joined their palms and prostrated themselves before those bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati took various supreme and exquisite flowers from that world of Immeasurable Merit-Jewel-Stainless-Splendid-Adornment—flowers named "Free from Sorrow, Delightful, Beloved, and Joyful to Behold," each one *krośa* in width and possessing hundreds of thousands of petals—and offered them to the Tathāgata as appropriate. This caused all the bodhisattvas who saw them to have their deep minds become stainless and their roots of goodness from past lives to be completely purified; thus, the entire assembly gave rise to joy, gladness of heart, and loving delight.
The flowers possessed radiance and a wondrous fragrance; having made offerings of these supreme flowers before the World-Honored One, they further rained down a vast and exquisite shower of blossoms.

Each individual flower was the size of seven men, filling and adorning the entire most excellent site of the Great Jewel Adornment Bodhimanda. All the great assembly attained the flavor of the joy of dhyāna that transcends ordinary birth;

from the sky, various drums spontaneously resounded, producing subtle, wondrous, and lovely sounds, and all those in the assembly who heard them attained the sublime bliss of meditative concentration.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, having performed such acts of offering, descended from the air and prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One. He circumambulated him seven times to the right, joined his palms in reverence, stood before the Buddha, and addressed him thus:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña inquires after the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni: Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your faculties at ease and your strength secure?
"Have you attained sublime bliss?

At that time, all the bodhisattvas who had come with him descended from the sky; they too each bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and each returned to sit upon his original seat.

At that time, in this trichiliocosm, there was a Great Brahmā King named Mahākaruṇācintin, who dwelt in this Brahma-world within these four great continents in a state of sorrowless peace and security. Suddenly, he beheld this trichiliocosm filled with vast waters, all blended together as one single ocean.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vast lotuses appeared, lofty and manifesting various sublime signs, and this site of enlightenment was filled with bodhisattvas.
Having seen this sign, he immediately reflected to himself:
"The kalpa-fire has not yet ignited its signs of destruction; how could there be such a great flood filling [the world]?
By what cause is this? Could it not be the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual transformations?"
"I should now go to question the Buddha, the World-Honored One, regarding this rare and extraordinary sign: what is its cause and what is its condition?

Having formed this thought, the Great Brahma King Mahākaruṇācintin immediately took sixty-eight thousand Brahma hosts and, remaining concealed within the Brahma realm, respectfully surrounded him as he approached the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, at the most excellent site of adornment, the Great Jewel Array. Standing in mid-air, he bowed his body, joined his palms, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed him thus:
"World-Honored One!"

For what reason has this great trichiliocosm now become filled with vast waters, merging into a single ocean, yet there have emerged hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immense lotus flowers rising high and manifest; and all the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are seated upon the thrones of these lotuses, while all the lands, cities, towns, and villages of this great trichiliocosm, as well as the populations of Jambudvīpa, the four continents, and the celestial palaces of the desire realm, down to the great oceans and Mount Sumeru, remain entirely undamaged and unobstructed?
Such signs as these are exceedingly rare; by what causes and conditions do they arise, and by what spiritual power?
We pray that the Buddha will explain this for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahmā Mahākaruṇācintin, saying:
"Great Brahmā, you should know!
In a world-system below there is a buddha-field named Immeasurable Merit Jewel Stainless Sublime Adornment. Its World-Honored Buddha is named Sāgarajayadhīvikrīḍitābhijña Tathāgata."

There is a bodhisattva there named Sāgaramati, who, together with a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas beyond all calculation, has come to this Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to me;
furthermore, he has something to inquire about within this sublime Dharma of the vast assembly.
"This is the power of that bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, which has first manifested auspicious signs in this world.
Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"In this great assembly, do you still preach the false dharma regarding all the true dharmas?
The Buddha said,
"Great Brahmā!"
The realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable; the wisdom, eloquence, and majestic spiritual power of all Tathāgatas should not be measured by limits.
If you see the Tathāgata remaining silent, do not think that he says nothing.
"And I constantly proclaim the vast, definitive, and true Dharma for the sake of the Bodhisattvas who come from the worlds of the ten directions.
At that time, the Great Brahma King Mahākaruṇācintin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Who, O Great Brahmā, is this Bodhisattva Sāgaramati whom the Buddha has described as one who manifests supernatural transformations?
The Buddha said:
“Great Brahmā!”

Within this assembly, there is a great lotus flower ten yojanas in breadth. Within the flower is a pedestal, and upon the pedestal is a lion throne adorned with various jewels. Seated upon it is a bodhisattva mahāsattva, his body the color of pure gold, his marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) perfectly dignified; except for the Tathāgata, he outshines all the physical forms of the other bodhisattvas. He is surrounded by countless thousands of bodhisattvas who circumambulate and prostrate before him—do you see him?
He replied, "I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Mahābrahmā!
He who possesses such marks of supernormal powers is none other than the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati.
At that time, the Brahmā Mahākāruṇyavitarka, having paid respectful homage by prostrating at the feet of the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who hear the name of this Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, you should know that such persons have attained great and wholesome benefit.”
Today, having heard the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and beheld such a physical form as his, I am deeply filled with joy and celebration, having attained excellent benefit.
Brahmā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For how long will this True Dharma of the Great Assembly remain?”
The Buddha said:
"Great Brahmā!
This True Dharma shall abide for as long as the lifespan of the Buddha endures."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bodhisattvas who receive, uphold, read, and recite this true Dharma, and extensively explain and expound it for others. Why is this?
"Mahābrahmā!
All the bodhi of all Buddhas in the past, future, and present worlds emerges from within this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, did so for the sake of bringing joy to the entire assembly gathered here.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of inspiring faith and reverence in the Great Brahmā King Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū through the contemplation of great compassion;
again, it is for the sake of adorning this True Dharma;
and also for the sake of manifesting the power of one's own wisdom and eloquence.
Immediately, together with that high and broad lotus flower and lion throne, they all surged upward into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees. Then, from within the sky, he spoke these verses:
"Below, past lands as numerous as motes of dust, There is a buddha-field named Glorious Merit;
That Buddha, the Lord of Transformation, dwells therein, His name is Ocean-Surpassing Supernatural Wisdom."
Within this land, all virtues are perfectly complete; the Bodhisattvas who rely upon it are free from fear.
As for the Dharma-gates taught by that Buddha-Tathāgata, having heard them, we are able to uphold and receive them.
We have come to this buddha-field for this very purpose, to gaze upon and pay homage to the Honored One of Ten Powers;
and as for these bodhisattvas who have arrived here, the Buddha, the Great Bull King, addresses each of them with inquiry.
Having now paid homage to this Dharma King, I also pay homage to the peerless Buddha of great wisdom;
according to what should be offered and whatever is bestowed, I extensively extend offerings to the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One.
If one can contemplate the Buddha’s form and formlessness, Free from sensation, free from formations, and also free from consciousness;
Even these three kinds of experience are absent therein— Within this, there is purity and eternal clarity.
If there are no physical marks or secondary characteristics, this is the correct contemplation of the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
with the pure eye of wisdom illuminating the Dharma-body, one then perceives the stainless, true meaning.
If phenomena are neither grasped nor abandoned, And both extremes are devoid of self and what belongs to self;
Abiding in the quiescent nature of the internal sense-bases, One brings to rest all objects of apprehension external to the mind.
Free from the discrimination of existence and non-existence, and transcending all conceptualization, this mind is as tranquil and silent as space;
it is thus able to make offerings to all the World-Honored Ones and firmly establish the banner of the True Dharma.
If one contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions, both the giver and the receiver therein are empty;
though one knows that all conditioned activities are fundamentally non-existent, one does not abandon or distance oneself from all phenomena.
They do not seek awakening with fixed determination, nor do they remain fixed in birth and death;
there is neither giver nor stingy mind, as they remain far removed from all faults within giving.
Body, speech, and mind are stilled, disciplined, and tranquil; the three karmas follow accordingly without affliction.
All defilements are removed and the burning heat is extinguished; with sharp wisdom, the faculties are ever serene.
Though they know that awakening is unattainable, they do not abandon sentient beings but abide in selflessness;
to deliver all those who have broken their precepts, they cultivate and maintain the vast practice of pure morality.
Realizing that all phenomena are momentary in nature, yet remaining unshaken by any external objects;
with an inner mind as tranquil as space, one views the world externally as being like an illusion.
Even as his body was severed limb from limb, he did not give rise to a single thought of anger;
until he sat beneath the tree and attained Bodhi, he steadfastly maintained the practice of patience as taught by the Buddha.
One is able to contemplate all phenomena as being like the moon reflected in water, like bubbles, like illusions, and like mirages;
one thoroughly understands that there is no life-principle and no person, nor any *maṇavaka* and so forth.
Although enlightenment and sentient beings cannot be attained, one seeks enlightenment for the sake of benefiting others;
if, upon hearing this principle, fear does not arise, one is able therein to give rise to diligent practice.
If one can remain unattached within the mind, Then one will not give rise to aversion toward external objects;
Knowing the mental activities of other sentient beings, One proceeds in accordance with them throughout the three periods of time.
Causing the hosts of Māras to be unable to know the movements of the mind as it turns;
having reached the other shore with a well-established mind, one fulfills meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and wisdom.
I have heard the Dharma taught by all Buddhas, and having heard it, I am able to receive and uphold it;
even throughout the course of boundless eons, the eloquence of the Buddhas cannot exhaust it.
Furthermore, within all Buddha-dharmas, sentient beings neither fall nor cling;
you are the Honored One of Power who possesses the treasury of wisdom, the one who is sovereign over the three realms and abides in silent stillness.
Detached from both the goer and the destination, within this there is neither going nor coming;
according to the mental activities of sentient beings, that which is headed toward has no abiding and no movement.
Though you have reached the other shore and are endowed with all virtues, You remain free from grasping at signs regarding those virtues;
O incomparable Śākyamuni, Great Bull-King, Therefore, I now prostrate before you.
Like the sun, pure and brilliantly radiant, able to eclipse the light of fireflies and the stars;
again, like the kalpa-fire reflecting all lights, ascending to the Brahma-world and descending to the earth.
Furthermore, like the great king of mountains, Sumeru, which supports the earth and all other mountains;
so from within the ūrṇā-kośa of Śākyamuni, the Bull among Men, emerges the most supreme radiance that transcends the three realms.
The assemblies of all bodhisattvas from the ten directions, having all come from hundreds of buddha-fields,
behold the Buddha’s physical marks and majestic radiance, and all give rise to great joy.
According to the mental inclinations and vows of sentient beings, the Tathāgata reveals the teachings to each one accordingly;
knowing the great majestic power of the Tathāgata, I have come from my own land to this realm.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet each sentient being understands it according to their own capacity;
even regarding the diverse voices of all beings, the Tathāgata universally teaches them as is appropriate for each.
The diverse mental dispositions of all sentient beings may be counted like dust motes or grains of sand;
yet the various wondrous sounds of the Muni are equal in measure to space and cannot be numbered.
Space cannot measure its limits; sentient beings cannot exhaust their number.
Even within the prior limit of birth and death, one likewise cannot know its boundary.
The limits of space and the number of sentient beings, even the prior limit of birth and death, may still be known;
yet within the sphere of the Buddhas' morality, concentration, and wisdom, one can never know even a small fraction.
Infinite sentient beings all take refuge in him— The Bull-King, Master of Dharma, Honored One among Men;
Having cultivated myriad virtues through many kalpas with diligent effort, His physical marks and limits are peerless and beyond measure.
Our Buddha possesses great majestic power, Thoroughly knowing the various inclinations and understandings of sentient beings;
Beholding this rare and inconceivable Honored One, I prostrate to the one who skillfully tames all realms of existence.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Two.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati had spoken these verses, he descended from the air, joined his palms toward the Buddha in reverent prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I have a question to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would grant me permission, I shall then ask my question."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
saying: "Good son,
ask whatever you wish."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, according to those who have doubts, is able to proclaim and expound each one for them, causing their minds to open and be enlightened.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Previously, I heard that there are certain bodhisattvas who themselves proclaim the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Seal of Purity (Vimalamudrā). If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they will be able to swiftly realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.”
How should a bodhisattva obtain such a gateway to the samādhi of the Pure Seal?
Furthermore, by what characteristics is it called "self-proclamation"?
And what is this "Pure Seal"?
How can one enter the gateway to that realm?
Furthermore, once bodhisattvas have heard of this samādhi, how do they swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously explain this for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
What you have now asked is most excellent and virtuous.
Well-spoken son of noble family!
"You should listen attentively and receive this with single-minded, profound, and firm attention; I shall now speak for you.
If any bodhisattvas attain this Samādhi of the Seal of Self-Expounded Purity, they will be able to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We are eager and desirous to hear.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "Sāgaramati!

If there is a bodhisattva who exerts diligent effort toward all roots of goodness, who dwells with a perfected virtuous mind within the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), and who, amidst birth and death, is able to accumulate various virtues through sharp faculties; who is sustained by spiritual friends and established by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas; and who is fully endowed with the power of causes—such a person should always draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, honoring and revering them with exquisite incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, thereby making offerings to them.
Furthermore, having seen the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, endowed with the [thirty-two] marks; or having heard the exquisite words of the True Dharma; or having seen the perfect and pure assemblies;
and furthermore, having heard the unimpeded wisdom, or having seen the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the knowledge of wondrous realms (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*);
or having seen the Tathāgata’s various transformations for taming sentient beings, or his miraculous displays of instruction, or his miraculous displays of praise.

Having seen this, one should always give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* toward all sentient beings out of great compassion; one should exert great diligence to earnestly seek wholesome dharmas, never forgetting the mind of omniscience, and purify the initial resolve through corresponding practice. Once the initial resolve is purified, one immediately attains that pure *samādhi*.
“Sāgaramati! It is like a great maṇi jewel produced from its source, which a skilled lapidary places in the palm of his hand, refines with exquisite skill, and further polishes;
once that jewel has attained complete purity, the lapidary himself declares:”
"This mani-jewel removes all that is false and is free from every flaw; it is a pure great mani-jewel, cherished by all who possess wisdom."

"Samudramati! It is just the same with the jewel of the mind set on omniscience that arises from the lineage of a bodhisattva; for it ultimately brings about the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

By means of those bodhisattvas’ former roots of goodness from past lives and their present hearing of the sublime Dharma, they polish and refine that jewel of the mind of omniscience; until that jewel has removed all false and provisional phenomena from within the mind and is free from faults, being cherished by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time, the bodhisattva may then declare for himself that he has attained the samādhi-gate of the Pure Seal.
“Sāgaramati! Furthermore, it is like a pure great maṇi-jewel, which is free from nine kinds of precious natures.
What are these nine?
First, the nature of gold;
second, the nature of silver;
third, the nature of crystal.
Fourth, the nature of vaidūrya;
fifth, the nature of agate;
sixth, the nature of coral.
Seventh, the nature of red pearls;
eighth, the nature of karketana gems;
ninth, the nature of auspicious treasury gems.

Once it is free from these nine kinds of precious natures, it is called the "Delightful, Pure Radiance Great Maṇi Jewel. It is supreme and priceless, to be used by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), and not to be used by any other king.
Furthermore, the light of that great maṇi jewel is exquisite and surpasses the light of all other jewels.
Sea-Mind!
The jewel of the bodhisattvas' mind of omniscience is likewise; it is able to transcend the nine kinds of precious natures.
What are the nine?
First, the jewel-nature of the ordinary being;
second, the jewel-nature of the follower by faith.
Third, the jewel-nature of those who practice in accordance with the Dharma;
fourth, the jewel-nature of those who practice the signless;
fifth, the jewel-nature of the srotāpanna;
Sixth, the jewel-nature of the sakṛdāgāmin;
seventh, the jewel-nature of the anāgāmin;
eighth, the jewel-nature of the arhat.
Ninth is the precious nature of the pratyekabuddhas.
Having transcended these nine precious natures, the tenth is called the precious nature of the profound mind and firm great compassion, which is sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas.

When a bodhisattva thus polishes and refines the jewel of the mind set upon omniscience, it surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is able to illuminate the seeds within the mental continuums of all sentient beings.
"Samudrareṇu! Furthermore, it is like a genuine great maṇi jewel, which can endure being polished and refined, withstands being crushed and pressed, and is not destroyed even when pierced."
That mani jewel is capable of performing beneficial functions within the world, bringing about meritorious deeds for all sentient beings.
It is the same with a bodhisattva who has long planted various roots of goodness.
Furthermore, that jewel of the mind set upon omniscience can endure being polished and refined, withstand being crushed and pressed, and remain unbroken even when pierced.
This jewel is authentic and free from all defects; this jewel of the mind set upon omniscience is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Samudramati!
What is meant by being able to skillfully polish and refine the jewel of the mind of omniscience?

It means that one should first fully cultivate the three types of ethical discipline and purify the ten virtuous actions; because one acts with a heart of loving-kindness, one regards all sentient beings with a pure mind."
Because it functions in accordance with compassion (*karuṇā*), one goes to assist and support whatever tasks sentient beings may be engaged in;
because it functions in accordance with sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one brings all the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings to fulfillment;
and because it functions in accordance with equanimity (*upekṣā*), one causes no harm to any sentient being.

Because he is free from flattery and deception, his mind is upright; because he is free from indolence, he applies himself with deep resolve to beneficial activities; because his mind is sovereign, he is able to give rise to all roots of virtue; because he has attained right mindfulness and clear comprehension and has well subdued his mind, his mind is harmonious and tranquil; because he always has few desires, he is able to cultivate the dhūta qualities in their entirety; and because he is well able to sustain the nourishment of contentment, he never severs the noble lineages.
Because one does not give rise to contempt or arrogance toward the venerable teacher and the noble ones, one is able to be humble and constantly maintain reverence.

Because the mind is settled, one can abandon conceit and overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Because there is no turbidity or confusion, there is no impure mind. Because one does not rely on oneself, one is able to know one’s own conduct; because one does not disparage others, one is able to protect sentient beings. Because one is free from overweening pride, one is able to draw near to the True Dharma and receive the medicinal teachings accordingly.

Because they are able to comprehend and understand all meanings, those who seek the Dharma possess a desire for the Dharma that gradually increases from the initial and shallow stages to the subsequent and profound, becoming ever more expansive within all phenomena.
Because they cultivate conduct free from contention, they constantly attain the joy of the Dharma.

Because they remain far removed from what is not the Dharma, they are able to diligently seek the True Dharma. Because they always maintain a sense of shame and remorse toward the Triple Gem, they are able to ensure that their pure faith is never interrupted. Because they believe in karmic retribution, they apply correct mental attention toward all wholesome dharmas. Because they practice right conduct, they remain concealed and tranquil in their deportment.

Because the mind is not haughty, it is ever supple; because one diligently practices śamatha, one is able to abandon restlessness; because wisdom is well-established, there is neither disparagement nor praise; and because one is serene and unmoving, the mind is like the king of mountains.

Because they are able to remain free from all dualistic oppositions such as high and low, their minds are like the earth; because their inner intention is pure, their minds are like water; because they are without divergent thoughts, their minds are like fire; because they are without attachment, their minds are like wind; and because they are wondrously stainless, their minds are like space.

Because they diligently seek to leave the household life, they are able to ensure that the Buddha-eye is never lost; because the body is able to be detached, they joyfully cultivate the practice of tranquility; and because the mind is able to be detached, they constantly cultivate the practice of the True Dharma.
Because they are not plundered by the objects of sensory realms in their various activities, they speak words of truth;
because their vows are luminous, they are able to act according to what they have said. Because they are not overcome by afflictions, their minds are always pure;

because they are ultimately indestructible, they are able to cultivate and accumulate pure precepts. Because they harbor fear even toward minor transgressions, they remain without deficiency or breach regarding the precepts; because they do not seek rebirth in the heavens, they do not sever their commitment to the precepts; because their conduct is purely white, their precepts are free from turbidity and defilement; and because they constantly associate with virtuous friends, they attain the illumination of the path to Great Bodhi.

Because the eye is pure, one attains unimpeded light; because the ear is pure, one attains unimpeded sound; because the nose is pure, one attains unimpeded fragrance; because the tongue is pure, one attains unimpeded flavor; because the body is pure, one attains unimpeded touch; and because the mind is pure, one attains unimpeded phenomena.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva! If one wishes to be free from the fetter of greed, one should constantly cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

If one wishes to be free from the fetter of hatred, one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-bhāvanā*). If one wishes to be free from the fetter of delusion, one should cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*). If one wishes to eliminate the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), one should skillfully contemplate the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). If one wishes to uproot all obstacles, one should purify the five powers (*pañcabala*). And because one wishes to dispel all presently arisen afflictions (*kleśa*), one should always maintain purity regarding the path of renunciation."

By practicing corrective conduct, one is able to abandon the fears of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; because of being free from stinginess, one is able to practice the gift of Dharma; because of being free from parsimony, one is able to practice the gift of material wealth; because the great bodhicitta is always firm and stable, one does not delight in the teachings of other vehicles; because the inner mind is tranquil, one is able to keep the sense faculties concealed; because external objects are tranquil, one skillfully observes all faults; because one is constantly fearful of birth and death, one commits no transgressions; and because the mind is free from weariness, one accumulates roots of goodness without ever feeling satiety.
To cross over the four floods, one constantly and skillfully repairs the Great Vehicle’s dharma-ship; to cause sentient beings to reach the other shore, one skillfully constructs bridges.
“Bodhisattvas always employ an untiring and non-regressive mind to uproot all sentient beings from the mire of birth and death and lead them to a place of peace and security. ‘Sāgaramati!

If a bodhisattva can fully cultivate such characteristics of practice, they will attain the perfection of the practice of giving and also purify the practice of ethical discipline; this is what is called a bodhisattva’s skillful polishing of the jewel of the mind of omniscience that has been generated.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"First, one should well restrain body, speech, and mind, Guarding the ten kinds of pure actions;
With a heart of loving-kindness, one regards all sentient beings, Thus polishing this mind of omniscience."
With a mind of compassion, one assists others in their undertakings; with a mind of joy, one brings the teachings of others to fulfillment;
with a mind of equanimity, one does not harm any sentient beings—thus is the mind of omniscience polished and refined.
Because free from flattery and deception, the mind is ever upright; ceasing transgressions, one is able to cultivate beneficial deeds.
As the profound mind increases all roots of goodness, the mind of omniscience is polished and refined thereby.
Through mastery over the mind, mindfulness and clear comprehension arise; by skillfully subduing the mind, the heart becomes harmonious and supple.
Capable of few desires, one practices the causes of dhūta austerity; thus is the mind of omniscience polished and refined.
Content with virtuous conduct regarding the noble lineages, and always showing reverence to teachers and elders;
being able to avoid a mind of contempt, one remains far removed from both pride and false arrogance.
With a concentrated mind, one does not give rise to overweening pride; because there is no turbidity or confusion, the mind is pure.
Because one does not rely on oneself, one understands by oneself; because one does not disparage others, one protects them.
One who approaches the profound, firm, and wondrous medicine of the Dharma, Leaving behind overweening pride, cures all ailments;
One who yearns for the Dharma is called a seeker of the Dharma, And by diligently seeking the Dharma, one possesses the desire for the Dharma.
Cultivating conduct free from strife is called delighting in the Dharma; by departing from what is not the Dharma, one is able to seek the Dharma.
Not destroying the Triple Gem and possessing faith, the mind of omniscience is here polished and refined.
Feeling shame within for what is unwholesome, And giving rise to a sense of modesty toward all Tathāgatas;
Endowed with such shame and modesty, guarding the sense faculties— This is how the mind of omniscience is polished and refined.
Clearly understanding the excellence of karmic retribution, with faith and resolve free from attachment to extreme views;
not contradicting the nature of dependently arisen phenomena—the mind of omniscience is thus polished and refined.
Guarding the majestic deportment and practicing right conduct, With a mind free from arrogance, one remains ever supple;
By not giving rise to restlessness and cultivating the practice of tranquility, The mind of omniscience is here polished and refined.
Because wisdom dwells well, there is neither disparagement nor praise; Tranquil and secure, they appear to all like the King of Mountains.
Within their firm vows, no mind of retreat arises; The mind of omniscience is thus polished and refined.
In suffering and pleasure, the mind is unmoving like the earth; the mind is pure like water that washes away the dust of affliction.
The mind is like fire, in which no divergent thoughts arise; the mind is like the wind, moving without attachment.
The mind is like space, wondrous and stainless; Diligently seeking renunciation, the Buddha-eye is clear.
With the body detached, one can cultivate a tranquil mind; With the mind detached, one always relies on the practice of the True Dharma.
In all his actions he always speaks words of truth; as he speaks, so he acts, for his vows are manifest.
Pure and unassailable by defilements, he cultivates the practice of ethical discipline because it is free from breach or destruction.
In the precepts, there is neither deficiency nor violation; even regarding minor offenses, one harbors a sense of great dread.
One guards the precepts not for the sake of seeking rebirth in heaven, but so that the precepts remain ever pure and free from defilement.
Constantly able to draw near to spiritual friends, They have all been enlightened regarding the bodhicitta;
Unobstructed radiance illuminates the world, All resulting from the attainment of the pure eye.
When the wise hear various sounds, they give rise neither to delight nor to aversion;
for within all sounds there is no expressed meaning—this is due to having attained the pure ear.
The nose and fragrance, the tongue and flavors are all likewise; the body and touch, the mind and phenomena are also thus.
When perceptions of high and low regarding touch and the rest do not arise, it is because one has attained the purity of the sense faculties.
To become free from the stains of desire, as well as hatred and delusion, one should cultivate the contemplations of impurity and loving-kindness;
furthermore, by skillfully practicing the contemplation of dependently arisen phenomena, the mind of omniscience is polished and refined.
If you wish to remove the five hindrances, you should skillfully contemplate the five faculties;
if you wish to uproot the entanglements of various obstacles, abide well in the purity of the five powers.
Knowing the path of renunciation removes present obstacles; Free from instability, one dwells in firm stability.
Always cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness with diligence; The right efforts and the bases of psychic power are likewise.
Furthermore, they constantly advance in the seven factors of enlightenment, And likewise cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path;
Free from greed and anger, fear does not arise, As they skillfully guard the sense faculties and abandon the fetters of delusion.
Free from stinginess, one is able to practice the gift of Dharma, Without giving rise to a mind of base parsimony or possessiveness;
Never grasping at wealth, one constantly gives it to others— Thus is that bodhicitta brought to fulfillment.
Having no desire to grasp at any wealth or treasures, they do not abandon bodhicitta nor seek a reward;
for the sake of gathering sentient beings, they constantly practice generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
Never abandoning the bodhicitta, nor taking pleasure in other vehicles;
constantly contemplating the gateway of the Tathāgata’s virtues, their mind is as firm and stable as Mount Sumeru.
With inner tranquility, one reflects upon one's own faults; outwardly, one protects others from error without reviling them.
Free from blemish in all actions, one refrains from committing transgressions out of fear of birth and death.
Diligently practicing wholesome dharmas without weariness, Adorning and purifying Buddha-lands without fatigue;
Protecting the Dharma without giving rise to thoughts of decline, Delivering sentient beings without falling back.
Constantly and diligently repairing the great Dharma-ship, To ferry beings across the ocean of the four currents and birth-and-death;
Furthermore, acting as a bridge to connect with sentient beings, Leading them to the secure and peaceful ground of Nirvana.
He pulls sentient beings out from the deep mire and establishes them in a place of purity and fearlessness;
he bestows consolation upon those who are terrified, crossing over himself and ferrying others to the further shore.
If one is well accomplished in this Dharma, one is a Bodhisattva of great fearlessness;
such a person can always purify the bodhicitta, so that the stains of the various afflictions cannot defile it.
Even the stainless void can be defiled, and even the tracks of birds can be seen in the sky;
yet the bodhicitta cannot be defiled by afflictions, for its self-nature is primordially and eternally pure.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
How is it that a bodhisattva is capable of withstanding the crushing pressure upon the jewel of the mind set forth for omniscience?
Moreover, what are the characteristics of this crushing pressure?"
Sāgaramati! If, within this jewel of the mind of omniscience of a bodhisattva, there should be those who break the precepts and are disagreeable,
or various Māras, or the retinues of Māra, or those in the palaces of Māra empowered by Māra’s strength—
O Noble One, even if a messenger of Māra should come to harass and torment you— shaking, agitating, threatening, striking, or hurling [you]— at that time,
the Bodhisattva shall make the great bodhicitta firm so that it remains unimpaired; likewise,
he shall not let the great compassion and diligence for liberating all sentient beings be impaired, nor shall he let his diligent effort in protection be impaired.

They maintain the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it is neither severed nor interrupted; they do not allow the diligent accumulation of all roots of goodness within the teachings of the Buddhas to be destroyed;
they do not allow the cultivation of meritorious deeds for the sake of accomplishing the primary and secondary marks to be destroyed;
and they do not allow their courageous exertion to increase for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields to be destroyed. Furthermore—

To protect the True Dharma, they do not spare their own bodies or lives; furthermore, in order to universally deliver all sentient beings, they do not destroy [their resolve] nor cling to their own happiness.

If a Bodhisattva can thus fulfill such a profound mind and give rise to such an intention, they will then be able to endure entirely any sentient beings who may encounter them with anger, striking, hurling insults, or slandering and disparaging them.

Or if they are oppressed and crushed by all sentient beings, they are able to endure it all; for the sake of universally rescuing and liberating all sentient beings, these bodhisattvas do not grow weary or indolent, nor do they retreat or sink, but rather increase their power, courageously arouse diligence, and sustain their minds by withstanding toil and enduring suffering.
If others should stubbornly come to provoke anger, the Bodhisattva at that time does not respond with anger.
Whether others come to strike, throw things, or even destroy [possessions], the Bodhisattva at that time does not respond to them at all, reflecting thus:
"I should now don the armor of Mahāyāna patience."
Why is this? Because this Mahāyāna Dharma is utterly contrary to all worldly ways.
Worldly beings follow the current of birth and death, whereas my Mahāyāna Dharma flows against the current of birth and death.
The sentient beings of the world are mutually antagonistic, whereas my Mahāyāna Dharma causes all sentient beings to sever such antagonism.
The sentient beings of the world are ablaze with intense hatred, whereas the power of patience in my Mahāyāna Dharma is greatly strengthened.
“Worldly beings deceive one another; my Mahāyāna Dharma shall cause the wisdom-mind of all sentient beings to become perfect.

Furthermore, in the world, there may be sentient beings who travel throughout the ten directions, carrying weapons and pursuing Bodhisattvas. Whether they are walking, standing, sitting, or lying down in various places, if there is even a single person who gives rise to the mind of great bodhicitta, or cultivates the mind of generosity, or cultivates the minds of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, or even hears of the arising of a single root of goodness, I shall follow them to those respective places and sever their bodies, dismembering them limb by limb and joint by joint, like the leaves of a jujube tree.
If a bodhisattva encounters such matters as these, they are able to endure them all.
Furthermore, if all sentient beings in the world were to give rise to anger and skillfully utter malicious words to revile, insult, and disparage them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to even the slightest thought of agitation toward sentient beings. Why is this?

Throughout immeasurable and innumerable births and deaths since the beginningless past, this body of mine has wandered through all realms of existence and done everything imaginable—whether in the hells, or among hungry ghosts and animals, and even now within the human realm—indulging in food and drink, enjoying various sensual desires, listening to what is not the Dharma, seeking with arduous toil, and sustaining itself through wrong livelihoods under many forms of oppression, all without any fruit or benefit for my own life.

Although I may engage in many activities, they cannot benefit myself nor others; therefore, from this moment until the very end of saṃsāra, even if all sentient beings were to cut and dismember my body, I would rather endure all such suffering than ever abandon the mind of omniscience, nor would I abandon any sentient being, nor would I abandon the aspiration for all wholesome dharmas.

Why is this? This body of mine, though currently subjected to various forms of affliction, pain, and destruction, does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even an *upaniṣad* part of the suffering experienced in the hells.
Therefore, within the Buddha-dharma, I shall never abandon it, nor shall I forsake the great compassion that takes as its object the deliverance of sentient beings. Why is this?

As the Buddha has taught, all wholesome dharmas encounter many obstacles and difficulties; worldly sentient beings are mostly able to provide assistance for unwholesome dharmas, while few are able to provide assistance for wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, I now exert diligent effort within wholesome dharmas to assist in their cultivation, rather than lending my strength to unwholesome dharmas.
For this reason, I am able to fully endure all instances of ill will and the like toward those sentient beings.
If sentient beings act according to whatever circumstances arise, I shall immediately bestow upon them the corresponding remedies.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to anger toward me and further harbor resentment, I shall immediately bestow upon them the Dharma of enduring humiliation.
Because I have bestowed upon them the Dharma of patience, and the power of patience is now manifest, I would rather sacrifice my own body and life than ever give rise to anger toward them.
Therefore, if a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it will not be difficult for them to attain the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, whenever anger arises due to some cause or condition, the bodhisattva should reflect: "I shall give rise to the method for severing anger.
What is this method for severing it?

That is to say, if one feels affection for the body, is bound to the body, or clings to the body—one completely abandons all such phenomena; because one is able to thus relinquish the body, malice does not arise.

“Sāgaramati! If a bodhisattva is able to skillfully contemplate and diligently cultivate such dharmas as these, they will be capable of enduring the oppression and subjugation of all sentient beings, and their mind of omniscience will remain unimpaired and undiminished.”
Sāgaramati, you should know that there are three kinds of endurance for being crushed and oppressed:

first, endurance for being crushed and oppressed regarding the body; second, endurance for being crushed and oppressed regarding speech; and third, endurance for being crushed and oppressed regarding the mind.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Second.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Third.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Translation Institute, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, and Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing et al., by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!..."
What is meant by a bodhisattva being capable of enduring physical oppression?
It means that if a bodhisattva should encounter the severing or destruction of their own body parts, they ought to observe other sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means, they are able to practice the six pāramitās to perfection.
What kind of practices constitute the perfection of the six pāramitās by a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means?

When a bodhisattva encounters a situation where his own body is about to be severed or destroyed, if he does not cherish that body, relinquishes it without attachment or longing, he is thus able to cultivate the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

Furthermore, if one encounters the time when the body is about to perish, by giving rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings and not abandoning them, this is precisely how one can cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

Furthermore, when encountering the time when the body is about to perish, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, may even endure the severing and destruction of the body; his mind remains unmoved as the power of patience manifests, and this is precisely how he is able to cultivate the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

Furthermore, if one encounters the time when the body is about to perish, one does not abandon the mind of omniscience; by exerting great diligence and heroic strength to gather and sustain it, one gives rise to various roots of goodness within the cycle of birth and death. This is precisely what constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of diligence.

Furthermore, if one encounters the time when the body is about to perish, one should not abandon the jewel of the mind set upon omniscience; rather, one should skillfully examine the great bodhicitta. Examining it in this way, one attains inner and outer tranquility, which is precisely how one cultivates the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

Furthermore, when encountering the time when the body is about to perish, a bodhisattva should examine the body as being like grass, wood, earth, stones, and the like, realizing that one's own body is unreal and like an illusion.
According to the true meaning: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all dharmas are selfless, and nirvana is tranquility.
If one can thus scrutinize the body with discernment, this constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Such a mode of practice is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the six perfections, whereby they attain non-retrogression from the Mahāyāna Dharma; these are called the bodhisattva’s capacity to withstand physical oppression.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
What is meant by a bodhisattva being capable of enduring verbal oppression?
It means that if a person comes to a bodhisattva with false or true malicious words, or with censure, defamation, anger, or insults."
At that time, the bodhisattva is capable of enduring and accepting [the provocation], not giving rise to anger, and severing those bonds of enmity.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means encounters others coming to revile, disparage, or insult him with harsh words, once he has heard them, he should practice to bring the six pāramitās to perfection.
What kind of mental engagement constitutes the skillful means by which a bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās?
It is as follows: when a bodhisattva encounters another who comes to speak harsh words, revile, or insult them, upon hearing this, the bodhisattva immediately reflects:

"This person, in previous lives, created the causes of stinginess; because of this, they are defiled by the stain of avarice. What is manifested now is likewise due to their never having associated with virtuous friends; therefore, this person does not abandon anger."
I shall now explain for you the method for severing anger. Why is this?

Because I am able to believe in and understand the Dharma of giving and renunciation, because I am not stingy or miserly, and because I have also personally associated with various spiritual friends; therefore, I now protect them from harsh speech and abandon all ill will.
This is precisely how one can cultivate the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, when others come to revile, disparage, or insult him, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
"This person’s transgressions of the precepts and evil karma have manifested; therefore, they have come to harbor anger toward me and to insult me."
Because I am now cultivating and accumulating pure precepts, I do not give rise to anger toward them.
Furthermore, it is because I guard the bodhicitta and keep in mind the retribution of karma.
"This is precisely how one can cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when others come to revile, disparage, or insult him, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
'This person possesses coarse and violent faults and is full of anger; therefore, he comes to revile, disparage, and insult me.'"
"I now possess the power of patience and extensively cultivate acts of loving-kindness; therefore, I do not give rise to anger toward them.
This is precisely what constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when others come to revile, disparage, or insult him, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
"This person is indolent and has distanced himself from wholesome qualities; therefore, he comes to me with anger and insults."

"Now I have initiated vast and great diligence, practicing with assiduity to plant all roots of goodness without ever becoming weary or satisfied; I vow that this person shall first sit at the site of enlightenment, and only then, as the very last, shall I realize the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If one is thus armored with such diligence, this constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when others come to revile, disparage, or insult them, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
"This person has lost mindfulness and lacks correct awareness; moreover, being unable to still their own afflictions (*kleśa*), they have come to me to express anger and to insult me."
Now, having stilled my afflictions, with right mindfulness and right awareness focused on a single object, I shall not forget the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
For the sake of benefiting these sentient beings who are unsubdued, unpacified, whose faculties are unguarded, and who have not attained cessation, I now don the armor of the Mahāyāna.
If one can thus stabilize the mind, this is precisely the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhipāramitā*).
Furthermore, when others come to revile, disparage, or insult them, the Bodhisattva then reflects:

"This person, being attached to the mark of a self (*ātman*) and possessing the views of emotional clinging, comes to revile and insult me because they perceive objects as having substantial existence."

Now, in accordance with the Dharma, I investigate as it truly is both the anger that has already arisen and the anger that has not yet arisen; within these two states, neither the one who feels anger nor the phenomenon of anger can be found.
"By investigating according to reality, one remains entirely free from both self and other; because of this, one is able to endure by being free from views that grasp at existence.
This is precisely the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Sāgaramati!

Such modes of practice constitute the skillful means by which a bodhisattva brings the cultivation of the six pāramitās to perfection, thereby attaining non-retrogression from the Mahāyāna Dharma; these are called the "bodhisattva’s capacity to withstand verbal suppression."
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
What is meant by a bodhisattva being capable of withstanding oppression and subjugation of the mind?
It means that when a bodhisattva encounters various māras coming to harass and destroy them, the bodhisattva should remain firm and unshakable in the great mind of awakening (bodhicitta)."

Furthermore, when all manner of heterodox and erroneous discourses come to disturb you through signs of acquisition and attachment, you should likewise dwell securely in your inner mind according to reality, never forgetting the mind of omniscience.
Why is this? Because that Māra possesses great power; he may even finally manifest before you in the form of a Buddha and speak these words:
"What power or capability do you have within the Mahāyāna Dharma?"
"You should cast off such a heavy burden and cease this arduous exertion of diligent effort.
Enlightenment is difficult to attain, and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to find; you have merely endured much suffering in vain within the cycle of birth and death."
"Now, O Great Being, if you wish to bring an end to this suffering, you should quickly realize the nirvāṇa of a śrāvaka.

When bodhisattvas encounter Māra and he attempts to harass and destroy them with such signs as these, they should not cast off their previously donned armor of firm resolve, nor should their inner minds waver or be corrupted.
If it is thus, then one cannot diminish or lose the unequaled mind.
At that time, the bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I shall certainly proceed to the site of enlightenment; having decisively crushed the armies of Māra with the power of great wisdom, I shall thereafter realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

I shall certainly turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; I shall certainly preach the vast Dharma throughout the entire trichiliocosm; and I shall invite all sentient beings to universally receive the gift of Dharma, bringing them all to fulfillment.

All Buddhas illuminate me with their knowledge of others' minds, and all worthy ones and sages bear witness to this great bodhicitta of mine, which is truly capable of enduring all forms of crushing oppression.
"I do not deceive all Buddhas, all worthy sages, or any sentient beings, nor do I even deceive myself.
O Samudramati!
If bodhisattvas practice in this manner, they will be able to withstand oppression within their minds and thus attain non-retrogression from the Mahāyāna Dharma.
These modes of conduct constitute the bodhisattva’s ability to withstand oppression regarding the jewel of the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) that they have generated.
If one dons the firm armor of the perfection of patience, one will not slacken or retreat from the perfection of diligence.
Furthermore, if one can bring these two perfections to fulfillment, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is capable of withstanding all crushing and oppression regarding the jewel of the mind of omniscience.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The mind of the path to Great Enlightenment is indestructible, And likewise, the mind of great compassion is not destroyed;
One skillfully protects and upholds the Three Jewels, Accumulating the Buddha-dharma without any loss.”
With the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his wondrous body is adorned with the ten powers;
having perfected merit and wisdom through manifold practices, he is capable of withstanding crushing pressure and thus never regresses.
The merits of the Buddha-fields are boundless; by the power of my vows, I shall adorn and purify them all.
The Dharma-jewel is the unsurpassed and most supreme gateway; with firm resolve, I shall always protect it.
May I cause hundreds of thousands of boundless sentient beings to attain universal liberation;
because the internal cause for their benefit and happiness is indestructible, I am able to endure all crushing oppression.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, Even unto the boundless realms of sentient beings;
If every single living being therein Were each to take up weapons and come to harass me.
Causing great terror and giving rise to anger, they struck and threw him with such intent;
yet for the sake of cultivating the causes of merit, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a courageous and superior mind and was able to endure it.
Having passed through countless hundreds of kalpas, ever since the beginningless limit of birth and death;
when sentient beings revile and insult them with evil words, those bodhisattvas’ minds remain free from affliction and harm.
For the sake of great wisdom, one is able to endure; One gives rise to neither anger nor malice.
Thus, by understanding the nature of such suppression, One is able to accept it and attain purity.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings without exception, each grasping weapons to inflict harm,
rend my body into pieces, even breaking it down bit by bit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains unmoved, Not giving rise to even a fraction of a mind of anger;
Holding fast to the resolve for great enlightenment with firm stability, He is capable of enduring this crushing oppression, remaining thus pure.
Whether the Bodhisattva is walking or standing, sitting or lying down—whenever they are in any posture, others follow them;
among those who watch for an opportunity, there may be someone who does not abandon the mind of great enlightenment.
Whether they practice acts such as giving, or give rise to other virtuous thoughts,
one shall immediately cut through that person’s body, dismembering it limb by limb until it is scattered.
When a bodhisattva encounters such suffering, they give rise to joy toward that person;
reflecting that throughout boundless hundreds of kalpas, there is no realm of existence they have not traversed.
Having passed through the three realms of suffering—hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—I have now attained birth among human beings;
though my body may be destroyed and yield no worldly fruit or profit, I shall cast it aside in order to seek the body of Buddha-wisdom.
Although I have now obtained this human body, I am constantly oppressed by countless sufferings;
yet compared to those within the Avīci Hell, these sufferings do not equal even one-hundredth part of that.
I would rather dwell within those hells, enduring their suffering for a hundred kalpas;
yet these three—the Buddha, the True Dharma, and sentient beings—I shall never abandon.
I contemplate this body as an impermanent phenomenon, Perishing in each instant like a phantom;
The four elements are a false composite, Which the Buddha has declared to be like the venom of a snake.
If I were to cast off this body, I would swiftly be freed from all the poisons within;
once those poisons of affliction are eliminated, I and others will naturally attain the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now this body of mine dwells in the world, where many fearful things give rise to terror;
for the sake of seeking the conditions for various physical pleasures, it is driven by desires such as food and drink.
If I were to cast off this body, all conditions would cease and all fears depart;
if one can understand and enter into this contemplation, one will be able to endure all forms of oppression.
Among the many hundreds of thousands of beings in the world, most constantly provide assistance within unwholesome dharmas;
few people can provide assistance within wholesome dharmas by applying diligent effort as is appropriate.
Therefore, regarding all unwholesome dharmas, I shall no longer assist them therein;
I shall instead assist in the cultivation of the gateway of patience, for "patience" is the word spoken by the Buddha.
All Buddhas of the ten directions, each and every one, bear witness for me:
that the resolute mind I have aroused shall never falter within the Buddha Vehicle.
Those sages of great power have likewise all witnessed my mind of endurance;
regarding the causes of oppression that I am able to bear, I commit no fault therein.
As the Buddha has taught regarding body, speech, and mind—these three are subject to many forms of suppression;
yet they can all endure with such vigor that none are destroyed, just as previously described.
This body possesses manifold sufferings, each of which is boundless;
if one can endure such suffering, this body will be purified through its subjugation.
If the body encounters suffering and is dispersed, when its joints and limbs are severed and destroyed;
if the six pāramitās are fully perfected, that is the virtue of great wisdom and skillful means.
What are called generosity and ethical discipline, Patience, diligence, and meditative concentration;
If one practices these together with supreme wisdom, They will all be perfected in a mere moment.
If at some time one is able to relinquish the body, neither loving nor cherishing it;
at that time, one should practice in this way to fulfill the perfection of generosity.
If one extensively practices loving-kindness toward sentient beings, One does not violate or destroy the practice of pure precepts;
As the cause for realizing awakening in the present life, One fulfills the perfection of pure ethical discipline.
Even when their body is about to be severed or destroyed, they should maintain the power of firm patience;
by diligently practicing through this power of patience, they will bring the perfection of patience to fulfillment.
Carrying the heavy burden of diligence without weariness, The inner mind likewise gives rise to no aversion;
Though the body may be destroyed, one maintains it with strength, Thus fulfilling the perfection of diligence.
Even when their bodies are about to be severed or destroyed, they do not think of abandoning the bodhicitta;
amidst the darkness of the dust of all afflictions, they exert diligent effort to cause them all to be extinguished.
For the sake of cultivating the power of meditative concentration and liberation, one would rather destroy one's own body;
universally causing all sentient beings to be free from defilement, one brings the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) to fulfillment.
I contemplate this body as truly selfless; this body is like an illusion and like a flash of lightning.
Both an agent and an experiencer are absent; herein there is not even the slightest dharma that exists in reality.
Amidst the entanglements of physical hardship and suffering, you skillfully bring liberation to sentient beings;
having reached the supreme further shore where self and others are perfected, you fulfill the pāramitā of supreme wisdom.
If one can skillfully contemplate and constantly cultivate this profound and firm Dharma,
they will be able to endure physical oppression and subjugation, and no faults will arise therein.
When a bodhisattva hears harsh words— unwholesome revilement and slander— if,
upon hearing them, they do not give rise to a mind of anger but can instead arouse a mind of loving-kindness and skillfully subdue themselves;
Abandoning the faults of anger and resentment is the pure perfection of generosity;
The vast and universal practice of a compassionate mind is the pure perfection of ethical discipline;
The manifestation of the power of patience as an antidote is the pure perfection of forbearance.
Constantly arousing diligence in the quest for Buddha-wisdom, this is the pure perfection of diligence;
Stabilizing the mind amidst all sensory objects, this is the pure perfection of meditative concentration;
Thoroughly realizing that all sounds are ungraspable, this is the pure perfection of supreme wisdom.
When a bodhisattva has heard various harsh words, they should contemplate the profound Dharma;
being able to withstand verbal abuse and suppression, they therefore do not cling to any faults.
Even if hundreds of thousands of hosts of Māras, with their various heterodox and external views, were all to come forth;
and even if they urged one to abandon skillful means and cultivation, claiming that the stages of enlightenment are difficult to attain—
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains unmoved; his power increases as he practices with ever-greater vigor.
Therefore, he is able to withstand oppression and crushing, remaining unbroken by all manner of such afflictions.

These two practices of patience and diligence, when well-cultivated and firmly established like the king of mountains, enable one to endure all that crushes and oppresses; such beings possess a single, unified courage.
The Tathāgata, possessing the ten powers, fully knows those who polish the jewel of their minds and subdue their oppressors;
they shall behold the Honored One who has realized manifest enlightenment and likewise receive the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
How is it that a bodhisattva’s jewel of the mind set upon omniscience is pierced yet remains unbroken?
