It is when a bodhisattva, regarding that mind of omniscience, does not experience anything, has no attachment, does not abide anywhere, neither emerges nor enters, is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and is without discrimination. Having destroyed all discrimination and established nothing, they should investigate the profound dharma as it truly is through right wisdom."
What is this profound Dharma?
It is the teaching that accords with dependent origination.

One realizes it as it truly is: without cause or object-condition; neither annihilated nor eternal; free from extreme views; and characterized by selflessness in its intrinsic nature, such that because the self lacks intrinsic nature, all phenomena likewise lack intrinsic nature.

All phenomena are originally unborn and have no place of birth; one understands emptiness, and with faith and compliance, one abides in signlessness, wishlessness, and non-seeking, performing no contrived action within true wisdom.

Ultimately impermanent: form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a floating bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusory phenomenon. The elements are unmoving; the sense bases arise from one another. The mind has no dwelling place and no volitional engagement; regarding what is superior and what is not superior, one realizes the dharmas of equality as they truly are. Without various modes of activity, they are identical in a single flavor, and all abide together on the path of the One Vehicle.
The practice of the path and the cultivation of wisdom rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); through wisdom, one understands that there is no attachment to objects.
All sounds are realized as being non-sound; wisdom knows all sounds because the limits of the past and future have been severed.

The two kinds of knowledge regarding words and meanings enter into non-duality; one directly realizes the ineffable meaning of all phenomena. The meaning of selflessness is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*); the meaning of ultimate exhaustion is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*); the meaning of non-conjunction is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); and the equal realization and entry into the conditioned and the unconditioned is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Detachment from the prior and subsequent limits is the foundation of mindfulness of the body; the non-abiding of arising and ceasing is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation; observing the absence of objective referents is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and the meaning of the equality and perfect equanimity of the dharma-realm, which is not a realm by nature, is the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas.
The meaning of mastery over the mind is the four right efforts; freedom from all obstacles is the four bases of psychic power. The meaning of giving birth is the faculty of faith;

the absence of discursive thought is the faculty of diligence; the absence of mental attention is the faculty of mindfulness; the transcendence of conceptual proliferation is the faculty of concentration; and the absence of reliance on others is the faculty of wisdom.

Unimpededness regarding the object of focus is the power of faith; penetrating all powers is the power of diligence; the mind’s abiding in stillness is the power of mindfulness; being unshakable is the power of concentration; and following mindfulness with mindfulness is the power of wisdom.

Equanimous correspondence with all phenomena is the factor of awakening of mindfulness; neither emerging nor entering is the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena; the absence of "mine" is the factor of awakening of vigor; the virtuous abiding of body and mind is the factor of awakening of joy; equanimous awakening is the factor of awakening of tranquility; detachment from dualistic phenomena is the factor of awakening of concentration; and distancing oneself from all views is the factor of awakening of equanimity.

To be free from all conceptual proliferation within both conceptualization and non-conceptualization is right view; to penetrate the equality of all sounds is right thought; to be free from the phenomena of body and mind is right speech; for all actions to attain pliancy is called right action; to be without high or low is right livelihood; to abide in equanimity after designating whatever is wholesome or unwholesome is right effort; to penetrate the equality of the mind’s objects of focus is right mindfulness; and to dwell peacefully in tranquil *śamatha* is right concentration.

The meaning of the non-arising of all that is seen and not seen is the meaning of impermanence; the meaning of primordial non-arising is the meaning of suffering; the meaning of non-activity is the meaning of non-self; and the meaning of cessation is the meaning of quiescence.

The meaning of generosity is the thorough taming of the mind; the meaning of ethical discipline is abiding in the nature of coolness; the meaning of patience is the knowledge that follows the exhaustion of phenomena; the meaning of diligence is the ability to skillfully discern all phenomena; the meaning of meditative concentration is the stilling of the internal mind; and the meaning of supreme wisdom is knowing, as they truly are, that all phenomena are signless.

That all sentient beings are fundamentally pure is the meaning of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); that they are equal to space is the meaning of compassion (*karuṇā*); that there is nothing to be attained is the meaning of sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and that all practices are ultimately perfected is the meaning of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The purity of the three spheres throughout the past of all phenomena is the meaning of emptiness; their purity in the future is the meaning of detachment; and their purity in the present is the meaning of non-self.
“Sāgaramati!

If bodhisattvas, regarding such profound dharmas as these, perceive neither arising nor cessation, are free from all letters, and are equal to space, they enter into equanimity through wisdom regarding both the favorable and the adverse.”
If one can thus contemplate and observe according to reality as practiced, that bodhisattva will be able to pierce the jewel of the mind set upon omniscience without it being damaged.
Although one thus pierces that mind of omniscience without any conceptual arousal, one is then able to realize it through direct perception within the principle of mastery over all phenomena.
Samudramati!

For example, the sun and moon each abide in their own palaces and illuminate the four great continents everywhere; yet those sons of gods, the sun and moon, have no conscious intention at all, nor do they form the thought, "I am going to various places," or "I am not going, yet I am shining. It is solely through the power of the ripening of the merit of all sentient beings that they shine in this way.
Sāgaramati! It is the same with that bodhisattva who possesses the wisdom of excellent discernment.

Although he extensively brings great benefit to sentient beings within immeasurable Buddha-fields, that bodhisattva has no conscious arousal of thought; he never repeatedly gives rise to conceptual intentions regarding his activities, yet whatever he does manifests in accordance with what is appropriate.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
A bodhisattva endowed with the wisdom of discernment should investigate, in accordance with reality, the perfection of meditative concentration and the perfection of wisdom."

Why is this? A bodhisattva dwelling in a state of meditative equipoise does not cultivate the dharma of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), whereas a bodhisattva cultivating the practice of contemplation does not dwell in meditative equipoise.
Furthermore, one who cultivates the practice of contemplation possesses wisdom; by virtue of possessing wisdom, they are able to investigate skillfully.
What is it that is observed?
It is the observation of the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas).
What is this true nature of all phenomena?
If one does not engage with any characteristics, this is precisely the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
What is the characteristic of all phenomena?
It is that which is manifested; this is the characteristic of all phenomena.
The mark of reality as it is within this exposition is also called the true mark of all dharmas (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*).
Furthermore, if one thoroughly understands all things in this way, one will be able to realize the signless (*animitta*) and the absence of the signless (*ananimitta*).
What is that which has characteristics?
What is that which is without characteristics?

That which has characteristics is birth; that which is without characteristics is cessation. If there is neither the absence of characteristics nor the absence of the absence of characteristics, then there is neither birth nor cessation.

If phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished, then the nature of all phenomena is primordially abiding, the dharma-realm is indestructible, true suchness is immovable, and the limit of reality is unchanging.
Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); this is precisely what is called "understanding dependently arisen phenomena as they truly are.

To awaken to the true characteristic of all phenomena and to directly realize the non-dual reality of the limit of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*)—this is known through the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
"Sāgaramati!
This is what is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses the wisdom of definitive discernment.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words concerning the dharmas of being receptive to polishing, capable of enduring crushing, and remaining unimpaired even when pierced, ten nayutas of devas and humans in this assembly all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and sixteen thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Scroll Three.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
Scroll Four.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Minister of State for the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Edict. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“If a Bodhisattva hears of the bodhicitta, They will then be able to penetrate all dharmas.”
This very wisdom that penetrates all things is unattached to any phenomena.
Although they thoroughly understand the profound Dharma, Bodhisattvas do not give rise to fear within it;
nor do they harbor any sense of dread or timidity, for they are able to attain the supreme path.
Whether as causes or as objects of perception, one awakens to all phenomena as they truly are—phenomena born of conditions.
Possessing wisdom that accords with the arising of all phenomena, one does not, in reality, cling to extreme views.
Whether phenomena are viewed as annihilated or eternal, the wise do not give rise to attachment or obstruction;
their awakening to the middle way is likewise so—therefore, the limit of reality is inconceivable.
If phenomena are by their very nature devoid of self, then within them the self likewise lacks intrinsic nature;
that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is likewise so—they are primordially unarisen and entirely empty and quiescent.
All phenomena are unborn and do not arise; Empty and without grasping, they are eternally pure.
Free from conceptual proliferation through the gate of signlessness, All are equal to empty space.
Without mind and likewise without aspiration or prayer, one remains far removed from all desire and greed;
by directly realizing the intrinsic nature of all forms, one knows them to be as unreal as a mass of foam.
Feeling is like a bubble, momentarily arising and ceasing; perception is like a mirage, giving rise to false appearances;
formations are like a plantain tree, lacking solidity within; consciousness is like an illusory phenomenon, not enduring for long.
The nature of all four elements is immovable, equal to the realm of empty space;
the internal and external sense bases are likewise so, their objects arising in mutual dependence yet remaining in profound stillness.
One should know that mental phenomena do not abide within, nor can they be found without;
the same applies to the mind and its objects, which are devoid of self, and herein all consciousnesses have no dwelling place.
All those phenomena are without mental engagement, and they are likewise free from the mark of self;
within the equality of all phenomena, one awakens to the true nature as it is.
The Dharma is fundamentally of one taste and without diverse natures; the single path and the single vehicle are all equal.
If one understands the wisdom of the path as it truly is, this meaning is revealed in the ultimate sense.
The wise are able to penetrate the meaning; observing both sound and non-sound, they attain awakening.
All sounds whatsoever in the world—both those of the past limit and the future limit—are severed.
Though one may well understand the words and their meaning, within them one must realize the non-dual dharma;
by understanding this gateway of the ineffable meaning, one is able to directly realize true suchness.
The non-arising of all phenomena is the knowledge of suffering; the equality of all phenomena is the knowledge of origination;
the meaning of the exhaustion of all phenomena is the knowledge of cessation; and the unconditioned nature of all phenomena is the knowledge of the path.
Within those [objects of] body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, one contemplates each phenomenon according to reality;
being without mindfulness and without the activity of mental attention—this is called the four foundations of mindfulness.
If one contemplates that the dharma-realm is not of the nature of a realm, it is equal and perfectly exhausted in its equality;
this gate of the true dharma, which is cessation without interruption, is called the four right efforts.
If one attains great mastery over the mind, this is called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
To transcend all minds attached to existence is what is termed the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*);
if one abides in the tranquility of all phenomena, this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
The thought of non-thought is the gateway to the True Dharma; this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
To realize that all phenomena are without volitional intent is called the faculty of concentration.
To transcend the gateways of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena is called the faculty of wisdom.
If one does not give rise to faith in others, One will be able to attain true wisdom.
When there is nothing to be perceived within the mind, This is called the power of faith and the power of diligence;
If one realizes the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing, This is precisely what is called the power of mindfulness.
When tranquility is settled so that the mind has no further activity, this is the accomplishment of the power of concentration;
when there is neither existence nor departure from conceptualization, this is what is called the power of wisdom.
Truly awakening to the meaning of all phenomena—this is called the seven factors of enlightenment.
To see the equality of phenomena without distinction—this is called right view.
To contemplate non-dual phenomena as they truly are—this unborn contemplation is the true path.
Non-arising is the meaning of impermanence; non-origination is the meaning of suffering;
non-activity is the meaning of non-self; and the state of cessation is the meaning of tranquility.
Taming the mind is itself generosity; A tranquil mind is itself ethical discipline;
Following the Dharma to its conclusion is the gateway of patience; Investigating with right wisdom is called diligence;
Ultimate stillness is meditative concentration; Knowing things as they truly are is wisdom.
The inherently pure mind of sentient beings— To fully understand this is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
To be equal to space is called compassion (*karuṇā*); Pure and joyful contentment is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*);
And a mind that dwells nowhere upon any object— This is said to be the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If, moreover, the three wheels are purified, one can then thoroughly understand all phenomena;
thus penetrating all dharma-gates, one further forever severs all views and attachments.
All concentration and wisdom contained herein—these two dharmas are able to penetrate through;
universally entering the gates of immeasurable realms, this is called the wisdom of the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:
“Sāgaramati! If a bodhisattva has attained such purity and universal purity, he gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind free from artifice.”
If one is oppressed by sentient beings, yet gives rise to no affliction or hindrance, attaining the wisdom of excellent discernment and definitive insight;
that Bodhisattva is then able, within this very state of non-abiding, to personally proclaim the root of the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
What is meant by abiding in the root of samādhi?
It means that because one is without obstruction toward all sentient beings, one gives rise to great compassion;
thus, even if one receives constant veneration from all sentient beings, the mind does not become elated, and if one is not venerated, the mind does not become dejected.

For this reason, phenomena do not arise, nor does one give rise to a conceited mind; thus, one is able to abide in accordance with all phenomena and does not abide in deluded phenomena, being able to produce the wisdom of phenomena and attaining it universally.

With wisdom as the precursor, they are perfected in physical action; with wisdom as the precursor, they are perfected in verbal action; with wisdom as the precursor, they are perfected in mental action. Whatever actions are performed by body, speech, or mind, all are preceded by wisdom, so that the bodhisattva is able to act in accordance with wisdom.
What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of bodily action preceded by wisdom?

It means that if there are sentient beings who should be transformed and disciplined by seeing the form-body (rūpakāya), the bodhisattva shall manifest the marks of dignified demeanor (īryāpatha) so that those sentient beings may achieve discipline of mind.
Although a bodhisattva thus manifests such signs, they have no awakening to them, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination.

Should the bodhisattva’s body give rise to faults—such as attachment to the body, the body manifesting divergent characteristics, the body engaging in crooked conduct, the body becoming agitated, or the body giving rise to speculative calculations—[these are likewise absent].
If it is thus, then whatever faults those bodhisattvas may have will arise before them, but like the cutting off of the heart of a tāla tree, they shall never again arise regarding all phenomena.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva attains purity of body, their entire form is adorned with all the supreme marks; their hands and feet are supple, exquisite, and lovely; they possess a body born of merit, with faculties that are not deficient and physical proportions that are perfectly complete.

Although the bodhisattva possesses such a body adorned with these ornaments, he does not take pride in or rely upon physical appearance; though his body is magnificent and beautiful, he does not give rise to the notion of a composite whole.

If a bodhisattva sees that any sentient beings have various physical forms that are deficient or impaired, the bodhisattva does not give rise to pride at that time; rather, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they remain humble and respectful.
Why is this? Because the dharma-nature of one's own body and the dharma-nature of the bodies of all sentient beings are entirely equal, both relying upon wisdom.
Once a bodhisattva has fully understood the body and the dharma-nature of the body, they immediately attain the dharma-body and no longer receive a fragmented,分段 (fen-duan) body.
What is called the Dharma-body?
It is that which takes the joy of meditation as its food and drink, rather than substantial, physical food.

Because Bodhisattvas wish to conform to the world and out of compassion for sentient beings, they manifest the acceptance of worldly food; it is not for the purpose of nourishing the body or curing emaciation and weakness.
Bodhisattvas rely solely upon the Dharma-body, sustaining themselves through the life-force of the Dharma rather than being sustained by the material food of the world.
What is meant by the "life-force of the Dharma"?
That which is sustained is not produced by causes and conditions, and thus does not transcend noble conduct.
What is called noble conduct?
It refers to non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; being free from all afflictions, one carefully guards the precepts according to their established prescriptions—this is called noble conduct.
Because the Bodhisattva’s physical actions are perfected with this wisdom as their precursor, they attain the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and achieve spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*).

Without a mind of deliberate arousal, they manifest their bodies universally throughout all Buddha-fields. According to each and every sentient being in those Buddha-fields who should perceive the Bodhisattva’s body adorned with the radiance of their physical form, the Bodhisattva—abiding in a state of non-arousal and non-discrimination—becomes fully endowed with that radiant, adorned body.
From within that body, they emit a great light, which shines universally upon immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-fields.
All sentient beings in the various hells and evil destinies, touched by the light’s radiance, attained complete happiness.

Because of this happiness, pleasant sensations manifested; through these pleasant sensations, the burning afflictions of all sentient beings were entirely stilled. They all attained refreshing coolness, their bodies and minds became harmonious and supple, and because those beings attained such harmony, they performed the work of the Buddha.
Sāgaramati!
Such dharmas as these are called the bodhisattva’s perfection of bodily action preceded by wisdom.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s verbal action being fully endowed with wisdom as its precursor?
It means that whenever a bodhisattva utters speech, they always remain far removed from all coarse and evil faults inherent in speech.
Sāgaramati!
What are called the coarse and evil faults within speech?
They refer to the sixty-four kinds of faults of speech from which a bodhisattva should always remain far removed.
What are the sixty-four?
First, the bodhisattva has no harsh or abrasive speech;
second, no turbid or confused speech.
Third, speech that is not of a disruptive tone;
fourth, speech that is not feeble;
fifth, speech that is not excessively loud.
Sixth, there is no speech with an excessively low tone;
seventh, there is no speech with a harsh or violent tone;
eighth, there is no speech that is rigid or abrasive.
Ninth, there is no stammering speech;
tenth, there is no speech that causes affliction;
eleventh, there is no speech that causes dissension.
Twelfth, there are no burning words;
thirteenth, there are no delusive words;
fourteenth, there are no resentful words.
Fifteenth, there is no secretive speech;
sixteenth, there is no defiled or attached speech;
seventeenth, there is no groaning speech.
Eighteenth, he has no childish speech;
nineteenth, he has no shouting or roaring speech;
twentieth, he has no harsh or violent speech.
Twenty-first, there is no speech that causes agitation;
twenty-second, there is no speech that lacks knowledge of the proper time;
twenty-third, there is no speech that follows after greed for base things.
Twenty-fourth, speech free from the obstacle of anger;
twenty-fifth, speech free from the delusion of madness;
twenty-sixth, speech free from alarm and fear.
Twenty-seventh, no speech characterized by arrogant attachment;
twenty-eighth, no speech that causes destruction;
twenty-ninth, no speech that is deceitful or crooked.
30. No speech of arrogance; 31. No speech of disparaging others out of pride;
32. No speech of concealment driven by attachment;
Thirty-third, there is no speech that is unpleasant or revealing of faults;
thirty-fourth, there is no speech that is untrue;
thirty-fifth, there is no speech that is deficient.
Thirty-sixth, there is no false speech;
thirty-seventh, there is no divisive speech;
thirty-eighth, there is no slanderous speech.
Thirty-ninth, he is free from harsh speech;
fortieth, he is free from frivolous speech;
forty-first, he is free from speech that causes estrangement among friends.
Forty-second, speech that is extremely sharp;
forty-third, speech that is extremely gentle;
forty-fourth, speech that is free from vulgarity.
Forty-fifth, there is no speech that is not guarded and concealed;
forty-sixth, there is no excessive speech;
forty-seventh, there is no speech of anger or malice.
Forty-eighth, there are no words of contention;
forty-ninth, there are no words of base inferiority;
fiftieth, there are no words of agitation and confusion.
Fifty-first, there is no frivolous speech;
fifty-second, there is no speech that ridicules others to their face;
fifty-third, there is no theatrical or playful speech.
Fifty-fourth, no singing or chanting;
fifty-fifth, no speech contrary to the Dharma;
fifty-sixth, no divisive speech.
Fifty-seventh, there is no speech of self-praise;
fifty-eighth, there is no speech of disparaging others;
fifty-ninth, there is no speech of contemptuous derision.
Sixty: no agitated speech; sixty-one:
no speech that contradicts the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha;
sixty-two: no speech that slanders the noble ones.
Sixty-third, there is no speech that realizes through irrational means;
sixty-fourth, there is no speech characterized by any coarse, evil, or faulty qualities.
Samudrareṇu!
Among these sixty-four kinds of verbal faults, the bodhisattva remains entirely free from whatever words they utter, thereby attaining purity of vocal action.

Whatever they speak, they always speak with continuity, speak words that accord with reality, speak words that are correct and true, speak words that express the stages of truth, and speak words that follow the turning of the truth.

They enter into the languages of all sentient beings, know the inclinations and intentions of all sentient beings, cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy, illuminate the faculties and natures of all sentient beings, and pacify all afflictions.

Abiding by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and upholding the True Dharma, the words they utter are distinct and clear, exquisite and lovely, and free from all faults; this is entirely because they are accomplished through the practice of merit.

Speech that does not arise from greed is the gathering of merit; speech that does not arise from anger is profound and bottomless; speech that does not arise from delusion is the conventional designation for the worlds of the ten directions.
It is not without purpose or benefit; wherever one goes, it is entirely devoid of the mark of volitional action.
Samudrareṇu!
This is the bodhisattva’s perfection of verbal action, preceded by wisdom.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati! What is meant by 'the mental activity of a bodhisattva being endowed with wisdom as its precursor'?
It refers to the bodhisattva’s ability, in a single moment of mind, to universally enter into the mental activities of all sentient beings and to understand them all with complete clarity."
Abiding in samāhita, he manifests all manner of dignified postures and activities, yet he does not arise from that samādhi.
None of the hosts of Māras can know the mental activity of the Bodhisattva.
He enters into the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet they do not know it.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva never gives rise to the thought of harming himself, harming others, or harming both.
It is not expressed by mind or thought, nor does it give rise to any obstruction within even the slightest phenomenon.
Within all phenomena, one gives rise to wisdom and realizes them.
Because that mind and thought are without expression or representation, there is nothing to be realized.
Not grasping what is not to be grasped, yet not failing to grasp when the Buddha-dharma is complete; furthermore, not extinguishing sensation to achieve realization—Sāgaramati!
This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of mental action, preceded by wisdom.
“Sāgaramati!
Such dharmas as these constitute the foundation for a bodhisattva’s abiding in the samādhi of the Seal of Purity Spontaneously Proclaimed.
This foundation refers to the fact that the bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind are all preceded by wisdom.”
Because their three types of action are preceded by wisdom, they are able to attain the samādhi-dharma of the Seal of Self-Expounded Purity.
Samudrareṇu, you should know that there are ten dharmas by which this samādhi is called "Self-Expounded."
What are these ten?
First, the initial arousal of practice, which is called "proclaiming the purity of one's own profound resolve";
second, the bodhisattva practice, which is called "proclaiming the purity of the six pāramitās."
Third, the practice of manifesting pure conduct, which is called "spontaneous declaration of the purity of all wholesome dharmas";
fourth, the practice of the perfection of the marks and signs, which is called "spontaneous declaration of the purity of unimpeded meritorious conduct";
fifth, the attainment of the faculty of eloquence, which is called "spontaneous declaration of the practice of following the heard Dharma to bring others to purity."

Sixth is the wisdom of mindfulness and concentration without distraction, which is called the self-proclamation of being far removed from all coarse heaviness and hindrances, because the manifest afflictions have been purified;
seventh is the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), which is called the self-proclamation of the purity of heedfulness (*apramāda*);
eighth is the wisdom that indicates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which is called the self-proclamation of the purity of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

Ninth is the wisdom of the sequential stages of the ten bhūmis, which is called "self-proclamation" because it completely purifies all obstacles within the establishment of dharmas that serve as remedies for everything;

tenth is the wisdom of the adornment of the great field of enlightenment, which is called "self-proclamation" because it purifies by severing all unwholesome dharmas and gathering all wholesome dharmas.
Sāgaramati!
Because it possesses these ten qualities, this samādhi is called "Self-Expounded.
Sāgaramati, you should know this!
Furthermore, there are twenty kinds of dharmas by which this samādhi is named "Pure Seal" (Vimalamudrā).
What are these twenty?
First, internal purity is called the Pure Seal, because the self is pure.
Second, the purity of the external is called the Seal of Purity, because that which belongs to the self (*ātmiya*) is pure;
third, the purity of the body is called the Seal of Purity, because it is entirely pure within all views;
fourth, the purity of the selflessness of all phenomena is called the Seal of Purity, because it is pure from the very beginning.
Fifth, the pure awakening to the equality of all phenomena is called the Seal of Purity, because it is the purity of a single flavor;
sixth, the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called the Seal of Purity, because all liberations are pure;
seventh, the purity of space is called the Seal of Purity, because it is ultimately pure.
Eighth, the purity of the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena is called the Seal of Purity, because it is free from all conditioned activities;
ninth, the purity of what is presently perceived is called the Seal of Purity, because the penetration of one's own wisdom is pure;
tenth, the purity of the radiance of the solar disc is called the Seal of Purity, because its constant illumination is pure.
Eleventh, the purity of unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the three periods of time is called the Seal of Purity, because it is pure in being free from all obstructions;
twelfth, the purity of the gateway of manifest realization is called the Seal of Purity, because consciousness and wisdom are pure in their non-abiding;
thirteenth, the purity of the unconditioned is called the Seal of Purity, because the intrinsic nature of the conditioned is pure.
Fourteenth is the pure seal called "thoroughly knowing the purity of dependent origination," because of skillfully contemplating the phenomena of conditions;
fifteenth is the pure seal called "the purity of the Buddha-dharmas of the powers and fearlessnesses as they are realized," because of the purity of unassailable, true wisdom;
sixteenth is the pure seal called "thoroughly knowing the purity of the characteristics of the Buddha-dharmas," because of the purity of prior karma.
Seventeenth, the purity of great loving-kindness and great compassion is called the Seal of Purity, because of the purity of not abandoning sentient beings;
eighteenth, the purity of subduing all māras and non-Buddhists is called the Seal of Purity, because of the purity of all practices;
nineteenth, the purity of destroying all seeds and habitual tendencies of affliction is called the Seal of Purity, because of the purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Twentieth: within a single moment of mind, one universally exhausts all gateways of the Buddha-dharma and knows them with purity; this is called the Seal of Purity (*śuddhamudrā*), because of the perfect accumulation of purity.
Sāgaramati!
Because it possesses these twenty kinds of dharmas, this samādhi is named "Pure Seal" (Vimalamudrā).
Sāgaramati, you should know this!
When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they are able to attain this samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, they shall obtain eight kinds of extraordinary marks of great supernormal powers (abhijñā).
What are these eight?
First, this great trichiliocosm suddenly transforms entirely into ground composed of vajra;
second, all the trees, flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves fully blossom and turn toward the Bodhi tree, bending low and curving to manifest an attitude of reverence.
Third, all sentient beings, in a single kṣaṇa, shall not be afflicted or harmed by any afflictions;
fourth, all sentient beings in the hells and evil realms shall see the Bodhisattva seated at the site of enlightenment, and having seen him, they shall all obtain perfect happiness;
fifth, throughout all worlds, a vast golden light shall manifest in the sky, shining brilliantly everywhere.
Sixth, the great earth shook in its entirety, yet not even a single sentient being therein was harmed;
seventh, all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, currently dwelling and teaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions, bestowed the gift of fearlessness upon him to comfort him, saying:
"O son of good family, you are most excellent, most excellent; you are a great leader."
"8. Within a single moment of mind, all Buddha-dharmas gather and appear before him. Sāgaramati!

Once this bodhisattva has attained that Pure Seal (*śuddhamudrā*) samādhi, he subsequently acquires these eight kinds of uncommon marks of great supernormal power (*abhijñā*), through which he is able to produce immeasurable meritorious deeds; all of them are identical in their supernormal power and majesty to this samādhi."
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Five.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, under imperial decree. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“This Dharma is virtuous, pure, and further luminous; Fundamentally without combination, it is equal to space.”
Without abiding, without cessation, and without arising—this seal is encompassed by the Buddha-seal.
Abiding in that fundamental source, one attains dhāraṇī and practices the conduct of compassion for a long time;
whether encountering respect or contempt in the world, one remains free from joy or anger within the wisdom of equanimity.
The knowledge of equality dwells in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), Neither dwelling in the darkness of delusion nor in deluded dharmas;
Though dwelling within wisdom, there is no attainment of a mind, Abiding securely in the knowledge of equality, eternally pure.
Wisdom constantly awakens to and understands the actions of the body, and through various modes of wisdom, it benefits the world;
if sentient beings behold this pure body, they shall all attain the supreme Buddha-wisdom that is free from defilement.
With dignified deportment and excellent precepts, free from distraction, one acts in accordance with the midst of both existence and non-existence;
though the physical faults of the body are limitless, they are fundamentally unarisen and thus require no severance.
He attains a body adorned with sublime marks, With hands and feet supple, graced by the equipment of merit;
A body with pure and perfect faculties, Not relying on physical form, but produced through wisdom.
If one sees sentient beings suffering from poverty and low status, one should treat them with humility and respect, never with arrogance;
by honoring those who know the Dharma and uphold the precepts, and hearing the Dharma from them, one attains the Noble Path.
Truly knowing the dharma-nature of one’s own and others’ bodies, Knowing the true nature-body of all sentient beings;
Having attained the pure, supreme, and wondrous dharma-body, One does not receive a fragmented body and is free from defilement.
He constantly partakes of the food of meditative joy within concentration; he does not augment his majestic radiance with solid food.
His acceptance of food accords with worldly custom and is not for the sake of physical strength; it nourishes his Dharma-life and matures into nectar.
Constantly attaining noble conduct and sublime tranquility, one is liberated from the defiled masses of greed, hatred, and delusion;
guarding the training in ethical discipline with secrecy, neither following nor violating it, one would rather sacrifice their own body than commit a transgression.
By his supernormal power, he can travel to billions of lands, manifesting bodies according to the needs of beings to preach the Dharma;
when those in the world behold his body of wondrous marks, they all attain a sublime and superior stature.
The body emits a wondrously pure radiance, Shining far and wide across boundless lands;
This light brings forth merit, victory, and soft touch, Causing all sentient beings to eliminate the harm of afflictions.
The sentient beings in the hells constantly suffer, yet upon being touched by the light’s radiance, they attain joy;
their bodies and minds become harmonious and refreshed, and their agonizing pains cease, whereby they are able to leave behind the suffering of hell.

Such and other bodily actions, infinite and excellent in accordance with wisdom, are able to open the gateway of Buddha-activities for the sake of subduing beings; thus is the bodhisattva’s bodily action purified.
Your speech is a wondrous sound, pure and pleasing to the mind; all who hear it in the world of gods and humans rejoice.
Whatever Dharma you preach bears fruit that is not in vain; this Dharma can bring about the nectar of extinction.
The faults of speech that follow from linguistic expression are skillfully severed by pure merit and wisdom;
the verbal karma and voices of sentient beings are made universally equal, bringing joy to all.
The continuity is taught as equal and true; his speech is free from turbidity and confusion, being entirely in accordance with reality.
Whatever he says is practiced with sincerity; his wisdom turns according to the truths and is perfectly pure.
His speech is sweet, for he has stilled craving; his words gather merit, for he is liberated from anger.
Profound and bottomless, he has severed ignorance, performing deeds of benefit and virtue throughout a thousand lands.
These spoken words are non-conceptual; without relying on strenuous effort, they accord with liberation.
They give rise to joy according to the faculties of sentient beings; such is the purity of speech produced by this wisdom.
Having well cultivated mental karma, they are always free from obstruction; in a single moment of mind, they know the entire world.
Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, they manifest majestic deportment; even Māra cannot know the intention of such a Bodhisattva.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom the profound path of the bodhisattva’s mind and intention;
they harbor no thoughts of harming self or others, possessing equalizing wisdom that is without pride or obstruction.
The Bodhisattva, following the world, possesses excellent awakening and knowledge; Without sensation, without thought, and without discursive investigation;
Not entering the gate of the blissful realization of the extinction-concentration, He is endowed with boundless eloquence and dhāraṇīs.
The wisdom practiced through hearing the Dharma abides eternally; with mindfulness and concentration free from distraction, one dwells in meditative equipoise.
All obstacles are purified and afflictions eliminated; not even the slightest trace of defilement is to be seen.
The factors of enlightenment are boundless, All of which universally encompass and eliminate negligence;
With wisdom ever abiding in śamatha and vipaśyanā, The stages of the ten bhūmis are now realized in succession.
Until the tree of enlightenment bears the fruit of wisdom, If one possesses these ten kinds of pure dharmas;
The Bodhisattva attains a concentration called "Self-Exposition," Manifesting the cultivation of all practices to their pure perfection.
All wholesome paths are pure, supreme, and exalted; according to the various stages, they purify the perfections.
All wholesome dharmas are transcendent and lofty; the marks and signs are exquisite, the perfect fruit of merit.
Seated at the site of enlightenment, he has perfected the ultimate good; he is able to sever all defiled dharmas, those supreme adversaries.
Having accumulated all roots of goodness like Mount Sumeru, he has achieved the purity of inconceivable light.
Attaining this samādhi brings forth merit; endowed with twenty qualities, it is called the Pure Seal (Vimalamudrā).
Like the radiance of the sun illuminating the world, it realizes great bodhi, the supreme wisdom of the Buddha.
Once the Bodhisattva has sat beneath the tree of enlightenment, he attains the eight extraordinary marks of supernatural power;
he is then able, within hundreds of Buddha-fields, to extensively perform deeds that bring benefit and happiness to the world.
All the Buddhas have come to bestow fearlessness upon you, praising you with these words: "O valiant one, you are most supreme!
You have already completely subdued all the armies of Māra and realized the unsurpassed, victorious Bodhi of a Buddha."
Having attained these supreme merits of body and mind, one will certainly be able to accomplish this seal of the Buddha;
if one wishes to cultivate this gateway of merit, one should be firm and courageous regarding the bodhicitta.
At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:

“Sāgaramati! For this reason, if any bodhisattvas wish to attain such a Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Spontaneous Declaration of the Pure Seal, as well as the Spontaneous Declaration of Stainless Wisdom, they should abide in two kinds of mind:”
First, the mind free from turbidity and agitation;
second, the mind free from dregs and impurities.
As for the mind free from turbidity and agitation, it means that the self-nature of the mind is pure and luminous, and does not admit adventitious afflictions.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding and primordially luminous; it is not accumulated through any mental formations (*manasikāra*). Because it is free from defilement, it is devoid of greed; because it is free from conceptualization, it is devoid of hatred;
because it is devoid of self, it is devoid of delusion; it is pure, universally pure, and ultimately stainless.
Just as the light of mastery is liberated, so too are all phenomena;
because they abide in accordance with the equality of suchness, just as liberation is, so too are all phenomena;
because they abide in accordance with the equality of the dharma-realm, just as liberation is, so too are all phenomena.
Because they abide in accordance with the equality of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), all phenomena are just as that liberation is;

because they abide in accordance with the equality of emptiness, and abide in accordance with the equalities of signlessness, wishlessness, non-activity, non-doing, non-arising, and non-origination, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are just as that liberation is;

and because they abide in accordance with the equality of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), this very abiding in the dharma of equality is without accumulation and without dispersion, and is not known by cognition—this is called the "unperturbed mind."
One should then clarify and reveal this very Dharma for other sentient beings and other individuals.
Not giving rise to thoughts of agitation or disturbance regarding one's own or others' dharmas—this is what constitutes a mind free from defilement.
“Sāgaramati!
One who possesses this mind free from turbidity and agitation, and a mind free from dregs and impurities, is able to attain the samādhi gate of the ‘Self-Expounded Seal of Purity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi is exceedingly profound.
The Buddha said:
"Because its limits and bottom cannot be found.
Samudramati spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"This samādhi is extremely difficult to perceive.
The Buddha said,
"Because it is free from dualistic phenomena."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
This samādhi is extremely difficult to realize."
The Buddha said:
"Because there is no self (ātman) and nothing belonging to a self (ātmīya).
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi is extremely difficult to understand.
The Buddha said:
"Because one knows the two dharmas of consciousness and wisdom to be equal.
It further says:
"World-Honored One!"
"This samādhi is free from turbidity and confusion.
The Buddha said:
"Because it has attained unimpeded liberation."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
This samādhi is exceedingly subtle and wondrous."
The Buddha said:
"Because it is free from all metaphors.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi is extremely refined and substantial.
The Buddha said:
"Because one has attained the diamond-like wisdom (vajropama-jñāna).
It further says:
"World-Honored One!..."
"This samādhi is indestructible.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is not broken before or after."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
This samādhi is entirely without attachment."
The Buddha said:
"Because all attachments are transcended accordingly.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi attains great radiance.
The Buddha said:
"Because they are free from all the darkness of delusion.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"This samādhi is utterly pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately free from defilement."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
This samādhi is by its very nature stainless."
The Buddha said:
"Because of being free from the dust of greed.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi has no activity.
The Buddha said:
"Because there is no activity in the three realms.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"This samādhi is without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The Buddha said:
"Because it transcends conceptual proliferation."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
This samādhi is immovable."
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately quiescent.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi enters into all places.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is equal to space.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If this is so, how can one initiate superior practice?
How shall one obtain the samādhi gate of the self-proclaimed seal of purity?
The Buddha said:
“Sāgaramati! For example, suppose there were a person who wished to engage in combat with space; at that time, that space would don armor.
It is the same for a bodhisattva: one who wishes to personally proclaim the samādhi of the seal of purity should don the armor and adornment of the equality of all phenomena.”
Why is this? Samudramati!
Wherever there is cessation, there is also arising.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

The seed of consciousness is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the seed of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This samādhi is not known by eye-consciousness, nor is it known by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness. This samādhi cannot be expressed; one should know that it is neither knowing nor non-knowing. This samādhi has no characteristic of being expressible, because it awakens equally to all phenomena; therefore, it is called *Samyaksaṃbuddha*.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
I do not perceive any dharma as having the characteristic of defilement such that I attain perfect enlightenment;
nor do I perceive any dharma as having the characteristic of purity such that I attain perfect enlightenment.
If a characteristic is defiled, that very same characteristic is pure, because it is the characteristic of intrinsic purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*).
That which is the characteristic of intrinsic purity is itself the absence of characteristics (*animitta*).

If there is no characteristic, then there is no aspect of activity; if there is no aspect of activity, then there is not even the slightest dharma that can be expressed or cognized. Because there is nothing to be expressed, all dharmas are without anything that can be known.
If a phenomenon lacks both that which expresses and that which is expressed, then within it there is no manifestation through the accumulation of syllables.
If there is no accumulation of syllables to manifest, that is the suchness of what is taught.
Furthermore, what is meant by "suchness" as it has been described?
It means that the later is suchness in relation to the earlier, and the middle is likewise so; this is precisely what is called the emptiness of all phenomena across the three periods of time.
Furthermore, what is called emptiness?
It is so-called non-action; this very non-action is also non-action, yet it is not non-action either. For this reason, it is described as emptiness.
As for what is called "non-action" (anabhisaṃskāra), what is its meaning?

"Non-action" refers to the absence of the manifest formative activity (*saṃskāra*) of all phenomena, because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be formed; therefore, this is termed "non-action."
Furthermore, what is meant by "absence of manifest activity"?
It refers to the absence of manifest activity of body, manifest activity of speech, and manifest activity of mind; this is called the absence of manifest activity.
If there is no present activity, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

if it is unconditioned, it is without arising and without cessation, and it has no location. Furthermore, this dharma that is without arising, without cessation, and without location is itself without a place.
What is meant by "non-abiding"?
It refers to the fact that all presently manifest conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no abiding place;
therefore, this is called "non-abiding. Why is this so?
What is called consciousness does not abide within form, nor does it abide within feeling, perception, or formations.
If consciousness has no place of abiding, that is right knowledge; and that right knowledge is a wisdom that is without reception.

If wisdom lacks apprehension, there is no superior intention (*adhyāśaya*); if there is no superior intention, there is no contention; if there is no contention, there is no agitation; if there is no agitation, there is no affliction; if there is no affliction, there is no burning; if there is no burning, one attains cessation; if one attains cessation, one abides in universal tranquility (*sarva-śānti*); if one abides in universal tranquility, one abides in proximate tranquility (*upaśama*); and if one abides in proximate tranquility, this is called attaining great silence (*mahā-tūṣṇībhāva*). Therefore, the aforementioned statement that "wisdom lacks apprehension" is what the Buddha taught.

“Sāgaramati! This Dharma is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand. If there are those who, upon hearing such a Dharma, give rise to faith and understanding, all their inverted views, afflictions, attachments, and fetters will be completely liberated. Such persons shall be able to uphold the Dharma-treasury of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present;
they shall become great guides, revealing the immeasurable right path to all sentient beings.”
He acts as a great king of physicians, skillfully healing the disease of all signless afflictions of sentient beings.
This constitutes being able to universally provide vast offerings to the Tathāgata; before long, he shall attain the samādhi gate of the "Self-Expounded Seal of Purity."
With resolute action, they are able to skillfully accumulate merit within this Mahāyāna Dharma.
Serving as great Dharma-ships, they are able to ferry across immeasurable sentient beings from the sea of birth and death.
"Having become a great sage who has subdued all Māras, he shall never again follow the words within the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva manage to subdue all māras and adversaries?
The Buddha said, "Sāgaramati!"
If a bodhisattva, with a mind that acts for no purpose, is able to universally embrace all beings, that bodhisattva is then able to subdue all maras and adversaries.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva, with a mind that does nothing, is able to give rise [to awakening] within all those signs of objective referents, that bodhisattva is then able to subdue all Māras and adversaries.
Sāgaramati, you should know that there are four kinds of Māras. What are these four?
First, the māra of the aggregates;
second, the māra of afflictions;
third, the māra of death.
Fourth is the celestial Māra.
If one examines the illusory nature of phenomena, one can subdue the skandha-māra;
by abiding in the dharma of emptiness, one can subdue the kleśa-māra.
Investigating phenomena that are unborn and unarisen can subdue the Mara of Death;
simultaneously relying upon all mental objects and tending toward the path of cessation can subdue the Mara of the Heavens.
Furthermore, knowing suffering can subdue the māra of the aggregates;
severing the origin [of suffering] can subdue the māra of afflictions;
realizing cessation can subdue the māra of death.
The cultivation of the path can subdue the celestial māra.
Furthermore, by investigating that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, one can subdue the skandha-māra;
by investigating that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, one can subdue the kleśa-māra.
By investigating that all phenomena are selfless, one can subdue the Māra of Death;
by investigating the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, one can subdue the Māra of the Deva Realm.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva internally severs the defilements of afflictions yet does not forget the Great Bodhicitta while practicing generosity, they are able to subjugate the Skandha-māra.

If a bodhisattva does not cherish their own body nor become attached to it, and having practiced giving, is able to dedicate the merit toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they can thereby subdue the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).

If a bodhisattva can contemplate that wealth is impermanent and thinks, "I shall share this with all beings," giving it truly and sincerely, and having given thus, is able to dedicate the merit toward omniscience, they can thereby subdue the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*).

If a bodhisattva, toward all sentient beings, does not lose the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and universally gathers in sentient beings with the wisdom of liberation, and having practiced giving, is able to dedicate the merit toward omniscience, they can thereby subdue the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*).
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Seal of Purity Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Scroll Five.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Seal of Purity Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
Scroll Six.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Commissioned Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under the Imperial Edict: "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!"

If a bodhisattva, though born into the various realms of existence, remains free from expectations and well guards their ethical conduct, they are able to subdue the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra).
If they have no reliance on the view of self and well guard their ethical conduct, they can subdue the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
If, through pure precepts, they cause all sentient beings to transcend old age and death while personally guarding their own ethical conduct, they can subdue the māra of death (mṛtyumāra).

If one gives rise to this thought: "I shall cause all sentient beings who violate the precepts to dwell entirely within the noble and pure precepts; by thus guarding my own observance of the precepts, I am able to subdue the celestial Māras."
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices patience with the non-apprehension of a self, they are able to subdue the māra of the aggregates;
when they practice patience with the non-apprehension of sentient beings, they are able to subdue the māra of afflictions;
and when they practice patience with the non-apprehension of birth and death, they are able to subdue the māra of death.
By practicing patience with the non-apprehension of nirvāṇa, one can subdue the celestial Māra.
Furthermore, because the body is tranquil, the bodhisattva arouses diligence and is able to transcend the skandha-māra;
because the mind is tranquil, he arouses diligence and is able to transcend the kleśa-māra.
Because they have thoroughly realized that there is neither birth nor arising, they initiate diligence and are able to transcend the Māra of Death;
because they never grow weary within the cycle of birth and death, maturing sentient beings and upholding the True Dharma, they initiate diligence and are able to transcend the Māra of the Heavens.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration without relying on the aggregates, they can transcend the māra of the aggregates;
when they practice meditative concentration without relying on the elements, they can transcend the māra of afflictions;
when they practice meditative concentration without relying on the sense bases, they can transcend the māra of death.
Regarding the remaining factors of dhyāna, he likewise dedicates each one toward bodhi and is thus able to transcend the celestial Māras.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, by means of right wisdom, thoroughly understands the aggregates (skandhas) and is thus able to subdue the māra of the aggregates;
he thoroughly understands the elements (dhātus) and is thus able to subdue the māra of afflictions (kleśa).
By skillfully knowing the sense bases (*āyatana*), one can subdue the Māra of Death;
though skillfully knowing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and is thus able to subdue the Māra of the Gods.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva understands the emptiness of all phenomena, the Māra of the Aggregates (*skandhamāra*) finds no opportunity to strike.
When the mind can faithfully accord with the signlessness of all phenomena, the Māra of afflictions finds no opportunity to interfere;
when one knows that all phenomena are without seeking or aspiration, the Māra of death finds no opportunity to interfere;
and when one knows that all phenomena are without fabrication and free from doubt, yet remains insatiable in virtuous conduct, the Māra of the devas finds no opportunity to interfere.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices by contemplating the body within the body as a foundation of mindfulness, they do not give rise to seeking in conjunction with the body, and are thus able to destroy the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra).

When they practice by contemplating feelings within feelings as a foundation of mindfulness, they do not give rise to seeking in conjunction with feelings, and are thus able to destroy the Māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).

When they practice by contemplating the mind within the mind as a foundation of mindfulness, they do not give rise to seeking in conjunction with the mind, and are thus able to destroy the Māra of death (mṛtyumāra).

One practices by contemplating phenomena within the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), yet does not give rise to seeking in conjunction with those phenomena; remaining unmoved in the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*), one is able to destroy the celestial Māra.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
You should now know that all such demonic activities as these have me as their root."
If a bodhisattva does not give rise to a fundamental self, then for them there is neither self nor non-self.
Within this, there is not even the slightest dharma that can arise; such is known through the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*).

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva dons the armor of the Mahāyāna for the sake of those sentient beings who lack wisdom, that bodhisattva should don that armor by not relying on self and other simultaneously.
The Bodhisattva then reflected to himself:
"How shall I obtain this armor so that it is firm and indestructible?
He further pondered:

"The armor I wear is not for the sake of destroying a self, nor does it destroy sentient beings; it does not destroy the life-principle (*jīva*), the person (*pudgala*), the nourisher (*poṣa*), the individual (*manuja*), or the mind-born (*manomaya*).
If one relies upon views of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-principle, or an individual, there is attachment; therefore, I now utterly renounce all such bases of reliance."
Upon what does it depend?
It depends on the inverted [view] regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements.
What is this inversion?
Because sentient beings give rise to the notion of permanence within the impermanent;
the notion of pleasure within suffering;
and the notion of self within the non-self.
Regarding the perception of purity in what is impure:
if a bodhisattva can correctly understand that perception, they should then teach the essential Dharma accordingly.
How does one correctly understand perception?
That is to say, if there is no feeling and no grasping, one is then able to have correct knowledge. Why is this?
If one does not feel this, one does not grasp that; if one does not grasp this, one also does not feel that.
"If it is thus, then there is no delusion, and one is able to correctly know perceptions.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
How is perception known?
Is it past, or is it future?
"Is it present?
The Buddha said:
"It is neither past, nor future, nor present."
Why is this? Because past perceptions have already ceased, future perceptions have not yet arrived, and present perceptions do not abide.
Therefore, one should know that within the three periods of time, no perception can be apprehended.

In this way, one is able to correctly know perceptions; by virtue of correctly knowing perceptions, one is able to purify all the practices undertaken by a bodhisattva, and furthermore, one is able to understand the various types of conduct of all sentient beings.
Sāgaramati!
If a bodhisattva cannot purify the conduct of a bodhisattva, they will not be able to know the conduct of sentient beings.
Furthermore, only if they can know the various conducts of sentient beings will they be able to purify the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Thus, by thoroughly understanding the conduct of sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma to them according to their needs; thereby, one is able to act in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings and fully knows how to manifest whatever is appropriate.
"Samudrareṇu, you should know that there are some sentient beings who practice hatred within a mind of greed, or practice greed within a mind of hatred;
there are those who practice hatred within a mind of delusion, or practice greed within a mind of delusion."
There is delusion within a mind characterized by greed; there is delusion within a mind characterized by hatred;
there is greed within a mind characterized by hatred and delusion;
and there is hatred within a mind characterized by delusion and greed.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who feign the appearance of greed while actually taking up hatred; feign the appearance of hatred while actually taking up greed;
feign the appearance of hatred while actually taking up delusion; feign the appearance of delusion while actually taking up hatred;
feign the appearance of delusion while actually taking up greed; and feign the appearance of greed while actually taking up delusion.
They manifest greed and anger while grasping at delusion; they manifest anger and delusion while grasping at greed;
they manifest delusion and greed while grasping at anger.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who first experience greed and later anger; first anger and later greed;
first anger and later delusion; first delusion and later anger;
first delusion and later greed; or first greed and later delusion.
First greed, then hatred, then delusion; first hatred, then delusion, then greed;
first delusion, then greed, then hatred; or first delusion, then hatred, then greed.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who give rise to greed toward forms and hatred toward sounds.
One gives rise to desire for sounds and aversion toward forms;
one gives rise to desire for fragrances and aversion toward tastes;
one gives rise to desire for tastes and aversion toward fragrances.
One gives rise to desire for tangibles and aversion toward mental phenomena;
one gives rise to desire for mental phenomena and aversion toward tangibles.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who achieve subduing through the separation from form, but not through the separation from sound.
There are those who attain discipline by being separated from sounds, but not by being separated from forms;
there are those who attain discipline by being separated from odors, but not by being separated from tastes;
there are those who attain discipline by being separated from tastes, but not by being separated from odors.
There are those who attain subduing through the separation from contact, but not through the separation from phenomena;
there are those who attain subduing through the separation from phenomena, but not through the separation from contact.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain subduing through the separation of the body, but not through the separation of the mind.
Some attain subduing through detachment of the mind, but not through detachment of the body;
some attain subduing through both detachment of the body and detachment of the mind;
and some attain subduing neither through detachment of the body nor through detachment of the mind.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are tamed by the sound of impermanence, but not by the sounds of suffering, non-self, or tranquility.
There are those who are tamed by the sound of suffering, but not by the sounds of impermanence, non-self, or tranquility;
and there are those who are tamed by the sound of non-self, but not by the sounds of impermanence, suffering, or tranquility.
There are those who are tamed by the sound of the cause of tranquility, but not by the sounds of impermanence, suffering, or non-self.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are tamed by the miraculous power of teaching the Dharma, but not by the miraculous power of instruction;
and there are those who are tamed by the miraculous power of instruction, but not by the miraculous power of teaching the Dharma.

There are those who are tamed through the miraculous power of supernormal feats (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), but not through the miraculous power of teaching the Dharma or the miraculous power of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*).
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who give rise to faith and understanding because of the miraculous power of teaching the Dharma;
and there are those who become free from the dust of defilement because of the miraculous power of instruction.
There are those who attain liberation through the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, though possessing sharp faculties, attain liberation through diligent practice with dull faculties;
and there are those who, though possessing dull faculties, attain liberation through diligent practice with sharp faculties.
There are those with dull faculties who attain liberation through diligent practice with dull faculties;
and there are those with sharp faculties who attain liberation through diligent practice with sharp faculties.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain liberation by means of causes, but not by means of conditions.
There are those who attain liberation through conditions but not through causes;
there are those who attain liberation both through causes and through conditions;
and there are those who attain liberation neither through causes nor through conditions.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain liberation by means of contemplating internal faults, but not by means of external ones;
some attain liberation by means of contemplating external faults, but not by means of internal ones;
and some attain liberation by means of contemplating both internal and external faults.
There are those who attain liberation neither by means of internal contemplation nor by means of external contemplation of faults.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who practice for happiness and realize liberation through happiness rather than suffering;
and there are those who do so through suffering rather than happiness.
Some exist because of suffering and also because of pleasure;
some exist neither because of pleasure nor because of suffering.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain subduing through the arousal of signs.
One attains taming through the sign of peaceful abiding;
one attains taming through the sign of subduing;
one attains taming through the sign of skillful gathering.
Some are tamed by means of wholesome characteristics;
some are tamed by means of unwholesome characteristics;
and some are tamed by means of characteristics of anger.
Some are tamed by means of the three characteristics of causality;
some are tamed by means of the characteristic of relaxed receptivity;
and some are tamed by means of the dharma of dependent origination.
Some attain subduing through conduct that accords with causes;
some attain liberation through silent conduct;
and some attain liberation through differentiated conduct.

There are those who attain liberation through the sound of the foundations of mindfulness, the sound of the right efforts, the sound of the bases of psychic power, the sound of the faculties, the sound of the powers, the sound of the factors of awakening, the sound of the noble path, the sound of śamatha, the sound of vipaśyanā, and the sound of the four noble truths.
“Sāgaramati! Such as these are the inconceivable activities of sentient beings, the inconceivable mentalities of sentient beings, and the inconceivable realms of sentient beings.”
If a bodhisattva enters inconceivable wisdom, having entered it, they are immediately able to universally enter the inconceivable realms of all sentient beings.
Samudrareṇu!

It is as if there were a person who, having spread a net made of rope throughout the four directions, suddenly entered that net due to certain causes and conditions; this person then desired to completely untie the net.

However, because of this person’s power of skillful incantations, the net was later overcome by the force of those spells and completely shattered; thus, the person emerged at will without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: by virtue of possessing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he enters the minds of all sentient beings;
having entered, he is able, through the power of the vidyā-mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā, to universally sever the fetters of affliction (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings.
"Yet the Bodhisattva likewise does not realize the Buddha-wisdom, but universally manifests and performs all Buddha-activities for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
The mental activities of all immeasurable sentient beings, up to and including the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddhas, are moreover most marvelous.
World-Honored One,

if bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds were to hear this teaching on the mental activities of immeasurable sentient beings and the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas, would they not become terrified upon hearing it?
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"
“Suppose there were a newborn lion cub; would it be terrified upon hearing the roar of a lion?
Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind is also like this: having heard the lion’s roar of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they do not give rise to alarm or fear;
and hearing the teaching on the mental activities of immeasurable sentient beings, they likewise have no dread.
Śāriputra! Furthermore,
just as the light of a small fire does not give rise to fear in any of those grasses and trees,
and the fire itself does not form such a thought:
"I do not have the power to burn all the grasses and trees.
A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind is also like this: although the light of their wisdom is still very slight, they feel no fear toward the afflictions possessed by all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva also does not form this thought:
"I am unable to pacify the afflictions of sentient beings. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva gives rise to profound and firm mental attention and observes with the wisdom thus accomplished exactly as it is, they will be able to pacify the afflictions of all sentient beings. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, it is as if there were a fire that made a pact with all the grasses, woods, trees, forests, flowers, and fruits of this great earth to engage in battle together for the duration of an entire kalpa, such that the conflict was to commence on the seventh day.
At that time, the grasses and trees of the great earth, along with all other multitudes of grasses, trees, and so forth, gathered together and said to one another:
"You possess the power and ability; grant us your assistance."
At that time, the heaps of grass and wood were so vast that they equaled Mount Sumeru in measure. Then, perhaps someone might come and say to the fire:
"The grass and wood are numerous, while you are all alone."
"Why do you not now seek more assistance?
How can your strength alone withstand a multitude of grasses and trees?
The fire replied:
"I have no need now to seek their assistance.
Why? Although these grasses and trees are numerous, I am able to withstand them all by my own power and cause those grasses and trees to be utterly extinguished without remainder."

In the same way, the Bodhisattva likewise accords with all the afflictions of those immeasurable sentient beings, immediately emitting immeasurable fires of wisdom whose power is superior and overwhelming.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to a profound and firm resolve, they observe the mass of afflictions within all sentient beings with the wisdom they have cultivated as it truly is, and are thus able to pacify the afflictions of all sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva were to realize the dharma of being free from afflictions and abandon the afflictions, they would immediately fall into the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Śāriputra!
For this reason, you should know:

if a bodhisattva, amidst any collection of afflictions, is able to apply deep and firm attention and investigate according to reality, they will be able to overcome the power of each and every one of those afflictions.

"Śāriputra! If there are those who, having heard such an exposition as this, are not struck with fear or alarm, you should know that they are bodhisattvas skilled in expedient means (upāyakauśalya). Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, just as snake venom, wherever it inflicts a wound, has no companion, so too it is with a bodhisattva who has newly resolved [for enlightenment]:

when practicing and accumulating the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they likewise proceed alone without a companion, merely practicing and accumulating the factors conducive to awakening by themselves.
Furthermore, just as a firefly cannot surpass the vast radiance of hundreds of thousands of solar discs, so too it is with all afflictions;
they cannot overcome the light of a bodhisattva’s wisdom.
Furthermore, just as a medicine that removes poison, though its form may be extremely small, is able to neutralize vast amounts of venom, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
although the medicine of their wisdom may be exceedingly small, it is capable of pacifying and eliminating the poisons of all afflictions.
Furthermore, just as when heaven sends down rain of a single flavor, the various vessels where it falls produce different flavors according to their differences, so too is it with the Bodhisattva:

they cultivate and accumulate the wisdom of liberation, which is of a single flavor, yet they preach the Dharma in various ways according to the diverse faculties and natures of sentient beings, each being distinct.
Furthermore, just as Jāmbūnada gold appears in the world and outshines all other precious jewels,
so too does the great jewel of the Bodhisattva appear in the world and outshine all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
