Furthermore, just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, all minor kings submit and turn toward him, so it is with the Son of the Dharma-King;
if he gives rise to the great bodhicitta, all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—each honor him upon their heads and turn toward him in submission.

Furthermore, just as sentient beings with meager merit obtain nothing even when encountering a rain of jewels, so it is with those sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness; though they may resolve upon bodhicitta, they achieve nothing.
Furthermore, just as in the world, if there were no seed of sugarcane, sweetness could not arise;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: if there were no seed of the great bodhicitta, one could not achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Seven.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree. Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“It is, for example, like Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, who surveys all the grasses and trees upon the great earth and sees that there is none that is not medicine.”
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is also like this: they contemplate that all phenomena are none other than bodhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is as if the asura king Rāhu, despite his power, cannot create an obstruction within the paths of the sun and the moon.

It is the same with all the hosts of Māras; although they possess power and influence, they cannot create obstacles within the path to enlightenment cultivated by a Bodhisattva who practices with diligent perseverance.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the palaces of all the devaputras in the realm of form abide supported by space;
so too it is with the assembly of bodhisattvas who cultivate profound practices—they are like space, equal and unimpeded.
All phenomena are likewise equal to space; it is in this way that one attains the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

For example, when various vessels and utensils in the world have been fashioned, the measure of space appears within them according to their respective sizes; yet that space neither increases nor decreases.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: having cultivated the power of various virtues until they reach maturity, he is able to receive the Buddha-dharma according to its depth or shallowness; yet that Buddha-dharma neither increases nor decreases.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is like a strong man who exerts all his strength to draw an arrow and shoot it into the sky; he can never reach the limit of space.
In the same way, a bodhisattva exerts all the power of their faith to give rise to faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma, yet they cannot attain the limit of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as a clay vessel from the world cannot yet receive the name of a "vessel for use" while it is not yet matured, so too it is with a bodhisattva:
as long as the roots of virtue for awakening are not yet matured, they cannot yet receive the name of a "pāramitā."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as a person who has seen a universal monarch (cakravartin) no longer takes pleasure in seeing minor kings, so too it is with a bodhisattva:
having seen the Tathāgata, the Great Dharma King, they no longer take pleasure in seeing śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as it is impossible for all kinds of precious jewels to emerge from the water in a cow’s footprint, so too it is with the precepts of the śrāvakas:
they cannot give birth to the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the great ocean is able to produce all manner of wondrous and precious jewels, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
within the ocean of the precepts they have heard, they are able to produce the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as a newborn crown prince is not yet called a king, yet is not not called a king;
so too is a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind: they are not yet called a Buddha, yet are not not called a Buddha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For example, just as people do not cherish a mani jewel that has not yet been polished and refined in the world, so too it is with a bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening:
although they may preach the Dharma, they have not yet attained fearlessness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as a mani jewel that has been polished and refined becomes pure, bright, and beloved by all people, so too is it with a bodhisattva who has fully cultivated sublime practices:
having attained fearlessness, they skillfully expound the Dharma, and all sentient beings give rise to joy and delight.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the small jewels produced in rivers and lakes should not be disregarded. Why is this?
Although this jewel is small, if it is within a house or even in the darkness, it can illuminate everything with its radiance.
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is just like this; do not treat them with contempt or negligence.
Why is this? Because once that bodhisattva has attained awakening, they are able to universally emit light that shines extensively throughout all buddha-fields.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as a priceless great maṇi jewel is supremely exquisite and free from all dust and defilement,
so too is the bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive, being free from all conceited thoughts.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the crops of the world, when fully ripened, have their ears of grain hanging down, so too is it with the bodhisattva:
having brought the wholesome dharmas they have cultivated to perfection, they remain humble and unimpeded toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as when the world-destroying fire suddenly breaks out, all grasses and trees upon this great earth are consumed by the flames without remainder, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

when the fire of wisdom blazes forth, all seeds of affliction and their habitual tendencies are incinerated without remainder; once these are utterly extinguished, he then realizes the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is like a fire, whether small or great, that burns the trichiliocosm; yet the nature of space is inherently such.

So too it is with a bodhisattva: whether there is a bodhisattva who attains equal and perfect enlightenment, or there is no bodhisattva who attains equal and perfect enlightenment, the self-nature of all phenomena is inherently such.
Śāriputra! Such various parables as these, spoken by the Tathāgata, are able to sustain the assembly of bodhisattvas.
If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this teaching, give rise to resolute faith, they will be able to achieve full accomplishment in all those metaphors.
When the Buddha had spoken these words on the Dharma of seeing the extremes, twenty-four thousand people in the assembly gave rise to the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The supreme Buddha-bodhi is difficult to attain; It is profound, wondrous, stainless, and non-existent."
If a person wishes to bring this to full perfection, they should not give rise to doubt or confusion therein.
Pure and wondrous wisdom is free from artifice; its true radiance shines everywhere.
Abiding within the stainless, sublime seal, one is able to perceive this Buddha-enlightenment.
The nature of the mind is pure and luminous; it is likewise so in the past and the future.
When the mind is defiled by afflictions, one should not abandon this profound and firm resolve.
Within this, there is no agent and no recipient; all phenomena are sovereign and without a master.
Because there is no self and no person, they are said to be selfless; they are like space and like a dream, lacking intrinsic nature.
One should contemplate this Dharma as neither bodily action, nor speech, nor that which is discriminated by the mind;
it is unconditioned, its true nature free from conceptualization, and cannot be expressed through metaphors or words.
Equal to space, its self-nature is pure; because it is not a form, it cannot be observed.
It is not known by the eye, ear, nose, or consciousness; it is not the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind.
Far removed from both the signless and the non-signless, Independent, tranquil, and as serene as the moon;
It is not the domain of the intellect nor of the mental factors, Neither consciousness, nor perception, nor conceptualization.
This cannot be known through the activity of ordinary wisdom; how could the conscious mind comprehend it?
It is by means of the Buddha’s unsurpassed great compassion that he provisionally employs words and letters to preach the Dharma.
Sentient beings who, through superior karmic deeds in previous lives, have been embraced by spiritual friends—
having heard the Dharma within such circumstances, they obtain incomparable joy free from attachment.
Those various māras shall find no opportunity to exploit them;
unable to fathom their minds or their spheres of experience, whatever they do or wherever they go, those deeds of Māra shall not prevail over them.
Once the Bodhisattva has transcended the four māras, practicing merit and wisdom according to reality and the teachings,
and abiding well within the realm of all Buddhas— this is called one who cultivates supreme bodhi.
Sentient beings cannot know their sphere of activity; The sphere of activity of those who cultivate bodhi is supreme.
Amidst the manifold gateways of practice they establish, They preach the Dharma according to each respective characteristic.
Thus, the various activities of the world are combined through mutual conditions;
with great wisdom one understands within these formations, and whatever is proclaimed proceeds without interruption.
There are sentient beings who are largely stained by greed, and others who are largely prone to anger—all these he fully understands;
seeing them oppressed by the affliction of anger, he perceives that various harms arise from within their very nature of delusion.
Thus, regarding the various activities of the world, the Bodhisattva understands them accordingly and is able to enter therein;
whether it be the characteristics of activity, the objects of perception, or the formation of conditions, he explains them by means of their respective characteristics and terminology.
Just as when a net is spread everywhere, a wise vidyādhara knows it well;
having thoroughly torn through all the nets, he emerges unimpeded wherever he looks at will.
The courageous wisdom of the Bodhisattva is likewise: it can enter all the mentalities of the world;
it causes all afflictions to be eliminated everywhere, and its conduct is pervasive and free from obscuration.
As the sun radiates its light without assistance, and as snake venom likewise has no companion;
so too it is with the lion’s roar—the practice of a Bodhisattva is performed without a partner.
The Bodhisattva is solitary and without a second, Accumulating all the supreme Buddha-dharmas;
With the power of diligence fully perfected, He destroys all the afflictions of the world.
Just as when fire encounters dry fuel, its power increases wherever it goes;
so too does the Bodhisattva increase the radiance of wisdom, fully able to illuminate and shatter all afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:

“If a bodhisattva can initiate diligence, remaining constantly firm in their application and aspiration, and if the diligence they arouse never ceases, then for such bodhisattvas, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.”
Why is this? Samudramati!
It is through diligence that one attains bodhi.
If one is indolent, they are far, indeed further removed, from the Buddha’s bodhi. Those who are not indolent are able to practice generosity;

those who are not indolent are able to maintain ethical discipline; those who are not indolent are able to arouse diligence; those who are not indolent are able to cultivate meditative concentration; those who are not indolent are able to accumulate wisdom; those who are not indolent are able to achieve their own benefit; and those who are not indolent are able to benefit others.
For this reason, you should now know:
if bodhisattvas are able to arouse diligence, then for those bodhisattvas, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.
“Sāgaramati!

I recall that in the past, incalculable great asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vīryavīra (Brave and Diligent) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The world was named Sudarśana, and the kalpa was named Puṣpasaṃcaya.”
For what reason is the eon named Flower Accumulation? Samudramati!

At that time, the great trichiliocosm was filled with vast waters, and from within those waters emerged eighty-four thousand immense lotus flowers. Each flower had hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of petals, and they were so exquisite and lovely that all who beheld them were filled with joy.
At that time, the assembly of Śuddhāvāsa devas, having seen these flowers, were all filled with joy and their minds became serene and delighted; they spoke these words together:
"Since these lotus flowers have appeared so vast, it is certain that a Samyaksaṃbuddha will arise within this kalpa."
"This eon is not empty; a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appears in the world, like a mass of flowers.
For this reason, this eon is named Puṣpasaṃcaya.
Furthermore, for what reason is that world named Sudarśana?"

Because that world was most supremely pure, immeasurable and innumerable assemblies of bodhisattvas from all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions all went to that world together to gaze upon it with reverence.
As they gazed upon it, the entire assembly in that world all attained the samādhi of the mark of joy, becoming fully endowed with every sublime bliss.
Because that world is observed to be virtuous and sublime, it is named "Sudarśana" (Good Vision).
"Sāgaramati! This world-system of Sudarśana is composed of the seven precious jewels; it possesses various jewel trees and jeweled pavilions, and the radiance of these jewels shines everywhere."
Furthermore, that world has no women; beings are not born from a womb but are spontaneously transformed within lotuses, sitting cross-legged.
Moreover, that world has no other vehicles; all practitioners dwell solely in the Mahāyāna.

The people of that land enjoy all manner of requisites as do those in the Tuṣita Heaven; whenever they require food or drink, they obtain it exactly as they wish, and furthermore, they attain supernatural powers for playful mastery, being able to walk upon the void.
Within the Dharma of that Tathāgata Vīryavīra, there were twenty-six koṭis of renunciant bodhisattvas who, being endowed with the bodhisattva path, entered the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable numbers of lay followers who practiced the Mahāyāna path; at that time, the Buddha expounded for those bodhisattvas the Dharma of diligent and energetic application.
That Buddha addressed them, saying:

"You great beings, you should be diligent and energetic, always firm and steadfast, exerting yourselves with profound intensity and desiring it with profound fervor, never allowing yourselves to rest."
“Sāgaramati! Within that Buddha’s assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Dṛḍhavarmā who rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One! ...’”
"How does a bodhisattva succeed in generating diligence?
Furthermore, by what Dharma do the Tathāgatas instruct the assembly of bodhisattvas?
At that time, the Tathāgata Viryavīra addressed the bodhisattva Dṛḍhavarmaka, saying:
“Good son! There are four kinds of diligence that are able to universally encompass all wholesome dharmas.
What are these four?
First, initiation;
second, diligent application;
third, investigation.
Fourth is cultivation.
These four kinds [of practices] are able to universally encompass all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, what is meant by "initiation"?
What is called "diligent application"?
What is called "investigation"?
What is called "cultivation"?
"Good son!
'Initiation' refers to initiating the great bodhicitta.
'Diligent application' refers to the vast accumulation of all roots of goodness."
Investigation consists of performing deeds that benefit all sentient beings.
Cultivation consists of abiding in patience toward whatever phenomena may arise.
Furthermore, exertion consists of diligently seeking out extensive learning.
Diligent application is being able to speak according to what has been heard.
Investigation is profound and firm mental attention.
Cultivation is the arising of noble right view.
Furthermore, "initiation" consists in restraining the mind of stinginess;
"application" consists in relinquishing all that one possesses;
and "investigation" consists in sharing all virtuous benefits with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward enlightenment.
The practitioner does not seek karmic retribution.
Furthermore, as for "initiating," it means raising the cry of great renunciation (*mahātyāga*).
As for "exerting effort," it means conceiving the thought of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) toward all who come seeking.
Investigation consists of contemplating the impermanent nature of all that is enjoyed.
Practice consists of being without regret after having given.
Furthermore, initiation consists of seeking all that is enjoyed in accordance with the Dharma.
Diligence means sustaining oneself through a pure livelihood.
Investigation means practicing true generosity.
Cultivation means not giving rise to conceptual thoughts at the time of giving.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to cleansing the defilements of broken precepts;
"diligent application" refers to maintaining the prohibitive precepts without deficiency;
and "investigation" refers to protecting sentient beings who have broken the precepts.
The practitioner, though endowed with the virtue of precepts, does not give rise to intentional thoughts.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to the purity of physical action (*kāyakarman*).
"Diligent application" refers to the purity of verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Investigation is the purity of mental activity;
cultivation is the purity of all phenomena.
Furthermore, initiation is the non-acceptance of any state of anger.
Diligent application is the manifestation of the power of patience;
investigation is the protection of oneself and others;
and cultivation is the absence of conceptual thought while abiding in patience.
Furthermore, as for "initiation," it means causing all those who are angry and resentful to become joyful and further attain purity.
As for "diligent application," it means causing all those who are angry and resentful to become joyful and harmonious.
Investigation means that the inner mind is cool and free from feverish affliction.
Practice means that neither self nor others are apprehended.
Furthermore, exertion means the elimination of indolence.
The one who exerts effort makes skillful discernment through the power of diligence;
the one who investigates provides protection for sentient beings who are indolent;
the one who practices dwells in patience regarding whatever phenomena may arise.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to the accumulation of wholesome dharmas;
"diligent application" refers to the accomplishment of wholesome dharmas;
and "investigation" refers to taking no pleasure in other vehicles.
The practitioner does not destroy any karma.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to mindfulness;
"exertion" refers to practice.
Investigation is wisdom;
cultivation is abiding.
Furthermore, initiation is principle.
Vigorous application is the instruction;
investigation is the gateway;
and cultivation is the path of deliverance.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to the accumulation of words and letters;
"diligent application" refers to the dhāraṇī of both words and their meanings;
and "investigation" refers to being entirely unattached to either sounds or words.
The practitioner realizes that all phenomena are ultimately ineffable.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to drawing near to virtuous friends;
"diligent application" refers to distancing oneself from evil friends.
Investigation means giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward both virtuous and non-virtuous friends.
Practice means retaining in memory whatever has been taught according to one's ability.
Furthermore, initiation means giving rise to the aspiration for renunciation.
Vigorous application consists in viewing with equanimity that which is pleasant and unpleasant.
Investigation consists in joyfully seeking whatever is wholesome.
Cultivation consists in attaining direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
Furthermore, "initiation" is delighting in dwelling in the wilderness;
"application" is remaining far removed from clamor and bustle;
"investigation" is delighting in abiding in tranquility.
The practitioner cultivates the practice of tranquility.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to having few desires;
"diligent application" refers to being content.
The one who investigates attains sublime bliss;
the one who practices knows the proper measure.
Furthermore, the one who initiates cultivates the training in higher ethics.
Diligent application refers to practicing without distraction.
Investigation refers to practicing the training in higher mind.
Cultivation refers to practicing the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, application is generosity;
diligence is kind speech;
investigation is beneficial conduct; and...
The practitioner practices through communal engagement (*samānārthatā*).
Furthermore, "initiation" is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*);
"diligent application" is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Investigation is great joy;
cultivation is great equanimity.
Furthermore, the initiator is the purification of the buddha-fields.
Vigorous application results in the perfection of the marks and signs;
investigation consists in the protection and upholding of the true Dharma;
and meditative cultivation consists in the deliverance of sentient beings.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to understanding the māra of the aggregates;
"diligent application" refers to transcending the māra of afflictions;
and "investigation" refers to distancing oneself from the māra of death.
The practitioner subdues the celestial Māras and worldly demons.
Furthermore, the one who initiates [the path] knows suffering;
the one who exerts effort cuts off the origin [of suffering].
The one who investigates cultivates the path;
the one who practices realizes cessation.
Furthermore, the one who initiates develops the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The practitioner of diligence cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
the practitioner of investigation cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
the practitioner of cultivation cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to faith;
"application" refers to diligence;
and "investigation" refers to mindfulness and concentration.
The practitioner’s wisdom.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to the prevention and abandonment of unwholesome dharmas;
"diligent application" refers to the perfect realization and arising of all wholesome dharmas.
Investigation refers to the physical and mental pliancy and harmony.
Practice refers to attaining the supernormal power of effortlessness (*anābhoga-ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, initiation refers to cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Diligent action means practicing the Eightfold Noble Path.
Investigation means cultivating tranquility and insight.
Cultivation means attaining clear understanding and liberation.
Furthermore, "initiation" refers to the initiation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Diligent application" indicates pure conduct.
"Investigation" is the attainment of mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
"The practitioner does not turn back from the wisdom that perceives the characteristics of the objective realm. Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
That Tathāgata Vīryavikrama again addressed the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavarmakaṅkaṭa, saying:
“Good son! Through diligence, the body and mind become pliant and at ease;
yet this very diligence—whether as cause or as view—one must entirely abandon.”
Furthermore, this diligence can bring about the full knowledge of name-and-form;
furthermore, this diligence can extinguish the views of "self" and "what belongs to self";
furthermore, this diligence can untie the bonds of that which is grasped.
Furthermore, this diligence can eliminate the five hindrances and all afflictions that presently arise;
furthermore, this diligence can sever regret and those doubts;
furthermore, this diligence destroys the maladies of the fetters.
Furthermore, this diligence is able to exert effort to sever all hindrances;
furthermore, this diligence is free from pride and overweening pride;
furthermore, this diligence transcends all bases of reliance and attachments.
Furthermore, this diligence is free from all joy and anger;
furthermore, this diligence is entirely unstained by ignorance or craving for existence;
furthermore, this diligence does not engage at all with the phenomena of greed or hatred.
Furthermore, this diligence constantly examines the phenomena of delusion;
furthermore, this diligence cognizes the twelve internal and external bases (āyatana);
furthermore, this diligence realizes that the five aggregates (skandha) and the eighteen elements (dhātu) are fundamentally unarisen.
Furthermore, this diligence abides in the mind’s tranquility, pervasive stillness, and proximate quiescence;
furthermore, this diligence definitively realizes that all phenomena are entirely unattainable;
furthermore, this diligence does not grasp at dualistic characteristics regarding any phenomenon.
Furthermore, this diligence realizes that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is primordially and eternally abiding;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena neither come nor go;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are without grasping and without relinquishing.
Furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are without activity and without cessation;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are without high and without low;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena neither emerge nor enter.
Furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither bound nor liberated;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither exertion nor indolence;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither negligence nor non-negligence.
Furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena have no agent and nothing to be done;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither observed nor unobserved;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither extinguished nor inflamed.
Furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena are neither to be protected nor not to be protected;
furthermore, this diligence knows that all phenomena neither accumulate nor disperse.

“Sāgaramati! When that Tathāgata Vīryavikrama taught such dharmas of diligent application and vigor to the bodhisattvas, ten thousand people in the assembly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
Having heard such a teaching on diligence from that Buddha, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavarmaka further aroused diligence to zealously seek the wholesome dharmas.
Thus, with such diligence, he remained without rest for ten million years (*koṭi-varṣa*). After this period had passed, he attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Continuing his diligent pursuit of wholesome dharmas for that duration of time, he passed away there; having passed away, he was again reborn by transformation before that same Tathāgata to hear and receive the proclamation of the *Mahāsannipāta* True Dharma, whereupon he once more applied himself with diligence to the diligent pursuit of wholesome dharmas.
Sāgaramati!

For these reasons, the bodhisattva Dṛḍhavarmaka, throughout that period of time, extensively attended upon eighty-four thousand buddhas; during that Flower-Heap eon, he gave rise to diligence and earnestly sought the wholesome dharmas, performing all such diligent practices for as long as that time lasted.
“Sāgaramati! Do not give rise to doubt now. As for that Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavarmaka at that time, could he have been anyone else?
It was none other than myself.”

In the past, I traversed the stages of many bodhisattvas, turning my back on birth and death while diligently seeking awakening; even until I now attained perfect enlightenment, I practiced extensive vigor and underwent profound hardships.
How much less could those worldly beings who are indolent and give rise to inferior diligence ever obtain the fruit of enlightenment? Samudramati!
If sentient beings are able to arouse diligence, they will attain purity within my Dharma; it is not possible for those who are indolent to achieve accomplishment.
"For this reason, you should now know that those who possess diligence and are heedful shall immediately attain Bodhi.

When the Buddha spoke these words concerning the dharma of past diligent practice, five thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and seven thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Scripture on the Dharma-Gateway of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
The Scripture on the Dharma-Gateway of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Eight.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Dharma Master of Radiant Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I recall a Buddha of the past who appeared in the world, Whose name was Honored One of Courageous and Diligent Effort;”
The kalpa is named Flower Accumulation, Wondrous and Delightful to Behold; the supreme world is named Good Vision.
Eighty-four thousand lotuses emerge, and a Buddha appears within that kalpa;
the world is like the Tuṣita heaven, where all food and drink are obtained according to one's wishes.
There are no women there, nor do beings dwell in wombs; all transformed beings are born spontaneously and are entirely magnificent.
Furthermore, they do not cultivate other vehicles; all bodhisattvas abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The assembly of bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions can be clearly beheld in those worlds;
they have all attained the wondrous gate of samādhi characterized by joy, experiencing unprecedented bliss.
Twenty-six koṭis of bodhisattvas adorn this assembly of the Honored One among bipeds;
furthermore, many other devas and humans all dwell securely in the supreme Buddha-vehicle.
That Buddha, the Great Sage Ocean of Wisdom and Virtue, Repeatedly proclaimed the gateway of diligence.
There was a bodhisattva named Firm Armor Who questioned the Buddha on this meaning:
"Those who wish to dwell securely in the power of diligence, How should a bodhisattva practice with diligence?"
"May the Buddha proclaim this meaning for me, so that I may dwell practicing within it.
Having understood his intention, that Great Dharma King spoke of the virtue of exerting diligent effort:
"One should initiate and apply oneself to practice, constantly examining and dwelling in cultivation."
Arouse what is called the bodhicitta, Diligently accomplish and perfect all wholesome dharmas;
Contemplate the benefit of all sentient beings, And practice patience in accordance with whatever dharma you abide by.
Generating reverence for this listening and receiving, Diligently proclaiming and elucidating it;
With profound and firm mental attention as the gateway of investigation, Its practice is said to be the arising of noble right view.
To initiate the cleansing of the stain of stinginess and to relinquish all that one possesses is diligent effort;
to possess the bodhicitta as the gate of investigation and to practice what is to be done without seeking reward is analytical discernment.
Initiation is the sounding of the great cry of renunciation; Compassion toward beggars is diligent application;
Investigation is the contemplation of impermanence regarding enjoyments; Cultivation is the absence of regret after having given.
That which is received according to the Dharma is called "initiation"; sustaining oneself through a pure livelihood is "diligent action";
giving with true sincerity is the gate of "investigation"; and being free from conceptual thought while practicing giving is "meditative cultivation."
To initiate the cleansing of the defilement of broken precepts, and to ensure that the prohibitions remain without flaw—this is diligent application;
to observe and protect those who have broken the precepts, while practicing the complete precepts without conceptual thought—this is cultivation.
To initiate what is called purity of physical action, Purity of verbal action is diligent application;
Purity of mental action is the gateway of investigation, And the practice thereof is the purity of all phenomena.
Not tolerating anger is called "initiation"; the manifestation of the power of patience is "diligent application.
Guarding oneself and others is the gate of "investigation"; practicing patience is "absence of mental preoccupation."
One who is free from anger is always pure; this is called "initiation.
To apply oneself diligently toward that without abandoning it is the "gate of inner purity and investigation," wherein one practices the non-apprehension of self and others.
Initiation means removing the stain of indolence; the power of discernment is diligence.
Vigilant observation is the gate for guarding against indolence; practice consists of abiding in patience toward whatever dharma arises.
Accumulating wholesome dharmas is called "initiation"; accomplishing wholesome dharmas is "diligent action.
Examining with no delight in other vehicles, one practices without undermining the retribution of various karmic deeds.
Arousing the awareness of right mindfulness, Diligently entering into the practice of the Dharma;
Thoroughly guarding the gateway of discernment through right wisdom— This is what is called practicing with firm abiding.
Initiation is principle; diligence is instruction; those various dharma-gates are investigation;
knowing the path of renunciation is practice—this is the skillful means of exerting diligence.
To initiate what is called the dhāraṇī of the text is "skillful exposition"; to proclaim its meaning is "diligent application.
To be unattached to sounds is the "gate of investigation," and to cultivate the realization that phenomena are ineffable is "practice."
Associating with virtuous friends is called "initiation"; distancing oneself from evil friends is "diligent application.
Contemplating the nature of good and evil is the gate of "investigation," while practicing and retaining all dharmas is "meditative cultivation."
Leaving the household life within the Dharma is called "initiation"; abandoning the pleasant and the unpleasant is "diligent application.
Seeking the sublime Dharma is the gate of "investigation," while practicing the Dharma without obstruction is "meditative cultivation."
To resolve to dwell in the wilderness is diligent application;
to delight in dwelling in solitude is the gate of investigation; and to practice is to cultivate the conduct of tranquility.
Having few desires and speaking wholesome words is called "initiation"; knowing one's lot with joy is "diligence";
obtaining and experiencing sublime bliss is the "door of investigation"; and practicing according to what is appropriate in measure is "meditative cultivation."
The training in higher ethics is called "initiation"; practicing without distraction is "diligent application.
The training in higher mind is the "gate of investigation," while the training in higher wisdom is "abiding in cultivation."
Generosity and ethical discipline are called "initiation"; patience and diligence are "exertion";
meditative concentration and the practice of wisdom are the "gate of investigation"; and their cultivation together constitutes the "skillful means of integrated knowledge."
The two gifts of material wealth and Dharma are called "initiation"; loving speech is what is meant by "diligent application";
beneficial conduct is the gateway of "investigation," and practicing with sincerity is "concordant activity."
The perfection of great loving-kindness is called "initiation," and the fulfillment of great compassion is "diligent application.
Great joy within the Dharma is the gate of "investigation," and practicing this is explained as the wisdom of "great equanimity."
To initiate the purification of Buddha-fields is the door of diligence; To perfect the marks and signs is the door of exertion;
To uphold the True Dharma is the door of investigation; To liberate sentient beings is the door of abiding in cultivation.
Non-attachment to the aggregates is called "initiation"; emerging from the afflictions is "diligent application";
subduing the mara of death is the "gate of investigation"; and crushing the celestial mara is "abiding in cultivation."
Thoroughly knowing the fruit of suffering is called "initiation"; not establishing craving is "diligent application.
Cultivating the path is the gateway of "investigation," while the knowledge of cessation is what is meant by "abiding in cultivation."
Arousing the foundation of mindfulness of the body brings liberation from bondage; observing the foundation of mindfulness of feelings is diligent application;
observing the foundation of mindfulness of the mind is the gateway of investigation; and the cultivation of practice is called the observation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The faculty of faith is what initiates; the faculty of diligence is what exerts effort;
the faculties of mindfulness and concentration are the gate of investigation; and the practice itself is the faculty of wisdom.
Preventing the severance of unwholesome states is called "initiation"; not destroying wholesome dharmas is "diligent application.
With physical and mental lightness and agility, one enters the gate of investigation; through the cultivation of wisdom, the four bases of psychic power arise.
Initiation refers to cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment; practicing the eightfold noble path is diligent application.
Cultivating the gateways of śamatha and vipaśyanā through investigation is the practice of true insight and liberation.
Arousing diligence to initiate all practices, The mind attains pliancy through the gateway of investigation;
Not wavering amidst the spheres of various signs— This is called abiding in cultivation.
Through the pliancy of body and mind, one shall emerge from views and their causes;
if one thoroughly understands name-and-form therein, the Noble Ones praise this diligence.
If one can extinguish "I" and "mine," one immediately releases all bonds of grasping;
the five hindrances that arise are entirely eliminated, and remorse and doubt are both severed and extinguished.
Furthermore, he is able to shatter the diseases of all fetters; by this power, obstacles are removed and nothing remains to obscure.
Arrogance and excessive pride are severed without remainder—all that is accomplished is through the power of diligence.
Eliminating all signs of existence, Cessating all conceptual proliferations,
And severing the causes of all afflictions— This is the diligence praised by the wise.
Having heard of these merits of diligence, they all resolutely exerted themselves and offered praise;
within the assembly of Bodhisattvas, ten thousand beings all attained the wondrous patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
Within this assembly, Śākyamuni Tathāgata has extensively proclaimed [the Dharma] for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
when they heard the teaching on the prior practice of diligence, five thousand bodhisattvas attained pure patience.
Furthermore, there were devas, humans, asuras, kinnaras, and all such members of the assembly;
at that time, hundreds of thousands within the gathering resolved their minds upon bodhicitta and dwelt therein with perfect stability.
In the past, I was named Dṛḍhavarmā, having attained the bodhisattva stage of supreme patience;
I abandoned body and life to practice with diligence, remaining ever untiring for such a long time.
He drew near to eighty-four thousand Buddhas, Abandoning his own body to serve them;
Attending upon all those Buddhas for the duration of one kalpa, He subsequently dwelt in the ranks of countless bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Great Brahma King Mahākaruṇācintin addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
“Noble son, what is the metaphorical designation for that which is called ‘the Buddha-dharma’?”
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“Great Brahmā!
This term ‘Buddhadharma’ is a synonym for all dharmas.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata realizes awakening by taking it as it is through the mark of non-discrimination.
The mark of non-discrimination is the mark of the equality of all dharmas; within this, the Tathāgata realizes awakening by taking it as it is.
Mahābrahmā!
If one realizes that all phenomena are equal, this is itself bodhi;
for this reason, it is said that all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma.
If all phenomena are thus, then the Buddha-dharma is also thus.
Whatever is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, that is the intrinsic nature of the Buddha-dharma.
Because all phenomena are detached, one should know that the Buddha-dharma is also detached.
Because all phenomena are empty, one should know that the Buddha-dharma is also empty.
Great Brahmā!

All phenomena arise through conditions; if one can awaken to the fact that all phenomena arise through conditions, that itself is bodhi. Just as the Tathāgata perceives all phenomena in this way, he perceives the Buddha-dharma in the same way.
Brahmā said: "Noble son!
Is it not the case that the Buddha-dharma transcends the three realms?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Great Brahmā!
The intrinsic nature of the three realms is itself the Buddha-dharma."
Why is this so? Great Brahmā!
Within the mark of equality of that Buddha-dharma, there is neither high nor low, just as in empty space there is likewise neither high nor low.
The Buddha-dharma is likewise; like that space, it has neither high nor low.
Great Brahmā!
All dharmas are also thus; within the emptiness of their own nature, they are equal and without high or low.
"Mahābrahmā!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to know the Buddha-dharma, they should know it in this way; yet, regarding the skillful means by which it is known, they should not become attached."
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
The Buddha-dharma has no spatial dimensions and no location; it is neither born nor extinguished, and it is neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white; therefore, it possesses no manifest color."

Because it has no physical form, it has no shape or color; because it lacks both shape and manifest color, it is signless (*animitta*). Great Brahmā! The meaning of "signless" is the meaning of the Buddha-dharma;

the meaning of the Buddha-dharma is the meaning of the "non-falling phrase"; the meaning of the "non-falling phrase" is the meaning of "quiescence"; the meaning of "quiescence" is the meaning of "detachment"; the meaning of "detachment" is the meaning of "emptiness"; the meaning of "emptiness" is the meaning of "non-attachment"; the meaning of "non-attachment" is the meaning of "true nature" (*tathatā*); the meaning of "true nature" is the meaning of "ultimate non-arising"; the meaning of "non-arising" is the meaning of "non-extinction"; and the meaning of "non-extinction" is the meaning of "having no place of abiding."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati spoke again in verse:
“The meaning of what is taught as signlessness is the supreme meaning of the Buddha-dharma;
that which is taught as the meaning of the Buddha-dharma does not fall into the realm of verbal expressions.”
The meaning of non-falling is the meaning of tranquility; the meaning of tranquility is the meaning of detachment.
The meaning of detachment is the meaning of emptiness; the meaning of emptiness is the meaning of non-attachment.
The meaning of non-attachment is the meaning of true nature; the meaning of true nature is the meaning of suchness.
Suchness is ultimate, the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
The meaning of non-ceasing is the meaning of no location; the meaning of the Dharma abides thus.
Just as the Dharma-realm abides, so too do all phenomena abide.
As all phenomena abide, so too does the Buddha-dharma abide;
as the Buddha-dharma abides, so too do the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Regarding the meaning of the non-attached Dharma and other such principles, True Suchness abides without distinction.
The dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas likewise abide in equality.
Abiding in such a manner within the dharma, the Buddha-dharma is supreme and unsurpassed;
because it has no spatial divisions or locations, the Buddha-dharma dwells in peace.
Do not, amidst arising and ceasing, contemplate the various Buddha-dharmas;
they are neither form nor manifest color, and not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Formless and without characteristics, the Buddha-dharmas are thus revealed and clarified.
Just as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is, so too is the Buddha-dharma.
This equality that is spoken of is without differentiation and without marks;
thus one should seek the Buddha-dharma, and one should likewise seek all phenomena.
If phenomena are unapprehendable, they are without conceptual differentiation;
so it is with the Buddha, the various Buddha-dharmas, and all phenomena.
The Great Sage, dwelling at the site of enlightenment, has attained the equal and true Dharma.
The Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas are observed at the site of enlightenment;
those Buddha-dharmas he has taught are eternal because they are equal,
being dharmas of equality without high or low, pure like space.
If the Buddha and the Buddha’s wisdom— what that Buddha has here taught—
is that all phenomena arise dependently and possess no intrinsic nature;
and if there is no intrinsic nature, then not even the slightest phenomenon arises.
If one knows this true reality (bhūtakoṭi), the world is likewise boundless;
within this limit, wisdom arises, following and turning in accordance with all phenomena.
These are the so-called past phenomena, as well as those future phenomena.
"This is called the present dharma; this is the dharma of all Buddhas.
Thus, throughout the three times, the Buddha’s wisdom is without attachment;
because his wisdom is unattached, the Muni then teaches the Dharma."
What are called the ten powers of a Buddha, And the four fearlessnesses;
The eighteen kinds of qualities Unique to all Buddhas—
Within these are universally subsumed All phenomena whatsoever.
"All such phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, the Great Brahma King Mahākaruṇācintin addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati once more, saying:
"O son of good family!
"In such a Dharma as this, what do you perceive?
The Bodhisattva said,
"Great Brahmā!"
"Is the Buddha-dharma, then, fallen into the categories of form?
Brahmā replied, "No."
The Bodhisattva said:
"If a phenomenon is not form, it is invisible; if it is without resistance, it cannot be manifested.
How, then, can there be anything seen therein?"
Brahmā said: "No, son of good family!"
The Bodhisattva said:
“Great Brahmā!
If the Buddha-dharma cannot be seen, then all dharmas are likewise.”
Why is this? Because phenomena are fundamentally non-dual.
This non-duality is precisely all phenomena.
Mahābrahmā!
If there is any phenomenon that is perceived, that is precisely a characteristic of existence; that is to say, one perceives the non-distinct as being non-distinct from the Buddha-dharma.
If one perceives in this way, that is the Buddha-dharma.
"If the Buddha-dharma is thus, then one sees it as such.
Brahmā said, "O son of good family!"
"If that is so, then the Tathāgata has no further views regarding any phenomena.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Great Brahmā!"
"If the Tathāgata had any perception within the Buddha-dharma, then that Tathāgata and all the Buddha-dharmas would possess a real, determinate nature that could be apprehended.
Brahmā said: "O son of good family!"
"If this is so, does it not follow that the Buddha-dharma does not exist?
The Bodhisattva said,
"Great Brahmā!"
"If dharmas lack a real, fixed nature, then within them both existence and non-existence are entirely inexpressible.
If a dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, then it is simply that which cannot be perceived.
Brahmā said:
“If that is so, for what reason does the World-Honored One now teach the Buddha-dharma within this assembly?
The Bodhisattva said,
“Great Brahmā!”
As it is said regarding space, that space does not possess a real, fixed nature;
so too it is with the Buddha-dharma: when one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, that Buddha-dharma does not possess a real, fixed nature.
The Brahmā said:
"How rare, O son of good family!
If a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening hears this teaching and does not give rise to fear or terror, that bodhisattva has donned the firm armor within the Buddha-dharma."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Great Brahmā!

If sentient beings have received the empowerment of the Buddha and have already resolved their minds toward awakening (bodhicitta), they will not give rise to fear or terror upon hearing these profound teachings of the Buddha-dharma as they are spoken."
Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
Those who have grasping and clinging give rise to fear; those without grasping and clinging do not give rise to fear.
Those who have dependence and attachment give rise to fear; those without dependence and attachment do not give rise to fear.
"Those who possess the view of 'self' and 'mine' give rise to fear and dread; those who are free from the view of 'self' and 'mine' do not give rise to fear and dread.
Brahmā said: "O son of good family!"
How many kinds of powers do bodhisattvas possess?
If bodhisattvas are endowed with these powers, they will not give rise to fear or trepidation regarding such profound Buddha-dharma.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Great Brahmā!
Bodhisattvas possess eight kinds of power."
If bodhisattvas possess these powers, they will not give rise to fear or terror regarding such profound Buddha-dharma.
What are the eight?
First is the power of unobstructed faith, because it gives rise to resolute conviction toward all Buddha-dharmas.
Second, the power arising from honoring spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), because one follows them with sincere intent as if they were venerable teachers.
Third, the power of wisdom arising from extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), because all supramundane dharmas are thereby brought to full perfection.
Fourth is the power born from the performance of meritorious deeds, because immeasurable meritorious practices are all brought to perfection.
Fifth is the power of wisdom born from profound and firm mental attention, because it destroys all Māras.
Sixth, great loving-kindness gives rise to the power of great compassion, because one is free from doubt regarding the dharma of non-self.
Seventh, stability gives rise to the power of skillful reflection, because the mind of great awakening is never forgotten.
Eighth, the power of patience born from confidence in nothing other than the Dharma, because of attaining the wondrous patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mahābrahmā!
These are the eight kinds of supreme powers of a bodhisattva.
“If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such power, they will not give rise to fear or terror regarding the profound teachings of the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Sāgaramati!
You have well explained these eight powers of a bodhisattva.
If bodhisattvas are endowed with these powers, they will not give rise to fear or terror regarding the profound teachings of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, one should not give rise to fear regarding whatever is heard.
Samudramati, you should know that all sounds of the Dharma are conceptual constructions; they cannot be expressed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of bodhi.
Why is this? That ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is not language, nor is it expressible; it is not even within the sphere of what is traversed by the accumulation of letters.
It cannot even be engaged by the mind or mental factors (*citta-caitta*), so how much less could it be traversed by letters?
Sāgaramati!

As you have observed, whatever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have spoken is solely for the sake of turning the wheel of great compassion for all inconceivable sentient beings. Having attained perfect awakening within such profound dharmas, they provisionally establish and proclaim them through words for the sake of other sentient beings and individuals, within a dharma that is without letters, without speech, without expression, and without designation.
Sāgaramati!

It is like a person who knows that this space cannot be seen because it lacks the characteristics of form, and is not manifest because it is not subject to obstruction; yet, within that space, one might paint various forms with diverse colors—namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and deities such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—manifesting all manner of appearances.
Sāgaramati! What do you think?
Is what this person has done difficult to achieve?
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What this person has done is most exceedingly difficult.”
The Buddha said,
“Sāgaramati! The Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, are even more difficult to surpass than that.”

Why is this? Because, having attained perfect enlightenment within the ineffable Dharma, one provisionally employs verbal expression to establish and proclaim it for the sake of other sentient beings and individuals (pudgala).
Because they have realized the ineffable meaning as it truly is, the Buddhas are able to accomplish what is difficult to accomplish. Sāgaramati!

If there should be anyone who, amidst these profound Buddha-dharmas, is not startled, not terrified, and does not give rise to fear, you should know that this person has deeply planted roots of goodness and performed various sublime practices under previous Buddhas; therefore, they do not give rise to fear regarding these profound Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, if there should be a person who, having understood as they truly are these profound sūtras—teachings difficult for all the world to believe and comprehend—upholds, recites, and extensively explains them to others, you should know that this person is able to uphold the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata and is able to uphold the portion of all wholesome dharmas belonging to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

If there is a bodhisattva who attains the illumination of the Buddha-eye and, within immeasurable buddha-fields, fills them with accumulated precious jewels to offer as worship, performing extensive acts of giving to each and every Tathāgata."
"What do you think?
Would that bodhisattva, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
Samudramati replied to the Buddha:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
Very much, Sugata!
This mass of merit is immeasurable and incalculable, such that even analogies cannot reach it.”
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!
I tell you now, as you should understand:

if there is a bodhisattva who can provide excellent protection for the Dharma of the Tathāgata, ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is neither interrupted nor severed; who does not abandon great compassion for all sentient beings; and who, having fully understood such profound sūtras and the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom, upholds and recites them—how much more so if they practice according to the principle within them—the mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva will be many times greater than that.”
Why is this? All material gifts are merely what is cherished and enjoyed by the world;
however, the gift of Dharma transcends all worlds.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
If there is a bodhisattva who is able to protect and uphold the True Dharma, that bodhisattva shall obtain four kinds of sustenance.
What are these four?
First, they obtain the protection of the Buddhas;
second, they obtain the protection of the devas;
third, they obtain the protection of merit.
Fourth is the attainment of being embraced by wisdom.
If bodhisattvas are embraced by the Buddhas, they shall attain four kinds of most excellent dharmas.
What are these four?
First, they shall always be able to behold and look up to the Tathāgata without being separated from him;
second, no host of Māras shall find an opportunity to harm them;
third, they shall attain the inexhaustible *dhāraṇī* gates.
Fourth, they swiftly perfect spiritual powers and abide on the stage of non-retrogression. Samudramati!
All bodhisattvas who are sustained by the Buddhas obtain these four kinds of most excellent dharmas.
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas are sustained by the deities, they shall attain four kinds of purity.
What are these four?
First, through the supernormal power of the assembly of deities, the assembly of those bodhisattvas is rendered pure.
Second, causing them to listen to and receive the True Dharma with single-minded concentration;
third, dispelling all hosts of Māras and externalists;
fourth, through the majestic spiritual power of the devas, enabling all who are not yet pure to attain a pure mind.
Sāgaramati! Those bodhisattvas who are sustained by the devas obtain these four kinds of purity.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who are sustained by merit shall obtain four kinds of marks of adornment.
What are the four?
First is the adornment of the body, which refers to the perfection of the primary and secondary marks;
second is the adornment of speech, which refers to surpassing the languages and sounds of all sentient beings.
Third is the adornment of the realm, which means being able to manifest all that is performed;
fourth is the adornment of birth, which means being born in various places as a Brahmā king, Śakra, a world-protecting deity (*lokapāla*), or the like.
Sāgaramati! Those bodhisattvas who are embraced by merit obtain these four kinds of adornments.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who are embraced by wisdom shall obtain four kinds of illuminating dharmas.
What are the four?
First, illuminating the faculties and natures of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate;
second, illuminating the diseases of all afflictions and accumulating medicinal teachings to treat them accordingly.
Third, illumination through supernormal power, being able to travel everywhere throughout other Buddha-fields;
fourth, illumination of the Dharma-realm, understanding all phenomena as they truly are.
Sāgaramati! Those bodhisattvas who are embraced by wisdom attain these four kinds of illumination.
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to obtain such qualities as being embraced and praised should diligently practice the protection and upholding of the true Dharma.
"If any bodhisattvas are able to diligently practice the protection of the true Dharma, they shall obtain immeasurable and most supreme merits.
