Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court for the Translation of Scriptures, the Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Radiant Dharma, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing, and others, by imperial decree. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Those who can protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas shall receive various kinds of virtuous praise;
I shall briefly proclaim that praised Dharma, like a single drop of water from within the great ocean.”
Those who know the kindness of all Buddhas and are able to repay it, To whom all Buddhas entrust the treasury of the Dharma;
Those who can protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas— This is itself the universal offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
With the Buddha-eye, one illuminates and contemplates the buddha-fields, making offerings of exquisite jewels to all the World-Honored Ones;
when one upholds the True Dharma of the Buddhas, this mass of merit is far superior to the former.
Though one may offer worldly wealth to the Buddha, one cannot thereby be liberated from worldly conduct;
yet when seeking the supreme Dharma that transcends the world, the wise person departs from worldly dharmas.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas shall be embraced by all Buddhas;
they will also be sustained by devas, nāgas, and others, attaining both the gathering of merit and the gathering of wisdom.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas attain the full perfection of mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct;
possessing vast and supreme insight that knows all things universally, these wise ones uproot the seeds of affliction.
Those who uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas cannot be caught off guard by any Māras;
having completely eliminated misdeeds and doubt, they are free from all obstacles and bonds.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas shall not pass their births in vain within the lands where they are born;
in every lifetime they shall behold the body of a Buddha, and having seen it, their minds will immediately attain purity.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas attain the dharma of great wisdom regarding past lives;
they frequently accomplish the excellent benefits of renunciation and cultivate genuine, pure conduct.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas, Possessing precepts and learning, give rise to supreme brahmacarya;
Attaining the five supernormal powers and wondrous pliancy, They are entirely unimpeded in meditative concentration and liberation.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas enter into the profound nature of all phenomena;
having no doubt that the realm of the Buddhas is empty, they have faith and understanding that sentient beings lack a self and [inherent] dharmas.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas attain unimpeded understanding and swift, sharp wisdom;
they obtain the gate of fearless speech that is unobstructed, thereby shattering the web of doubt and confusion of all sentient beings.
Those who uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas attain the supreme and virtuous benefits of great dhāraṇī;
though they may not have been able to hear or receive it for a hundred kalpas, by virtue of possessing eloquence, they are entirely without hindrance.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas are constantly praised by the wise;
the devas, asuras, and others rejoice in their hearts, and the Buddhas praise and protect them as their own children.
For those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas, it is not difficult to attain the status of Śakra or Brahmā,
nor that of a universal monarch among men, even unto the supreme and wondrous bliss of Bodhi.
The upholder of the True Dharma of all Buddhas possesses the thirty-two marks of excellence;
with a perfectly accomplished body of great wisdom that is indestructible, no one who beholds it can ever be satiated.
For those who uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas, it is not difficult to find virtuous friends;
they shall proclaim and clarify the gateway of the Dharma-seal, and one shall hear and receive the inexhaustible treasury of the True Dharma.
Those who uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas have purified their actions of body, speech, and mind;
likewise, their morality, concentration, and wisdom are pure, and they attain the sublime purity of the knowledge of liberation.
Those who uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas never abandon the bodhicitta;
they do not forsake the practice of the pāramitās and are able to universally encompass manifold wholesome dharmas.
If one were to extensively praise the merits of those who uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas,
even if they were to remain for the duration of an eon, they could not describe its ultimate limit.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Guṇaprabharāja who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously spoke these words:
"I have attained perfect enlightenment within the dharma that cannot be taught.
World-Honored One!
“If dharmas are ineffable, for what reason do you now speak of protecting and upholding the true Dharma?
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”
“Good son! It is as you have said:
I have attained perfect enlightenment within the dharma that cannot be spoken.
Yet, good son!”
That which is "inexpressible" means that it cannot be expressed by means of conventional characters or speech within the realm of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
However, if one employs characters and speech to expound the gate of dhāraṇī, establishing, clarifying, and revealing it, then there is indeed something spoken;
this is precisely what constitutes the protection and upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Furthermore, noble son!

There may be a Dharma teacher who, regarding such profound sūtras as these, extensively upholds them, expounds them for others, and practices them according to the principle. If one can show reverence, respect, and service toward such a Dharma teacher, making various offerings and providing secret protection; if one skillfully provides gifts of food and drink, clothing, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for illness; if one can protect the wholesome Dharma and skillfully guard their speech while concealing what is not fit for speech—this is precisely what it means to uphold the True Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!

If there is anyone who can comprehend emptiness, who has faith in and accords with signlessness, wishlessness, and non-seeking, and who truly abides in the state of non-application—this is what it means to protect and uphold the true Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!

If there is one who can regard both their own words of non-contention and excellence, and the unrighteous speech of others, as being equally subsumed within the Dharma—this is precisely what it means to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!

If a person can, with an unobstructed mind, continuously and universally embrace all sentient beings and lead them into the wisdom of liberation, and bestows the gift of Dharma upon others without a mind for worldly wealth or profit—this is precisely what it means to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If there is anyone who can sacrifice their own body and life to secretly provide protection for such profound sūtras, dwelling in a place of tranquility and practicing according to the Dharma, this is precisely what it means to uphold the True Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!

If there is anyone who, for the sake of listening to the Dharma or for the sake of expounding the Dharma, can focus their mind even while taking a single step, or during a single inhalation or exhalation, this itself constitutes the protection and upholding of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!
If one realizes that all phenomena are without anything to protect and without anything to grasp, this itself constitutes the upholding of the true Dharma.
"Moreover, King Śrīguṇaprabha!
You should understand these and other such conditions!

Son of good family, I recall that in the past, beyond incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and even further beyond those incalculable numbers of kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Mahājñānabalaśvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The world was named Viśuddhaprabhā, and the kalpa was named Priyottama.
"Good son!
That World of Pure Light is composed of lapis lazuli; it is vast, pure, and its radiance illuminates the ten directions.
Therein dwell a multitude of pure great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who rely upon and sport with great supernormal powers, having been born from the most profound Dharma."

All the requisites and enjoyments of those bodhisattvas were like those of the sons of the gods in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations; they all appeared in the form of such sons of the gods, listening to and receiving the teaching of the Dharma from that Buddha, without any further distinctions of various forms such as householder or renunciant.
At that time, the Tathāgata Great Power and Wisdom Sound constantly proclaimed for the assembly of bodhisattvas the vast protection and upholding of the True Dharma, saying:
"O sons of good family, you should diligently practice the protection and upholding of the True Dharma, without begrudging even your bodies or lives."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in that assembly named Dharmavādin, who addressed the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Mahājñānabala-svara, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How is it that these bodhisattvas are able to protect the true Dharma?
Furthermore, what is this Dharma that is to be protected?
That Buddha replied:

“Good son! If, within the sphere of form and mind, one skillfully guards against all hindrances, concentrates single-mindedly on a single object, and dwells in the dharma of tranquility through subduing and ceasing [distractions], this is precisely what it means to uphold the True Dharma.”
Why is this? Because these three—the eye faculty, the object of form, and eye-consciousness—are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.

This is because the ear faculty, the object of sound, and ear-consciousness; the nose faculty, the object of odor, and nose-consciousness; the tongue faculty, the object of taste, and tongue-consciousness; the body faculty, the object of tangibles, and body-consciousness; and the mind faculty, the object of phenomena, and mind-consciousness are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
If one can thoroughly understand that the eye and forms are empty, then there is no conceptual differentiation regarding the eye and forms, and the visual consciousness has no abiding;

this is the True Dharma (*saddharma*). If a bodhisattva, within the knowledge of reality as it is, skillfully enables others to attain such a dharma, this constitutes the protection and upholding of the True Dharma.

In this way, having realized that the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects are empty, one then has no further discrimination regarding the mind and its objects; the mental consciousness abides nowhere—this is the True Dharma.
If a bodhisattva, within the knowledge of reality as it is, skillfully enables others to attain such a Dharma, this is precisely what constitutes the protection and upholding of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If there were any phenomenon among all phenomena that could be transmuted, that phenomenon would be neither to be protected nor to be grasped.
One who understands in this way is precisely one who protects and upholds the True Dharma.
Furthermore, among all views, for one who relies upon wrong views, those very views are neither to be protected nor to be grasped.
One who understands in this way is precisely one who protects and upholds the True Dharma.
Furthermore, because of the obscuration of ignorance and delusion, the mind is not pure.
If, within that obscuration of ignorance and delusion, one neither guards nor grasps at anything, and understands it in this way, this is precisely what constitutes upholding the True Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!
If a phenomenon has accumulation or dispersion, it is neither the Dharma nor the Vinaya; if there is no accumulation and no dispersion, that is the Dharma and that is the Vinaya.
What are the phenomena that aggregate and disperse?
They are the conditioned dharmas of the Path that aggregate and disperse.
If they were neither Dharma nor Vinaya, how could there be no aggregation and no dispersion?
Therefore, you should know this:
if there is no grasping, there is no arising; because there is no arising, there is neither accumulation nor dispersal.
Because there is neither accumulation nor dispersal, this is the Dharma and this is the Vinaya.
What is this Dharma and what is this Vinaya?
It is that which is non-arising by its very nature, such that no afflictions or the like are allowed to arise; this is precisely what is called the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If, because it is this Dharma and this Vinaya, it is neither arising nor ceasing, then it is inexhaustible.
This inexhaustibility is precisely the Dharma and Vinaya of non-arising; such a Dharma of non-arising is that which requires no protection.
"This state of having nothing to protect is itself the true protection and upholding of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, O King Puṇyaprabha!
When that Tathāgata Mahābalajñānasvara preached this Dharma, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas within that assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Having heard the Dharma from that Buddha, the Bodhisattva Dharmavādin felt his heart and mind become light and joyful; leaping for joy and filled with gladness, he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One! You have so well expounded this profound Dharma-gate for upholding the True Dharma."
World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, and as I have realized it, all dharmas are non-dharmas; yet where there is no dharma, there is dharma.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are subject to grasping and attachment, then they are non-dharmas; if there is no grasping or attachment, then they are dharmas.
By means of the two perceptions of "dharma" and "adharma," one can perceive that within all dharmas there is neither the perception of dharma nor the perception of adharma.
World-Honored One!
As for all dharmas and non-dharmas, if considered within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), not even a dharma can be found, nor can a non-dharma be found.
Because there is neither the perception of dharmas nor the perception of non-dharmas, no dharma can be reckoned.
Because no dharma can be reckoned, one abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); to abide in the limit of reality is itself to be without limit.
Why is this? The limit of space (*ākāśakoṭi*) is itself the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena. Because space comes from nowhere, it is therefore without limit.

Just as space is without limit because it comes from nowhere, so too are all phenomena; because they come from nowhere, they are also without limit. Thus, one says that all phenomena are themselves the limit of space.
"Bhagavān!

If there is a bodhisattva who, having heard such a dharma of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), understands it as it truly is, that person will thoroughly realize that all dharmas possess no dual characteristics."
“World-Honored One!
I do not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; since no dharma exists, it is for this reason that I speak of upholding the true Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
When I teach this Dharma, does it accord with and conform to what the Tathāgata has spoken?
Is it the true Dharma?
Am I teaching correctly, speaking in accordance with the Dharma that follows the Dharma?
The Buddha said: "Good son!

What you have spoken is truly in accord with the words of the Tathāgata; it is the true Dharma-discourse, a teaching of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and this constitutes the correct exposition."
"Furthermore, Puṇyaprabhāsa-rāja!
When that Bodhisattva Dharmavāk preached this Dharma, ten thousand devaputras among that assembly of devas attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti)."
"King Guṇaprabha!
Do not give rise to doubt. Was that Bodhisattva Dharmavādin at that time anyone else?
He was none other than you, King Guṇaprabha."

Since you have now entreated me before this great assembly, I hereby entrust to you the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over incalculable koṭis of kalpas; you should receive and uphold it, and widely proclaim, expound, and disseminate it for others.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, there were sixty koṭis of great bodhisattvas in this assembly who all stood before the Buddha and, with one voice and in unison, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
“We vow to protect and uphold the Tathāgata’s true Dharma of Bodhi, and to propagate it far and wide.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“O sons of good family!
"Upon abiding in what dharma do you all practice, such that you protect and uphold the dharmas of enlightenment accumulated by the Tathāgata over incalculable koṭis of kalpas?"
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Śikhin-rāja who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one cherishes and guards one’s own body and life, one will be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
"Because I do not begrudge my own body or life, I am thus able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭarāja said,
"World-Honored One!"
If one harbors any longing for gain and offerings, one is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma;

I have completely renounced matters such as fame, gain, and offerings, and have distanced myself from all that is not permitted by the Noble Ones—it is only in this way that one can protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Mahādhvaja said:
“World-Honored One!
If one harbors the dualistic notion of ‘dharma’ and ‘non-dharma,’ one will be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
"If one attains the equality of all phenomena by being free from the two types of conceptualization, only then can one protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Bodhisattva Jinasena said:
"If one is oppressed by the sickness of afflictions, one will be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma."
"Having attained the power of the noble ones' wisdom, I shall overcome and subdue the afflictions; only in this way can I protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Holder of the Torch said, "World-Honored One!"
If one dwells within the realm of ignorance and darkness, one is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma;
having attained the light of unimpeded wisdom and being free from all ignorance and darkness, it is only then that one can protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vidyuddeva said:
“World-Honored One!
If one gives rise to knowledge based on inference within the Dharma, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
“I have realized the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) and do not rely on the faith of others regarding all phenomena; it is in this way that one can uphold the True Dharma.
Bodhisattva Samantagupta said:
“World-Honored One!...”
If one possesses worldly faculties and a distracted mind, one will be unable to uphold the True Dharma;
I have skillfully and profoundly regulated my faculties, gates, and sense bases, and it is by means of this that I am able to uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Pure Light said:
“World-Honored One!
If sentient beings and dharmas possessed various natures and various perceptions, they would be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
"I give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, and I also attain equanimity regarding all phenomena; in this way, one is able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Bodhisattva Supreme Gait said, "World-Honored One!..."
If one gives rise to a distracted mind that is not in meditative equipoise, one will be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma;
I abide in meditative equipoise with an undistracted mind, and in this way, I am able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Guide said:
“World-Honored One!
If one does not understand the Dharma of the right path and instead practices a deviant path, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the true Dharma.”

"I have already realized the Dharma of the knowledge of the true path; by placing sentient beings on the wrong paths upon the path of reality, it is in this way that one can protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Bodhisattva Suprajña said, "World-Honored One!"
If a mind of hesitation gives rise to discrimination, one is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma;

I have now already abandoned the mind of hesitation and severed all discrimination, and furthermore cause all sentient beings to eliminate the disease of doubt—only in this way can one protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha said:
"World-Honored One!
If one dwells in what is not the Dharma and ruins the path of practice, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma."
I abide in the true practice of the True Dharma and further establish all sentient beings within the path of reality; in this way, one is able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vimaladarśana said:
"World-Honored One!
If one possesses defiled wisdom and is separated from the light of the Dharma, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma."
“Having attained decisive wisdom, perfect skillful means, and being endowed with the light of the Dharma, it is only in this way that one can protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Wisdom said,
“World-Honored One!”
If one possesses an obstructed mind and cannot follow and protect the wisdom of sentient beings, one is unable to uphold the True Dharma;
by means of an unobstructed mind, I follow and protect sentient beings so that they may abide in supreme wisdom—it is in this way that one can uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati said:
“World-Honored One!
If one does not skillfully understand the faculties of sentient beings and cannot know the conduct of sentient beings, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
“Having entered into the wisdom and understanding of the faculties and conducts of all sentient beings, I am thus able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva King Adorned said,
“World-Honored One!”
If one harbors conceptual discriminations regarding phenomena, relying upon a self, a person, or upon phenomena themselves, one is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.

When I am entirely free from all conceptualization and non-conceptualization, having abandoned all pervasive imaginings, and when the three spheres are pure—being without reliance on a self, a person, or phenomena, and being without volitional construction—it is only in such a state that one can protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhadhvaja said:
“World-Honored One!
When the sentient beings of the world hear that all dharmas are unarisen and unproduced, they are all struck with alarm and fear; thus, they are unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.”

I have realized that all phenomena are without birth and without arising; I no longer experience alarm or fear, nor do I perceive any phenomenon as being near or far. Abiding thus in accordance with reality, I am then able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!
If one conceives of awakening as being remote and distant, such a person will be unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma."
If there is a bodhisattva who reflects thus:
"Although I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I do not perceive that bodhi; whether it be body or mind, there is nothing that is joined together, nor anything that is not joined together."
"Only such a bodhisattva as that is truly able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Guṇaprabharāja said:
"World-Honored One!"
If one dwells in non-virtue and departs from true virtue, and does not seek the supreme virtues of a Tathāgata, such a person is unable to protect and uphold the True Dharma.

I have already distanced myself from all non-virtues and dwell securely in the true virtues of a Bodhisattva; by diligently seeking the most supreme virtues of a Tathāgata, it is in this way that I am able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
it is like a person who is deranged in this world who speaks as follows:”
"To say, 'I am able to protect and uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata,' is not a statement of sincerity. Why is this so?"
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sat at the site of enlightenment, there was no dharma to be obtained and nothing to be realized.
How, then, could there be any dharma therein to be protected?
World-Honored One!

I have nothing at all to protect regarding any phenomena; free from all attachments, I uphold the nature of all phenomena through great compassion, yet I neither accomplish nor fail to accomplish any phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”

It is so, it is so, just as you have said: when I sat at the site of enlightenment, not even the slightest dharma was to be obtained; it was precisely because there was nothing to be obtained that I spoke these words while dwelling at the site of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
at what time will you sit upon the site of enlightenment?”
If there were anything upon which one could sit, then there would be something attained regarding bodhi.
This would constitute duality, with distinctions between opposition and obstruction and distinctions within bodhi itself.
The World-Honored One taught that this is because the Buddha and bodhi are non-dual and free from opposition.
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! Having fully realized the intrinsic nature of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I therefore sit upon the site of enlightenment.”

Because my own nature is the very nature of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and the nature of enlightenment is the nature of all sentient beings, and that nature of all sentient beings is the nature of all phenomena (dharmas).
Mañjuśrī! Because they share the same single flavor within the identical nature,
when I attained perfect awakening at the site of enlightenment, I observed that not even the slightest phenomenon existed within the site of enlightenment that was not liberated.
This means that because awakening is equal, one realizes all phenomena as equal.
Yet, within this equality of phenomena, one does not fall into numerical categories, for both number and non-number are entirely transcended.
That dharma of equality is why the Tathāgata calls it the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Mañjuśrī!
Having attained this unconditioned, the Tathāgata transcends all conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī gave rise to profound faith and understanding, as did the entire assembly, who believed and understood the Tathāgata’s teaching on liberation.
By virtue of their faith and understanding, they universally do not transgress against the equal Dharma.

At that time, the great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had previously come to this Sahā world together with Sāgaramati Bodhisattva—having heard this Dharma—felt their hearts leap with joy and delight; all were filled with gladness and spoke these words in unison:
"We have come to this Buddha-field and have swiftly attained excellent benefit."

They beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and also saw the Great Being Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; they heard the preaching of this profound and sublime Dharma, witnessed the appearance of the Buddha in the world, and saw this true Dharma currently abiding in the world as it turns the great wheel of Dharma.
“World-Honored One!
Wherever this True Dharma is widely disseminated, those sentient beings therein will obtain great and wholesome benefit.

Furthermore, if there are people who, whether during the Buddha’s lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa, are able to hear and receive this True Dharma, and having heard it, believe and understand it, upholding, reciting, and extensively explaining it to others—it should be known that such persons will obtain great benefit.”
The Buddha said:
“Sons of good family!
According to what you know, how many kinds of great benefits does a bodhisattva well obtain?”
That bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva well attains ten kinds of great benefits; these are turned by inconceivable and virtuous benefits.”
What are the ten? They are:
first, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world and being able to draw near to him, thereby attaining this great benefit;
Second, having seen the Buddha, their deep mind becomes pure;
third, they give rise to a pure mind to hear and receive the true Dharma;
fourth, having heard the true Dharma, they are freed from all doubts and delusions.
Fifth, having abandoned doubt and confusion, one leaves the household life;
sixth, having left the household life, one sustains oneself through a pure livelihood;
seventh, because one sustains oneself through a pure livelihood, one is able to skillfully expound the Dharma.
Eighth, having skillfully taught the Dharma, they resolve their minds on enlightenment;
ninth, because they do not forget the bodhicitta, they are able to hear and receive the teachings of the Bodhisattvapitaka;
tenth, having heard the profound Dharma of the Bodhisattvapitaka, they practice in accordance with the Dharma and thereby attain this great benefit.
“World-Honored One!
Such dharmas as these constitute the ten kinds of great benefits for bodhisattvas.
These are turned by inconceivable and virtuous benefits; if bodhisattvas abide in this manner, it is said that they have well attained great benefit.”
Then the Buddha praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You great beings!"
“Excellent is this discourse on the great benefits attained by Bodhisattvas.
When this Dharma was being taught, thirty-six thousand people in the assembly resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Minister of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Fan (Sanskrit), Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Edict. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
It brings great benefit to those who cultivate the Mahāyāna.

All sentient beings—including gods and humans—though they may enjoy the pleasures within the realms of gods and humans, are thereby able to draw near to the supreme and wondrous bliss of unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
"Bhagavān!
How many kinds of dharmas are there that can follow along with and sustain the Mahāyāna?
Furthermore, how many dharmas are there within the Mahāyāna that can perform much?"
Furthermore, how many dharmas are extremely difficult to practice within the Mahāyāna?
Furthermore, how many dharmas cause the Mahāyāna to increase?
Furthermore, how many dharmas constitute obstacles and difficulties within the Mahāyāna?
“World-Honored One!
For what further reason is it called the ‘Great Vehicle’ (Mahāyāna)?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now speak for you.
Samudramati, you should know this!"
There is one dharma that encompasses the Mahāyāna.
What is this one?
It is the non-forgetfulness of the mind set on great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta), coupled with the absence of negligence.
Sāgaramati!
Furthermore, there is one dharma that encompasses the Mahāyāna: namely, the conviction that all actions inevitably fall within the retribution of karma.
Again, there is one dharma: namely, the arising of right view, which does not contradict the phenomena of dependent origination.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to be free from both love and non-love, giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to abide in great compassion and thereby deliver oneself.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to give rise to great compassion and not be attached to one's own pleasure.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to yearn for the Buddha-body and practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to practice the true cultivation according to the Dharma and practice mindfulness of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: dwelling among those who have reached non-retrogression, one attends to the assembly with mindfulness.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: having eliminated all afflictions, one attends to equanimity with mindfulness.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: because one never forgets the bodhicitta, one practices mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, there is one dharma: abiding in the pure dharmas, one practices mindfulness of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*).
Furthermore, there is one dharma: abiding in benefit and happiness so as to cause others to rejoice.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: abiding in a firm resolve with an extremely wholesome aspiration.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: giving rise to a joyful mind to effect liberation for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to earnestly seek the true Dharma, arising from the profound Dharma in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to practice the gift of Dharma without a mind for material gain.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: regarding those who listen to the Dharma, one should conceive of them as being like patients.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: regarding the Dharma that is taught, one should conceive of it as being like excellent medicine.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: regarding oneself as the teacher of the Dharma, one should conceive of oneself as being like a king of physicians.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: constantly practicing protection so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is neither severed nor interrupted.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: maintaining a continuity free from greed, always giving rise to contentment.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: relinquishing all that one possesses without giving rise to attachment.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: although one maintains one's own precepts, one constantly protects those who have broken their precepts.
Furthermore, there is one more dharma: those who perform evil deeds dwell in patience without examining the faults of others.
Furthermore, there is one more dharma: those who perform wholesome deeds dwell in patience by manifesting benefit for others.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to give rise to the wisdom of compassion toward those who are ungrateful.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to give rise to reverence and pity toward those who are grateful.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: not to give rise to arrogance toward those who lack wisdom.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to study and learn from those who possess wisdom according to their instruction.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to deeply and firmly cultivate roots of goodness with a mind free from weariness or abandonment.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: for the mind to always follow and turn toward all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: because of being free from guile and crookedness, the three precepts are pure.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: toward those who preach the Dharma, one should love, respect, serve, and regard them as a venerable teacher.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to abandon the texts of all non-Buddhists and listen well to the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to cultivate all roots of goodness, remaining untiring even amidst the hardships of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, there is one dharma: to serve and make offerings to all the Tathāgatas, both those currently dwelling in the world and those already entered into parinirvāṇa, without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to act as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is one more dharma: to cultivate the four means of attraction with a mind that is without dependence, without grasping, and without attachment.
Furthermore, there is one more dharma: having thoroughly understood the various faults of the household life, to always delight in leaving home.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: the constant self-development of the deeds of a true being (*satpuruṣa*).
Furthermore, there is one dharma: making one's actions decisive, abiding in the path of enlightenment (*bodhimārga*), and further cultivating superior practices.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: not giving rise to vexation or anger toward those who dwell together in the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: teaching the dharma of the bodhicitta without becoming weary or indolent.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to skillfully guard the secret teachings so that they do not disperse.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to always diligently seek the craftsmanship of wisdom regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to establish the banner of the Dharma through truthful speech.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: that the vows one has undertaken should be brought to ultimate fulfillment.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to practice giving with a mind free from regret or change of heart.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to always remain clearly aware of the activities of Māra.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: one should constantly initiate the mental activity of wisdom that is free from pride.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to distance oneself from worldly acquaintances and delight in dwelling in tranquility.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to be free from overweening pride and arrogance, and not to give rise to slander against others.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: although one has thoroughly understood all afflictions, one nevertheless accords with the modes of worldly conduct.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: sustaining one's life through pure livelihood, free from all greedy attachments.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to remain constantly in meditative seclusion while being deeply and firmly integrated with practice.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: although possessing great learning, to remain constantly in tranquil concentration.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to correctly cultivate the stages of yogic practice in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: the dharma of investigating the realm of emptiness as it truly is.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: maintaining a mind free from fluctuation—neither elated nor dejected—in the face of gain or loss.
Furthermore, there is one dhaa: fearing the clamor and bustle of crowds, dwelling alone in gardens and groves.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: if one attains the benefit of the Dharma, one shares it equally with others.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: skillfully understanding the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: having no secretiveness or stinginess regarding any dharmas of wisdom.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: for the sake of accomplishing the training of those who have not yet trained, one’s mind is free from pride or superiority.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: whether gain or loss occurs, because one has faith in karmic retribution, one does not give rise to feverish distress.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: listening to the Dharma with reverence and skillfully expounding the Dharma for others.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: being free from all craving and attachment toward kinsmen and friends, and giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: not giving rise to a mind of flattery toward the Dharma-preacher, but constantly praising them.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: bearing the burden of all sentient beings by means of a mind that is disciplined and compliant.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to diligently seek that which corresponds to the various pāramitās.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to cultivate the practices of the path to enlightenment through diligence.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: establishing the faculty of faith so that it remains unshakable.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: not receiving food in vain within the city and its districts.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: accumulating the seven kinds of noble wealth so as never to be destitute.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: making the internal mind truly firm and stabilizing the life-faculty.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: maturing sentient beings through skillful means.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: properly gathering the Dharma by practicing the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to abandon all contentious debate and preach the supreme Dharma.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to listen to and receive the true Dharma with a mind of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to become a śramaṇa by being free from the defilements of a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, there is one more practice: entering royal cities and villages with a mind free from attachment.
Furthermore, there is one more practice: one should constantly examine one's own faults and protect all sentient beings well.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to abandon all worldly and miscellaneous arts.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: to always be sincere toward spiritual friends. Furthermore, there is one dharma:
having purified one’s own mind, to give rise to wisdom and further cause the minds of all sentient beings to attain purity.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: because it is free from artifice, the internal mind is pure.

Furthermore, there is one dharma: because it tends toward the most excellent path, the profound mind is pure; and this one dharma, by skillfully performing supreme deeds, is pure in its expedient means.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: once merit is purified, the physical marks are purified.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: once wisdom is purified, the afflictions are purified.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: once sentient beings are purified, the buddha-fields are purified.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: although one contemplates signlessness, one skillfully dedicates [the merit].
Furthermore, there is one dharma: cultivating the patience that accords with reality (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there is one dharma: one should constantly investigate and cultivate renunciation through the three gates of liberation.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: dwelling in non-dwelling.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: realizing the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and sporting therein.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: abiding in śamatha and vipaśyanā, accomplishing what is to be done, and attaining clear liberation.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: wisdom encompassed by the diligent cultivation of skillful means.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: abiding within the wheel of the triple world while attaining the adornment of the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is one dharma: the manifestation of perfect awakening to the equality of all dharmas.

Furthermore, there is one dharma that encompasses the Mahāyāna: knowing that all dharmas are by nature without self-nature, unarisen, and unoriginated; having known this, one immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Sāgaramati!
This single dharma is able to encompass the Mahāyāna; once such a single dharma has encompassed the Mahāyāna, all other forms of encompassing and reliance are entirely abandoned.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
There are two kinds of dharmas that can be extensively practiced within the Mahāyāna.
What are these two?
First, to give rise to pure faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma;
second, not to delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
There are two kinds of dharmas that are extremely difficult to practice within the Mahāyāna.
What are these two?
First, having attained liberation oneself, one skillfully protects those who are not yet liberated;
second, one preaches the Dharma of liberation to them accordingly.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, never allowing the great bodhicitta to be destroyed or extinguished;
second, investigating sentient beings and skillfully establishing them [in the path].
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to contemplate the bodhicitta as being like an illusory phenomenon;
second, to contemplate all sentient beings as being entirely without self.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced extensively:
first, a mind free from weariness or aversion;
second, that the skillful means one cultivates are not hypocritical or artificial.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, taking internal purity of mind as the foundation;
second, cultivating various meritorious practices because there is neither "non-doing" nor "not non-doing."
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, the skillful means of diligently cultivating roots of goodness;
second, bringing the skillful means thus cultivated to ultimate completion.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to cultivate skillful means because of the absence of conceptual proliferation;
second, for the mind to be tranquil because the skillful means one cultivates abide in the ultimate.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, to direct the profound mind toward the supreme path;
second, to take the most excellent dharmas as the supreme object of focus.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to confess and repent for one's own transgressions;
second, to bring others out of their transgressions.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, relinquishing all that one possesses;
second, not seeking karmic rewards.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to practice giving with an impartial mind;
second, to be skillful in dedication.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, maintaining the precepts without deficiency;
second, not seeking rebirth in the heavens.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to give rise to a heart of compassion toward those who violate the precepts;
second, to possess the virtue of one's own precepts without becoming arrogant.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, taking genuine delight in patience;
second, dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to abandon a haughty mind;
second, to respect those who practice patience.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be frequently practiced:
first, to arouse diligence in seeking all wholesome dharmas;
second, to give rise to a mind of joy toward all roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, the tranquility of body and mind;
second, the mind’s freedom from dependence and attachment.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced extensively:
first, the accumulation of the factors of dhyāna;
second, the harmonious cultivation of mental activity.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, not becoming attached to the flavor of dhyāna;
second, not feeling weary of the desire realm.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced frequently:
first, diligently seeking the true Dharma;
second, constantly giving rise to the aspiration for the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the investigation of phenomena;
second, meditative absorption in phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, associating with virtuous friends;
second, increasing one's respect toward teachers and elders.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to serve with dedicated diligence;
second, to comply with kind words.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, to constantly inquire at the proper and improper times;
second, to internalize within the mind the meanings as they are received.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, cultivating the wisdom of meaning;
second, cultivating the wisdom of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced extensively:
first, insatiability regarding the wealth of hearing;
second, insatiability regarding the wisdom derived from hearing.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the investigation of profound and firm dharmas;
second, the distancing from those that are not profound and firm.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, to expound the Dharma to others in accordance with the truth;
second, to give rise to a heart of compassion toward those who listen to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, not being stingy with the Dharma;
second, not preaching the Dharma to others with a mind intent on material gain.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, the cessation of external listening;
second, the gathering and sustaining of the mind.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the cessation and removal of the five hindrances;
second, the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced frequently: first, attaining joy;
second, being associated with the feeling of joy.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, knowing the Dharma and knowing the measure;
second, knowing one's own sphere of experience.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, faith in the retribution of karma;
second, the skillful cultivation of superior practices.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to understand that all things are not the result of karmic retribution;
second, to increase all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, speaking words of sincerity;
second, not deceiving the noble ones.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to be able to act according to what one says;
second, not to impair the Buddha-eye.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, purity of physical action;
second, abstaining from the three unwholesome deeds.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to contemplate the body as being like a reflected image;
second, to contemplate it as being like grass, wood, tiles, and pebbles.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced extensively:
first, the purification of verbal karma;
second, the avoidance of the four faults of speech.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to realize and understand that the Dharma is ineffable;
second, to know through wisdom that all sounds are like echoes.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, the purification of mental karma;
second, remaining far removed from greed, hatred, and false views.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, the stilling of the internal mind;
second, the absence of external activity.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness;
second, the arising of an impartial mind toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, a mind as pure and stainless as space;
second, delivering oneself and others while skillfully dedicating the merit.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, never becoming weary of or abandoning the mind of great compassion;
second, diligently cultivating roots of goodness without indolence or fatigue.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the investigation of non-arising;
second, the skillful protection of renunciation.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, sporting in the garden of the Dharma;
second, eliminating the mind of weary detachment.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to bring the dharma of profound silence to perfection;
second, to cause those who have not yet attained the dharma to practice it.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, relinquishing attachment and defilement;
second, severing all forms of harm.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the cultivation of the practice of equanimity;
second, observing sentient beings without experiencing weariness or distress.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, the cultivation of the contemplation of the Buddha;
second, abiding in non-thought while giving rise to the mind of thought.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, contemplating the Dharma-body;
second, perfecting the body of various marks and signs.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, the cultivation of the contemplation of the dharma;
second, the accomplishment of the dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to investigate and remain free from greed;
second, to give rise to great compassion for sentient beings who act out of greed.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, to keep in mind the assembly of all bodhisattvas;
second, to take refuge in and turn toward the assembly of those who are non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to contemplate the unconditioned;
second, to protect those who have attained the fruits [of the path].
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, mindfulness of ethical discipline;
second, never forgetting the mind of great enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to examine the precepts without deliberate effort;
second, to embrace and protect sentient beings who have broken the precepts.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, mindfulness of equanimity;
second, not giving rise to regret after having relinquished something.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to eliminate one's own afflictions;
second, to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may sever their afflictions.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, mindfulness of the devas;
second, not seeking rebirth in the heavens.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to abide in right mindfulness and wisdom;
second, to cause those with distracted minds to abide in the foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, the further cultivation of meritorious conduct;
second, the further cultivation of wisdom-conduct.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, skillfully cultivating non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*);
second, not giving rise to weariness or revulsion toward meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, to transcend all attachments;
second, to be fully able to liberate oneself from all cravings and clingings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to practice:
first, having an exceedingly wholesome aspiration;
second, not giving rise to flattery or deceit.
Furthermore, there are two practices that should be frequently cultivated:
first, recognizing kindness;
second, repaying kindness.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to sever desire and greed;
second, to never grow weary of or abandon the aspiration for wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, confessing and repenting for all transgressions;
second, refraining from committing any transgressions.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, not giving rise to regret;
second, not giving rise to latent tendencies.
Furthermore, there are two practices that should be frequently performed:
first, rejoicing in the merit of others;
second, never being satiated with one's own merit.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to give rise to the wisdom of exhaustion and cessation regarding all faults;
second, to give rise to the wisdom of cultivation and increase regarding all merits.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, exhorting and requesting all Buddhas;
second, upholding and protecting the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, although one knows that the dharma-realm is fundamentally without discrimination;
second, using wisdom to skillfully discriminate and explain the meanings of various phrases and principles.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced frequently:
first, skillfully understanding dedication;
second, sharing whatever is dedicated with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the definitive discernment of the signless;
second, the cultivation of all that possesses signs.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that are frequently practiced:
first, although one contemplates emptiness;
second, one contemplates and illumines sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, the arising of wisdom in which nothing is found to be pleasurable;
second, the application of skillful means in which something is found to be pleasurable.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, the aspiration for roots of goodness;
second, the accomplishment of roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, the cultivation of wishlessness;
second, the accumulation of the wisdom that arises [therefrom].
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, non-attachment;
second, immovability.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to practice:
first, the absence of pride;
second, the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced frequently:
first, delighting in dwelling in tranquility;
second, experiencing the merits of tranquility.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, practicing the conduct of tranquility;
second, delivering oneself and then delivering all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced frequently:
first, having few desires;
second, knowing contentment.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to examine and reflect upon one's own afflictions;
second, to scrutinize and observe the severing of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced frequently: first, stabilizing;
second, investigative analysis.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to constantly examine one's own faults;
second, not to observe the faults of others.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, to personally distance oneself from arrogance;
second, not to give rise to slander against others.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to contemplate the self as being without self;
second, to contemplate sentient beings as being without sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, to constantly practice giving oneself;
second, to accept the gifts of others.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to transcend saṃsāra;
second, to deliver all sentient beings within saṃsāra.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced extensively:
first, to diligently seek the pāramitās;
second, to abide according to the teachings in accordance with whatever pāramitās one seeks.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, attaining the wisdom of direct perception;
second, bringing about the wisdom of others.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, not seeking worldly fame, reputation, profit, or sustenance;
second, diligently seeking the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to do:
first, to provide benefit to those who do not benefit one;
second, to cause those already benefited to increase to the utmost degree.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, the great loving-kindness one cultivates is boundless;
second, the great compassion one practices is uninterrupted.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to cause those who have already attained deliverance to realize awakening;
second, to bring across those who have not yet attained deliverance.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, to bring merit and virtue to accomplishment for all sentient beings;
second, to give rise to great compassion toward those sentient beings who lack merit and virtue.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to act for the benefit of those who do not benefit one;
second, to have no ulterior motive after having already acted for their benefit.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, constantly practicing the contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness;
second, abiding in the purity of the body.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to practice the mindfulness of the body within the body;
second, not to give rise to discursive thought (*vitarka*) or deliberation (*vicāra*), nor the path of such discursive thought, in conjunction with the body.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, constantly practicing the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding sensation;
second, being without subjective reception toward sensations such as suffering or pleasure.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to practice the mindfulness observation of feelings while experiencing them;
second, not to give rise to discursive thought (vitarka) or investigation (vicāra), nor the path of such discursive thought, in conjunction with feeling.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas to be practiced frequently:
first, constantly practicing the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness;
second, the mind abiding in purity.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to practice the contemplation of mindfulness according to the mind’s center even while acting;
second, not to give rise to discursive thought (*vitarka*) and deliberation (*vicāra*), nor the path of such discursive thought, together with the mind.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, constantly practicing the contemplation of the application of mindfulness to phenomena;
second, constantly giving rise to the wisdom that discriminates phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, although one practices the mindfulness of dharmas within the sphere of dharmas;
second, one does not give rise to discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*), nor the path of discursive thought and investigation, together with those dharmas.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, to completely eliminate all unwholesome states that have already arisen;
second, to be able to protect and preserve all wholesome states that have already arisen.
Furthermore, there are two things that are difficult to perform:
first, to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising;
second, to cause all wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced frequently:
first, to constantly cultivate the four bases of psychic power—desire, effort, mind, and wisdom;
second, to skillfully deliver those sentient beings who are to be delivered by means of these psychic powers.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to attain supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) without deliberate application;
second, to manifest various miraculous responses within all Buddha-fields while remaining unmoved from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced extensively:
first, to remain unshakable in the faith one has attained;
second, to cause those who have not yet attained faith to possess it.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to have one's own mind free from defilement;
second, to cause sentient beings with defiled minds to attain purity.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas to be frequently practiced:
first, to arouse the faculty of diligence;
second, to abide in the faculty of mindfulness so that no distraction arises.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to decisively discern and skillfully observe the faculty of diligence;
second, to give rise to mindfulness without clinging to the mark of emptiness.
Furthermore, there are two things to be practiced extensively:
first, to diligently cultivate all practices within the faculties of concentration and wisdom;
second, to give rise to no weariness or indolence regarding the practices one cultivates.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, wisdom that has no sphere of activity;
second, maturing sentient beings while having a sphere of activity.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, contemplating the separation from all afflictions;
second, diligently seeking liberation once afflictions have arisen.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, that all dharmas are non-composite because they are fundamentally free from afflictions;
second, to enter into harmony within the triple world for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor for the Transmission of Sanskrit, Court Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, recipient of the purple robe, under imperial decree. "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that can be extensively practiced within the Mahāyāna:
first, to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment with diligence;
second, to teach the dharma of the factors of enlightenment with a profound mind.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, not dwelling in the knowledge of exhaustion;
second, the patient acceptance of the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently cultivated:
first, practicing the right path well;
second, knowing well what is not the path and refraining from it.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, cultivating the knowledge that leads toward the path;
second, establishing the true path.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that should be practiced extensively:
first, to accord with the principle of dependent origination;
second, to remain free from the views of the two extremes.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, skillfully knowing the defiling causes and defiling conditions of all sentient beings;
second, skillfully knowing the purifying causes and purifying conditions of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced frequently:
first, recognizing the activities of Māra;
second, distancing oneself from the deeds of Māra.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, to emerge from all māras;
second, to cause the māras to remain hidden and concealed.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that are frequently practiced:
first, that which is already exhausted has nothing further to be exhausted;
second, that which is inexhaustible cannot be exhausted.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, that which is fundamentally inexhaustible;
second, to contemplate with precision that all phenomena are destroyed moment by moment.
Furthermore, there are two practices to be frequently performed:
first, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one should immediately investigate the site of great awakening;
second, because one investigates the site of awakening, one takes no pleasure in other vehicles.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to accomplish:
first, at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, it becomes the cause for giving birth to the site of awakening;
second, although one gives rise to various wholesome states of mind, one remains free from grasping and attachment.
Furthermore, there are two things that should be practiced frequently:
first, for those whose continuity of birth and death persists, to sever all fetters;
second, for those whose continuity of roots of goodness persists, to cause them to resolve their minds so that they do not give rise to weariness or renunciation.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, whether things possess spatial dimensions or lack them, to dedicate all roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi;
second, although one dedicates them toward bodhi, to give rise to a mind that clearly contemplates all things as being like illusory phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas to be practiced extensively:
first, to cause all sentient beings to universally contemplate bodhi;
second, to cause those sentient beings who have already contemplated bodhi to contemplate liberation.
Furthermore, there are two things difficult to perform:
first, to investigate that because awakening is equal, sentient beings are also equal;
second, to bring sentient beings to maturity with tireless diligence.
Furthermore, there are two things that can be extensively practiced within the Mahāyāna:
first, to generate the resolve to rationally discern all wholesome dharmas;
second, to give rise to the mind of great compassion, thereby establishing all sentient beings upon the path to nirvāṇa.
Sāgaramati!
These two dharmas can be practiced extensively within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that are extremely difficult to practice within the Mahāyāna:
First, arising from the non-arisen;
second, arising from the unarisen.
Sāgaramati!
These two dharmas are extremely difficult to practice within the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati,
there are three kinds of dharmas that cause the Mahāyāna to increase."
What are these three?
First, to resolve upon bodhicitta and further cultivate roots of goodness;
second, to be sustained by spiritual friends and not give rise to weariness or indolence.
Third, establishing great compassion without retreating.
These three dharmas increase the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are another three dharmas that increase the Mahāyāna.
What are the three?
First, diligently cultivating superior practices;
second, investigating all conditioned phenomena.
Third, within the supreme practices, one skillfully accomplishes them for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, to restrain and cease the mind of stinginess;
Second, extensively practicing giving and relinquishment;
third, dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
First, one personally accumulates pure precepts;
second, one protects those who have broken the precepts;
third, one dedicates [the merit] toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, a mind free from hindrances;
second, causing sentient beings who are prone to anger and resentment to attain purity.
Third, dedication toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, diligence without weariness;
Second, being able to protect and sustain indolent sentient beings;
third, dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, arising from meditative concentration;
second, non-attachment to meditative concentration;
third, dedicating [the merit] toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, diligently seeking extensive learning;
second, investigating and examining according to what has been heard.
Third, dedication toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, giving rise to compassion that takes sentient beings as its object;
Second, the arousal of compassion directed toward conditioned phenomena;
third, the arousal of compassion that is without an object.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, one gives rise to compassion because of what one has done oneself;
second, one gives rise to compassion because of what one has done for others;
third, one gives rise to great compassion because of being free from the two extremes.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, diligently seeking the wisdom for one's own benefit;
second, diligently seeking the wisdom for the benefit of others.
Third, by exerting diligent effort, one brings both [self-]benefit and [benefit for others] to fulfillment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, the wisdom that has already exhausted the past;
Second, the wisdom of the future that has not yet arrived;
third, the wisdom of the present abiding in the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, they give rise to the compassion of skillful means toward those beings fixed in the right path;
second, they give rise to the compassion of liberation toward those beings who are not yet fixed;
third, they give rise to the compassion of great deliverance toward those beings fixed in error.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, because one attains pleasant sensations, the activities of the body are harmonious and supple;
second, because one skillfully protects others, one’s speech is sweet and pleasing.
Third, because their conduct is upright, their mental karma is capable and resilient.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, although they practice the contemplation of impurity, they do not give rise to revulsion or detachment toward those among the class of sentient beings who act out of greed.
Second, although they cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness, they do not give rise to weariness or revulsion toward sentient beings who act out of anger;
third, although they cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination, they do not give rise to weariness or revulsion toward sentient beings who act out of delusion.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, cultivating superior practices for the sake of benefiting others;
second, being constantly content with joy.
Third, it is cool and refreshing because it is forever free from the affliction of heat.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, to retain and uphold what one has heard;
Second, the retention of words and phrases;
third, entering into the sound of wisdom because the prior and subsequent limits are severed.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
First, because they gather and accumulate the seven noble riches, they are never in want;
second, because their Dharma-giving is without obstruction, they are able to practice great relinquishment;
third, because they distribute all wealth and profit equally among the multitude, they always attain great prosperity.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, being truthful because one enters the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
second, being real because one is free from falsehood and deception.
Third, because it is as it always has been and is without change.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, knowing for oneself: "What am I now?"
Second, knowing what various sentient beings should practice;
third, knowing the timing, understanding the appropriate and inappropriate moments, and all their respective states.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the equality of the aggregates and the aggregate of dharmas;
second, the equality of the elements and the realm of dharmas;
third, contemplating the sense bases as an empty village.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, not undermining cause and effect;
second, being able to skillfully nurture all conditions.
Third, they are harmoniously integrated and mutually interpenetrating.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, not being in opposition to the Buddha;
Second, not slandering the Dharma;
third, not treating the assembly with contempt, but always honoring, revering, and serving them.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, to bring rest to greed;
second, to distance oneself from anger;
third, to illuminate and dispel delusion.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, entering into conventional truth;
second, the characteristic of speaking according to ultimate reality.
Third, the non-abiding in ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, not giving rise to contempt or arrogance toward sentient beings;
Second, one should always give rise to respect for arhats;
third, one should not be subdued by afflictions.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, they are not defiled by the desire realm;
second, they do not delight in the form realm;
third, they do not cling to the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, when encountering decline, censure, disparagement, or suffering, the mind does not sink;
second, when encountering gain, praise, fame, or pleasure, the mind does not become elated.
Third, they are unstained by the eight worldly dharmas, remaining as firm and unmoving as a mountain king.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, the concealment of the sense faculties;
Second, being skillful in understanding all fetters;
third, being skillful in disciplining one's own mind.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the merit of establishing the stages;
second, the ability to abandon the faults of the stages;
third, the skillful advancement through each stage.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, the arising of supreme wisdom within the inner mind;
second, the arising of discerning wisdom from the profound mind.
Third, the wisdom that establishes through skillful means.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
