first, having attained purity of concentration, one attains the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Second, having perfected wisdom, one attains the training in higher mind;
third, having perfected liberation, one attains the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, through pleasant feelings, one eliminates craving;
second, through painful feelings, one eliminates aversion;
third, through neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, one eliminates ignorance.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, although one transforms the causes, there is no deliberate application;
second, although one transforms afflictions, there is no conceptual discrimination.
Third, although they transmigrate through the three realms, they harbor no aspirations or cravings.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, to discern emptiness and remain far removed from all views;
Second, the discernment of signlessness and the cessation of applied and sustained thought;
third, the discernment of wishlessness and the quiescence of the three realms.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the eye is empty;
second, the objective realm of forms is devoid of intrinsic nature;
third, visual consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, the emptiness of the ear;
second, the nature of detachment from the objective sphere of sound.
Third, auditory consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas: first, the nose is empty; [the second is... [the third is... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated).
Second, the objective field of fragrance is devoid of intrinsic nature;
third, olfactory consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the tongue is empty;
second, the objective realm of flavors lacks inherent nature;
third, the gustatory consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, the emptiness of the body;
second, the detachment from the nature of sensory objects.
Third, the body-consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas: first, the emptiness of the mind; [the second is the emptiness of the body; the third is the emptiness of consciousness].
Second, the objective realm of phenomena is devoid of intrinsic nature;
third, the mental consciousness has no abiding place.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the secret cultivation of ethical discipline;
second, the skillful protection of meditative concentration;
third, the definitive discernment of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, cultivating mindfulness to uphold the True Dharma;
second, cultivating wisdom through profound and firm investigation.
Third, practicing and fully awakening to the meaning of conduct.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, abiding in accordance with the noble truths of the śrāvakas and preaching the dharma of liberation within their sounds;
Second, he teaches the Dharma of liberation while abiding in accordance with the dependent origination of the pratyekabuddhas;
third, he teaches the Dharma of liberation while abiding in accordance with the various supreme practices of the bodhisattva’s six pāramitās.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, relinquishment, which means relinquishing all precious treasures;
second, great relinquishment, which means relinquishing one’s wife, children, slaves, and retinue.
Third is ultimate relinquishment, which means giving away parts of one's body, such as the head, eyes, hands, and feet.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, upholding and protecting the True Dharma;
Second, to protect and uphold all Dharma-preachers;
third, to protect and uphold the Mahāyāna teachings.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, not allowing birth and death to continue in succession;
second, awakening to the faults of birth and death;
third, distancing oneself from the karmic offenses of birth and death.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, listening to and receiving the true Dharma with a mind free from hindrances;
second, constantly sitting in meditative seclusion with a mind free from latent tendencies.
Third, one is able to practice correctly with a mind of renunciation.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, to rely on the meaning of what has been heard;
Second, observation based on wisdom;
third, liberation based on the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, being learned and delighting in dwelling in tranquility;
second, having dwelt in tranquility, applying the mind with deep firmness;
third, through such application of the mind with deep firmness, being able to realize the equality of all phenomena.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, to revere those who possess wisdom;
second, to inquire of those who have heard much.
Third, protecting those who cultivate meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, not practicing the gift of Dharma with a mind seeking personal gain;
Second, to embrace those who listen to the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness;
third, to manifest all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā-citta) in all present actions.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, because the mind is equal, sentient beings are equal;
second, because there is no diversity of natures, all phenomena are equal;
third, because wisdom is equal, all Buddhas are equal.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, wisdom (*jñāna*), which knows the equality of the three periods of time;
second, insight (*prajñā*), which understands the equality of the three gates of liberation.
Third, to clearly realize and awaken to the equality of the three realms.
Furthermore, there are three further dharmas:
first, to skillfully contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and also suffering.
Second, skillfully contemplating that all phenomena are without self;
third, skillfully contemplating the tranquility of nirvana.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, the vow is true because it abides in the ultimate;
second, that which has been heard is true through practice according to the principle;
third, samādhi is true because it gives rise to transcendent wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, not concealing sins already committed;
second, preventing uncommitted sins from arising.
Third, to cause all present transgressions to be repented of and extinguished.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, to remain far removed from regretful remorse.
Second, being free from latent tendencies;
third, being free from doubt.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, delighting in dwelling in tranquility;
second, being free from craving and attachment;
third, giving rise to the desire for wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, abiding in the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti);
second, expounding various teachings; [and third, ...].
Third, attaining the eloquence of thorough penetration in all places.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, the definitive retention of all that is heard;
Second, attaining the eloquence empowered by the Buddhas;
third, having all the teachings one expounds protected by the noble ones.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
First, from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one is as level and even as the earth;
second, all practices are brought to ultimate completion and these practices continue in succession;
third, although one transforms all conceptual perceptions, one dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, the perfection of the patience resulting from hearing;
second, the patience resulting from reflection that does not dissipate.
Third, they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that cause the Great Vehicle to increase:
first, practicing all paths through the harmonious union of skillful means and wisdom;
Second, through the union of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they bring sentient beings to maturity;
third, through the union of diligence and heedfulness, they protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Samudramati!
These three dharmas are able to increase the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute obstacles and hindrances within the Mahāyāna."
What are these four?
First, evil learning, which refers to seeking out the texts of non-Buddhist paths;
second, having no inclination to listen to or receive the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the six pāramitās.
Third, through an arrogant mind, they give rise to various demonic activities;
fourth, being pursued by karmic obstructions, they slander the true Dharma.
Samudramati!
These four dharmas constitute obstacles and difficulties within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas that constitute obstacles and difficulties within the Mahāyāna.
What are these four?
First, craving;
second, hatred; third, delusion.
Fourth, when afflictions increase and overflow, one does not seek the merit of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, envying others for their gains; [and so forth].
Second, they associate with Dharma teachers through deceit and crookedness;
third, they give rise to sharp and clever intelligence to practice deception while appearing to provide benefit;
fourth, they act with fraud by means of an insincere mind.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, conceiving the notion of an evil friend toward a virtuous friend;
second, conceiving the notion of a virtuous friend toward an evil friend.
Third, conceiving the notion of true Dharma regarding what is not the Dharma;
fourth, conceiving the notion of what is not the Dharma regarding the true Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, constantly giving rise to a mind defiled by stinginess;
second, immediately giving rise to a mind characterized by the fault of malice upon seeing a beggar;
third, giving rise to a mind of regret after having given.
Fourth, they give rise to a mind that turns its back on omniscience.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, they practice giving with a desirous mind;
Second, giving with a mind of fault-finding;
third, giving with a mind of fear;
fourth, giving with a mind of delusion.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, giving for the sake of seeking reputation;
second, giving for the sake of seeking fine praise.
Third, giving for the sake of seeking a good reputation;
fourth, giving for the sake of seeking praise.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, giving out of worldly sentiments and obligations;
second, giving for the sake of some specific purpose;
third, giving without making it manifest.
Fourth, not giving with one's own hands.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, giving coarse things;
Second, giving without regard for its value;
third, giving without reverence;
fourth, giving with overweening pride.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, giving with a sharp blade;
second, giving with poison.
Third, giving the Dharma in an improper manner;
fourth, giving with a harmful mind.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, conceiving a mind of anger toward those who uphold the precepts;
second, giving rise to a mind of harm and a lack of protection toward those who break the precepts;
third, one's own cultivated precepts being constantly confused and disordered.
Fourth, conceiving thoughts of killing toward those who recite the precepts.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, being fond of seeking wealth and profit through hardship;
Second, if one obtains the benefits of the Dharma, one does not withhold them from others;
third, one does not desire the gains and offerings obtained by others;
fourth, one does not give rise to contentment with the gains one has received for oneself.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, crookedness of body, which is contrary to dignified deportment;
second, crookedness of speech, wherein what is said is not truthful.
Third, a crooked mind that desires to commit various transgressions;
fourth, being crooked in all matters because one does not sustain oneself through a pure livelihood.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, giving rise to a mind of anger toward those who dwell together in the Mahāyāna;
second, being unable to discern the activities of Māra due to overweening pride;
and third, immediately delighting in practicing what has not been correctly taught upon hearing it.
Fourth, they feel vexation upon hearing an exposition of various virtuous merits.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, being arrogant toward the True Dharma and unable to draw near to it;
Second, they do not give rise to respect for the Dharma-preacher;
third, they do not develop reverence toward their parents, elders, or preceptors;
fourth, their bodies and minds are stubborn and wild, such that all their actions are constantly in opposition [to the Dharma].
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, extolling one's own virtues;
second, concealing the virtues of others.
Third, the blazing of pride;
fourth, stubborn and fierce anger.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, laziness; second, lethargy;
third, lack of rectitude.
Fourth is attachment.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, lack of self-discipline;
Second, lack of tranquility;
third, lack of secrecy;
fourth, lack of gentleness and goodness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, entering cities, towns, and villages with little learning;
second, seeking gain and offerings while not being fully endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline.
Third, entering the houses of women without guarding one's physical deportment;
fourth, not abiding in a state of meditative equipoise while discerning and entering into the root dispositions of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, being unable to diligently practice the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu);
second, abandoning the maturation of sentient beings.
Third, slandering the true Dharma and failing to provide its protection;
fourth, giving rise to vexation toward those who preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, being deluded, they constantly give rise to much desire;
second, being full of hatred, they delight in committing various transgressions;
third, being possessed by craving, they do not give rise to contentment.
Fourth, the mind seeking profit is never satiated.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, lack of faith accompanied by constant restlessness;
Second, associating with evil friends and not abandoning sinful deeds;
third, being indolent and causing wholesome dharmas to decline and vanish;
fourth, being heedless and thereby losing all roots of goodness that have been cultivated.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, because one is unable to engage in internal observation, one is constantly devoid of shame;
second, because one's wisdom and understanding are not clear and lucid, one is constantly devoid of remorse.
Third, because they are equal to those who commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), they do not recognize kindness;
fourth, although they perform even small acts of benefit for others, they destroy them through self-aggrandizement and instead give rise to slander.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, anger; second, resentment;
[third, hostility; fourth, malice].
Third, resentment;
fourth, malice. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, deceiving the noble ones;
second, failing to protect the noble ones;
third, treating donors with contempt.
Fourth, they give rise to overweening pride toward arhats.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, their physical actions cannot be purified;
Second, they are unable to properly guard their verbal karma;
third, their mental karma is defiled;
fourth, they give rise to weariness toward the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, to engage in divisive speech within a gathering;
second, to utter harsh words toward one's teachers and ācāryas.
Third, engaging in frivolous speech toward those who come seeking [help];
fourth, deceiving humans and devas.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, failing to protect the aggregate of ethical discipline;
second, not transcending to future lives;
third, losing and dispersing one's roots of goodness.
Fourth, destroying the cultivation of superior practices.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, giving rise to a mind of competitiveness within the great assembly;
Second, maintaining a mind of arrogance in assemblies;
third, constantly uttering harsh words while wishing to distance oneself from transgressions;
fourth, expounding worldly treatises with confused and incoherent speech.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, dwelling in a quiet place with a mind that lacks diligent practice;
second, dwelling amidst bustle and clamor with a mind full of harm.
Third, not having planted roots of goodness yet conceiving the notion that one possesses merit;
fourth, usurping the name of a bodhisattva to seek profit and sustain one's life.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, the mind is not supple;
second, the mind is coarse and wild;
third, the mind is not disciplined.
Fourth, giving rise to a sense of hardship and distress toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, being arrogant and self-reliant on the observance of precepts;
Second, being conceited and relying on extensive learning;
third, being conceited and relying on dwelling in an araṇya;
fourth, being conceited and relying on the merits of dhūta practices.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, reckoning oneself as superior;
second, reckoning the Dharma as superior.
Third, to consider a small root of goodness as superior and not dedicate it toward Bodhi;
fourth, to have previously practiced the path of the Mahāyāna, yet later take pleasure in the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, attachment to the body;
second, attachment to the mind.
Third, attachment to precepts;
fourth, not directing oneself toward the supreme path.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, begging at the homes of friends and relatives for use in non-household matters;
second, seeking gain and offerings while claiming to be pure, yet taking pleasure in seeing those who break the precepts;
third, being addicted to the pleasures of lay households.
Fourth, to give rise to anger toward those who possess the precepts, and to engage in various entanglements through the hardships one undertakes.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, to engage in many activities;
Second, seeking many profits;
third, engaging in much speech;
fourth, having many acquaintances.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:

first, the view of self and attachment to a self; second, the view of sentient beings and attachment to sentient beings; [third, the view of life and attachment to a life; fourth, the view of a person and attachment to a person].
Third, the attachment to the view of nihilism and the grasping at non-action;
fourth, the attachment to the view of eternalism and the grasping at body and life.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, although one initiates various activities;
second, having initiated them, one is unable to maintain them;
third, because one does not maintain them, weariness and indolence arise.
Fourth, because of indolence and laxity, one gives rise to fear.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, not cultivating the wisdom that ascends through each successive stage (bhūmi).
Second, they are unable to skillfully cultivate meditative concentration;
third, they abandon the supreme wisdom that benefits sentient beings and fail to practice it;
fourth, although they cultivate aspiration and skillful means, they give rise to the notion of attainment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that constitute obstacles and difficulties within the Mahāyāna:
first, the latent tendency of dharma-obstructions combined with dull faculties;
second, the latent tendency of karmic obstructions combined with a lack of diligence in practicing various roots of goodness.
Third, the latent tendencies of the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa-anuśaya) operate in accordance with the three aggregates;
fourth, demonic activities pursue one, causing the loss of the bodhicitta.
Samantamati!
"These four dharmas such as these constitute obstacles and hindrances within the Mahāyāna.
Thus concludes the eleventh fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-vimala-mudrā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*.
Fascicle Twelve.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Fan Translation, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree.

When the World-Honored One spoke these teachings on the "Acceptance of the Mahāyāna" and other dharmas, forty-four thousand sentient beings and one thousand devas within the assembly all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and twenty-eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Then this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great radiance shone widely throughout the ten directions; a thousand devas and humans stood in the air, their voices rising in mutual exhortation as they leaped for joy and circled about.
Furthermore, they rained down various exquisite celestial jewel-flowers, and with the sounds of drums, flutes, and songs, they performed sublime celestial music as an offering.
With wondrous verses, they praised him, saying:
"This most supreme treasury of the Great Dharma, The Tathāgata has today personally revealed."
"Having long since dwelt securely in the mind of great compassion, you have made it clearly manifest for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having spoken this verse, he further said:
"World-Honored One!"

If a person is able to receive and uphold even a very small portion of this great treasury of the Dharma-jewel spoken by the Tathāgata, that person will swiftly be liberated from all terrors of the hells and shall, in due course, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person who, not far from a certain state, city, or village, saw that within a hidden treasure trove in the earth there was an abundance of inexhaustible precious jewels. Because this person possessed a mind intent on benefiting others, upon seeing this, he immediately went into the city and said to the people:
‘Welcome, all of you! If you wish to seek various precious jewels, I know their location; I shall show you the inexhaustible hidden treasury.’”
"World-Honored One!
In that city, there are some people who, although they hear these words, do not believe or accept them.

There are others who believe what is said; they immediately accompany those people to the location of the hidden treasure and, according to their own strength and ability, take as many jewels as they please. Having obtained jewels in accordance with their wisdom and capacity, they return."

However, that hidden treasure is inexhaustible once taken; furthermore, there is no discrimination as to whether this person shall be given it and that person shall not, or whether this person should take it and that person should not.
Why is this? Because this hidden treasure is free from discrimination,
World-Honored One!

The great treasury of the sublime Dharma taught by all Buddhas is likewise so: over incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, the Buddha accumulated such a supreme, vast, and wondrous treasury of the Dharma; having accumulated it, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment to realize the fruit of perfect awakening, and thereafter turned the Great Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī.
Today, the World-Honored One has once again turned this Dharma-assembly of the True Dharma, revealing the unsurpassed great treasury of the Dharma-jewels.
With a mind free from grasping, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, gives rise to the practice of great compassion toward all sentient beings and performs deeds for their benefit.
To those who do not know, he universally proclaims to the devas, humans, asuras, and others with his wondrous Brahma-voice, declaring:

"Come here and receive and uphold this unsurpassed, vast jewel of the Dharma; this Dharma can bring an end to all sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and can bestow all inexhaustible, sublime bliss."
"World-Honored One!

There may be certain individuals who are lacking in faith and are deluded; they do not give rise to resolute understanding toward this True Dharma, nor do they accord with it correctly or discern it, and thus they do not produce faith."

There may be a certain class of faithful individuals who are able to skillfully discern this True Dharma, giving rise to resolute conviction and further engendering right compliance; because they are able to discern it, they develop profound pure faith.
Such persons are then able to take up the Dharma-jewels from the great Dharma-treasury of the Buddha-Tathāgata, according to their capacity and strength.
Having taken the jewels for themselves, they further cause others to develop faith and understanding in those various vehicles and the Dharma of liberation—

some who delight in abiding in the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle, some who delight in abiding in the nature of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and some who delight in abiding in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
However, the unsurpassed and most supreme great Dharma-treasury of the Buddha-Tathāgata is inexhaustible and free from discrimination.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,

although this unsurpassed great Dharma-treasury has been thus extensively opened, revealed, and displayed, there are sentient beings who are unable to take even a small portion, or even a very slight fraction, of this Dharma-treasure.
Because these people do not obtain the treasure, they shall wander through the three evil realms for a long night without end.
World-Honored One!

If there should be another person who, regarding this unsurpassed great Dharma-treasury, can even briefly receive and uphold a single four-line stanza, that person will be fully endowed with the seven kinds of noble wealth and shall not be destitute; how much more so for one who can, within this vast assembly of the True Dharma, briefly believe in and uphold even a single chapter, or two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, up to seventy chapters, or even until the very end, being able to receive and uphold it—the merit obtained by such a person is beyond measure.
Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate is not separate from the bodhicitta, and because it is impelled by the arousal of great compassion for all sentient beings.

Therefore, one should know that if a person can give rise to a pure mind and receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain it to others, that person shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, shall sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and subdue all Māras, and shall attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) within the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the sons of the gods, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
O assembly of sons of the gods!"
"You have spoken well.

You should know that those who are able to properly uphold, recite, and develop resolute understanding of this True Dharma, and who practice according to the principle, will establish all the most sublime merits of speech;
such persons shall reach the pinnacle of omniscience."

Furthermore, he knows that this person will extensively act as a light of wisdom for all the world, illuminating it everywhere, and will soon proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Why is this? Because they are able to mount and drive this Great Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Having established this most supreme, vast vehicle of the Buddhas—
like the radiance of space, for it transcends all worlds—
one departs from the three realms of existence and proceeds to the site of enlightenment.”
Free from that mind of attachment, having already abandoned all fetters and clinging;
through vast and pure teachings accumulated over millions of eons,
the gates of generosity, discipline, and tranquility cause the inner mind to become firm and stable.
Through the precepts, one restrains all transgressions, And body and mind attain purity;
Free from all fearful thoughts, One proceeds to the site of enlightenment.
With a mind and intention of equanimity, One embraces all sentient beings.
Surpassing all other vehicles— namely the various lower vehicles—
he enters this Mahāyāna Dharma to bring joy to sentient beings;
he erects high the great banner of the Dharma and controls his divine feet like a horse.
Hearing the Dharma with continuous diligence, taking meditative concentration as one’s seat,
attaining the power of patience, and receiving the empowerment of great wisdom;
having subdued all external factions and shattered the armies of Māra.
They proceed to the site of pure enlightenment and advance toward the Mahāyāna Dharma.
With a compassionate mind as their armor, they cannot be destroyed by enmity or evil;
practicing steadfast great compassion, they advance toward the profound principle of the Dharma.
The four dhyānas and the four bases of psychic power, Riding upon the practice of the four immeasurables,
Taming and governing the bodhicitta, Without abandoning any of the true paths.
Throughout the boundless ten directions, Across the entire realm of sentient beings;
All within this Mahāyāna, they ride and advance upon it.
There is neither suffering nor pleasure; there is neither decrease nor increase.
Within this supreme Buddha-vehicle, such spiritual powers are fully possessed.
One practices the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the four right efforts;
the same applies to the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
As the Buddha has praised and taught, one is endowed with the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Wandering upon the Eightfold Noble Path, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment.
Having stilled all afflictions and perfected the radiance of the Dharma,
he shattered all darkness and dust, manifesting himself beyond the three realms of existence.
By the power of their spiritual transformations, they can universally summon Śakra, Brahmā, and the rest;
may you each skillfully govern this peerless Mahāyāna.
The various pāramitās—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—
Through the gates of diligence and meditative concentration, The power of supreme wisdom and spiritual faculties,
And those practices of skillful means, As well as the true vows they encompass—
Even if hundreds of thousands of demonic armies were to arise, All of these could be utterly subdued.
Sentient beings who violate the precepts diligently create various sinful karmas;
Exalted and supreme Bodhisattvas accumulate manifold merits.
If the various states of mind that arise are the vast bodhicitta;
Those who are able to master the Mahāyāna can fully observe all worldly treatises,
their various meanings and practices, as well as the supramundane, true, and virtuous dharmas.
Those in training and those beyond training, the Pratyekabuddhas and all the noble ones;
those who abide in the Buddha-vehicle—all enter their respective gates.
Whether it be various afflictions or various mental activities;
All sentient beings afflicted by suffering, revolving within the realm of conditioned existence—
those who abide in the Buddha Vehicle, the Bodhisattvas are able to observe them all;
they cause them to cease their suffering and proceed toward the ultimate vehicle.
Furthermore, those who are indolent, weak,
and lacking in power are unable to direct their minds toward the end of the suffering of all sentient beings.
Having heard the Mahāyāna, such fear arises in their hearts.
Seeking only the causes of one’s own happiness, one performs no deeds for the benefit of others.
But if there is a Bodhisattva of great wisdom who possesses clear understanding and great power,
and whose strength of diligence is fully perfected, they constantly bring benefit to sentient beings.
Practicing the skillful means of great compassion, with an inner nature that is pure;
because they ride upon the Supreme Vehicle, their minds are filled with joy.
Throughout all worlds, they engage in infinite and diverse activities.
The distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, as well as their faculties and inclinations—
by means of this supreme vehicle, the Bodhisattvas endowed with great wisdom are able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings in a single instant.
The body attains the marks and signs of excellence, adorning all its parts;
from the speech issues a delightful and beautiful sound, which all who hear find joy in.
The mind attains purity, endowed with meditative concentration and supernormal powers.
By riding upon the Supreme Vehicle, one attains vast merit.
This most supreme Buddha-vehicle is heard throughout the three realms;
thus, for all Buddhas, the noble Buddha-eye remains uninterrupted.
They increase the supreme eye, namely the blazing Dharma-eye;
transcending the multitudes of the triple world, they are the Arhats.
This vehicle is pure and subtle, and does not fall into the defiled lands.
When Bodhisattvas ride this vehicle, they behold all Buddhas in an instant;
having traveled through the worlds of the ten directions, they feel neither fatigue nor diminution.
Behold this peerless vehicle—such are its miraculous transformations.
The Great Being who rides the Buddha-vehicle travels throughout all worlds;
though one seeks a superior or an equal, neither can be found.
This world’s sole hero is the Bodhisattva of great majestic power.
By mounting the Supreme Vehicle, one can terrify the hosts of Māra’s armies;
one obtains physical strength, majesty, and power, as well as vast wealth;
or one becomes Śakra, Brahmā, a Wheel-turning King, a World-Protector, and so forth.
Even up to the gods and humans, they obtain the pleasures of these three realms;
by riding the Supreme Vehicle, they are fully endowed with wondrous bliss.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is neither haughty nor humble;
They are able to give away all that is dear, and having given, they do not seek recompense.
With a joyful and compassionate mind, they even give their own head and eyes;
because they ride upon the Supreme Vehicle and dedicate [the merit] toward Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva upholds the pure precepts, or is fully endowed with the holy life;
the pure radiance of these prohibitive precepts shines forth more brilliantly than the sun and moon.
Regarding physical appearance and worldly prosperity, he harbors no desire for them at all.
Riding upon the Supreme Vehicle, for the sake of rescuing and delivering sentient beings,
when a Bodhisattva hears harsh words, they feel neither anger nor resentment;
even if their body were to be shattered to pieces, they would still protect all living creatures.
This body is easily obtained, but encountering a Dharma King is extremely difficult;
by riding the Supreme Vehicle, one attains this purity of patience.
For countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the Bodhisattva has [practiced].
Cycling through the miserable realms, They wander within the world of birth and death.
Generating the power of great diligence To rescue and deliver sentient beings;
By means of the Supreme Vehicle, The power of diligence is perfected.
The Bodhisattva attains tranquility, And experiences soft, sublime bliss;
Knowing the qualities of meditative concentration, He gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness.
Within this state, there is not the slightest Attachment to the flavor of the joy of dhyāna.
Through mere recollection and aspiration, one attains the vision of all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and are empty;
as for self, dharmas, and sentient beings, none of them can be apprehended.
All views are thoroughly purified, and the mind is subdued by supreme wisdom;
by means of the Supreme Vehicle, this sublime wisdom is purified.
All the Four Noble Truths, the four immeasurables, and the four meditative concentrations—
As well as the five kinds of supernormal knowledge, the four analytical insights, and so forth;
among the four means of integration, the gift of Dharma is supreme.
Such gateways of merit all emerge from the Buddha Vehicle.
All the ten powers and other Boundless qualities of the Buddha-dharma;
The Buddha, the lion among men, Preaches the Dharma like his roar.
From between his brows and from his mouth, And from the invisible crown of his head, he emits light.
By riding upon the Supreme Vehicle, Bodhisattvas do not find it difficult to attain.
The Buddhas possess three kinds of most excellent and great supernormal powers;
they subdue the world and illuminate all minds and intentions.
The Dharma taught by all Buddhas brings fruits and benefits that are never in vain;
by means of the Supreme Vehicle, one swiftly attains them all.
The Buddha’s words are consistent with their meaning, untainted and free from fault.
The *kiṃnara*’s Brahma-voice is soft, beautiful, and delightful;
it universally encompasses the various worldly sounds and the speech of all sentient beings.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s wondrous voice, everyone is filled with joy.
Before long, the Bodhisattvas shall obtain such sounds of the Buddha’s speech;
throughout the entirety of the Buddha-fields, which are equal to space, all shall be made manifest.
Universally they shall be able to hear the words that accord with the meaning of the Dharma.
When sentient beings hear this, they all rejoice, and their afflictions are entirely eliminated.
Even if one were to use supernatural powers to reach the very edge of space,
one might even be able to know the measure of the waters in the oceans of the ten directions.
"The conduct of boundless sentient beings, He knows even in a single moment of mind;
Only the Buddha’s Supreme Vehicle— Its merits can never be fully told.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:
“Sāgaramati! Therefore, you should know this:
if there are bodhisattvas who wish to secretly protect and uphold such a vast and sublime Dharma so that it may endure for a long time;”

Once one's own mind is purified, one should uphold the meaning of these words: that one is able to fully know all the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and individuals.
These are the so-called gate-phrase, the seal-phrase, and the vajra-phrase.

Having received and upheld them, one understands them according to their meaning, accords with them through wisdom, and investigates them with the most excellent skillful means in accordance with reality.
Sāgaramati! What is called a "gate-word" (dvārapada)?
It refers to the gates of all designations (prajñapti), which express the meaning of the differentiation of all phenomena (dharma).
The letter A-gate signifies that all phenomena are unarisen;
the letter Pa-gate signifies that all phenomena are the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
the letter Na-gate signifies that all phenomena are understood through the names and forms (nāma-rūpa).
The syllable NA represents the meaning that all phenomena are tamed and quiescent;
the syllable SA represents the meaning that all phenomena transcend all attachments;
the syllable TA represents the meaning that all phenomena abide in accordance with suchness.
The gateway of the letter KA signifies that all phenomena are fully understood in terms of the meaning of karmic retribution;
furthermore, the gateway of the letter SA signifies that all phenomena are equal and without distinction;
the gateway of the letter MA signifies that all phenomena are the meaning of great compassion.
The gateway of the syllable Ga signifies that all phenomena are most profoundly deep and difficult to fathom to their source;
the gateway of the syllable Ja signifies that all phenomena transcend old age and death;
the gateway of the syllable Dha signifies that all phenomena are non-discriminative within the dharmadhātu.
The syllable-gateway "Śa" represents the meaning that all phenomena are the perfection of śamatha;
the syllable-gateway "Kha" represents the meaning that all phenomena are the radiant clarity of emptiness;
the syllable-gateway "Cha" represents the meaning that all phenomena are universally exhausted and non-arising.
The syllable-door *nya* signifies that all phenomena are characterized by wisdom free from attachment;
the syllable-door *tha* signifies that all phenomena are well understood in terms of what is possible and what is impossible;
the syllable-door *ṣka* signifies that all phenomena are fully understood as the aggregates (*skandha*).
The gateway of the syllable *ccha* signifies that all phenomena are ultimately without limit;
the gateway of the tranquility of body signifies that all phenomena are free from attachment and defilement;
the gateway of the tranquility of mind signifies that all phenomena have subdued anger and delusion.
The gate of cessation signifies that all phenomena converge upon the meaning of non-attachment;
the gate of profound stability signifies that all phenomena transcend the three periods of time;
the gate of abiding in true nature signifies that all phenomena abide within the dharma-realm.
The gate of non-appropriation signifies the meaning of the liberation of all phenomena;
the gate of non-attachment signifies the meaning of all phenomena being free from contention;
the gate of non-defilement signifies the meaning of the purity of all phenomena.
The gate of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) signifies the meaning that all phenomena are primordially luminous and pure;
the gate of wondrous radiance signifies the meaning that all phenomena are brilliantly manifest;
the gate of contemplative visualization (*bhāvanā*) signifies the meaning that all phenomena are free from dispersion.
The gate of non-concealment signifies the meaning of the non-combination of all phenomena;
the gate of bodhi signifies the meaning of the equal single flavor of all phenomena;
the gate of nirvāṇa signifies the meaning of all phenomena being free from all afflictions.
Sāgaramati!

One who can receive and uphold such gateways and phrases will attain purity of their own mind, and thereafter be able to fully discern the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and individuals.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
What is called a 'seal-word' (mudrā-pada)?
It refers to that which is sealed by the seal of liberation of all phenomena."
Dharmas are fundamentally non-dual, because duality is pure.
All dharmas are sealed by the seal of neither limit nor boundlessness, because both the extremes of annihilation and permanence are pure.
All dharmas are sealed by the seal of being entirely free from craving, because within the gateway of exhaustion and the limit of exhaustion, there is neither exhaustion nor boundless limits.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of being neither high nor low, because the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of equality is pure.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of being like space, because they transcend the path of the five eyes.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of abiding in space, for the dharma-realm is itself the realm of space.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of non-discrimination, for the dharma-realm is characterized by mutual penetration.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of the dharma-realm, for phenomena possess no characteristic of discrimination.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of suchness, for they are as they truly are throughout the past and future limits.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because they are primordially pure.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because conditioned things are equal.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of signlessness (*animitta*), because they are far removed from all differentiated objects of cognition.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of wishlessness, for they are free from all seeking.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of impermanence, for their intrinsic nature is non-existent and signless.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of suffering, because the five aggregates are characterized by their well-accumulated nature.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of selflessness, because their intrinsic nature is devoid of self.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of tranquility, for they are ultimately immovable.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of truth, for they are universally subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of immovability, because their seeds have no abiding place.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of indestructibility, because they are ultimately and definitively settled.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of suchness (*tathatā*), because there is no interruption between the prior and subsequent limits.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of the equality of the three times, because they are of a single flavor in all places.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of non-arising, because their intrinsic nature is non-existent.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of non-cessation, because their intrinsic nature is unarisen.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of mutual non-dependence, because they are free from overweening pride.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of non-proliferation, because all discursive thoughts and investigations are without accumulation.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of clarity and signlessness, for they cannot be represented by any marks of form.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of non-defilement, for their basis has been severed.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of non-accomplishment, because their antidotes are unapprehendable.
All phenomena are sealed with the seal of non-karmic retribution, because all are without volitional construction.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for they are entirely free from all states of arising and ceasing.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*), for all phenomena are equal to space and entirely without distinction.
Sāgaramati!
These are called the words of the seals (*mudrā-pada*).
These words of the seals are the seals of the awakening of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
From these seal-words, all eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma arise.

These seal-words universally encompass the supreme wisdom-seals of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through which one swiftly realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Sāgaramati!
Such seal-words as these cannot be heard by any sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness;
furthermore, this Dharma-gate is well able to subdue all demonic activities.
Sāgaramati!
All the inexhaustible jewel caskets of dhāraṇī are able to contain and encompass all those dharmas; these dharmas all emerge from the phrases of the seals.

Furthermore, the eighty-four thousand gateways of samādhi, the universal entry into the mental activities of eighty-four thousand sentient beings, and the thousand gateways of pāramitās all emerge from such seal-words (mudrā-pada), and these seal-words likewise enter into each and every one of those dharma-gateways.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Number Twelve.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Number Thirteen.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Translation Institute, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, and Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Venerable Weijing and others, by imperial decree: "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!..."
What is the vajra-word?
It is that one's own body is the vajra-word, because its intrinsic nature is non-conceptual. Samudramati!
This vajra phrase functions as a definitive discernment among all views.
Ignorance is a vajra phrase, because it enters into all forms of knowledge.
This vajra phrase functions through the thorough knowledge of the objects of perception.
The limit of the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*) is a vajra phrase, because it is equal to the absence of application (*anabhisamskāra*).
This vajra phrase functions through the thorough knowledge of all applications.
The limit of desire (*rāga*) is a vajra phrase, because it is equal to the limit of freedom from desire.
This vajra phrase functions with equanimity toward desire and freedom from desire.
The limit of hatred is a vajra phrase, because it is equal to the limit of loving-kindness.
This vajra phrase shatters all forms of hatred.
The limit of delusion (*moha-paryanta*) is a vajra-phrase, because the radiance of wisdom is equal.
This vajra-phrase reveals and clarifies luminous wisdom.
That all sentient beings are one sentient being is a vajra-phrase, because it penetrates the equality of all sentient beings.
This vajra phrase awakens to the self-nature of sentient beings.
The mind of all sentient beings is the mind of a single sentient being; this is a vajra phrase, for it enters into the state of no-mind.
This vajra phrase is that which accords with the realization that the self-nature of the mind is originally luminous and transparent.
"All Buddhas are one Buddha" is a vajra phrase, because they universally enter into the equality of suchness.
This vajra phrase is the realization of the wisdom of equality.
All buddha-fields are one buddha-field; this is a vajra phrase, because it pervades all inexhaustible fields.
This vajra phrase is known to accord with the equality of space.
That all dharmas are a single dharma is a vajra phrase, because it enters into the equality of the nature of all dharmas.
This vajra phrase is understood accordingly as the dharma-gate of non-duality.
That all phenomena are Buddha-dharmas is a vajra phrase, because wisdom enters into and understands them in every respect.
This vajra phrase is that which realizes the vajra-like samādhi.
That the activities of Māras are the activities of all Buddhas is a vajra phrase, because by entering into the activities of Māras, one is awakened accordingly.
This vajra phrase transcends all activities of Māra.
All speech that is the speech of the Tathāgata is a vajra phrase, because it universally enters all sounds and is understood accordingly.
This vajra phrase is to be understood as the ineffable nature of phenomena.
That all phenomena are unborn is a vajra phrase, because they enter into non-extinction.
This vajra phrase transcends the path of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
That all phenomena are without arising is a vajra phrase, for they enter into non-ceasing.
This vajra phrase is able to accord with and turn toward the quiescence of all phenomena.
"Sāgaramati!..."
These various vajra-words are words that are indestructible; they are words of sublime excellence;
they are words of equality; they are words of the noble truths; they are words of firmness; they are words of non-differentiation;
they are words of delight; they are words of non-interruption; they are words of tranquility, universal tranquility, and proximate tranquility.
This is the phrase of non-action; this is the phrase of non-conjunction; this is the phrase of entering the destinationless destination; this is the phrase of non-practice;
this is the phrase of true nature; this is the phrase of suchness; this is the phrase of not turning away from the Buddha;
this is the phrase of not slandering the Dharma; this is the phrase of not breaking the Saṃgha; this is the phrase of being as it has been taught.
These are the phrases of the purity of the three wheels; they are the phrases of valor; they are the phrases of the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

they are the phrases of emptiness and stillness; they are the phrases of space; they are the phrases of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); they are the phrases of signlessness (*animitta*); they are the phrases of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*);
they are the phrases of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); they are the phrases of the non-abiding of mind, thought, and consciousness; they are the phrases for subduing all Māras.
The phrase of the non-Buddhists is the phrase of purity, stainlessness, and lucidity; it is the phrase of the contemplation of bodhi; it is the phrase of the light of wisdom;
it is the phrase of the non-manifestation of phenomena; it is the phrase of ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing;
it is the phrase of the purity of one’s own realm; it is the phrase of entering the realm of the Buddha; it is the phrase of non-conceptualization.
Discrimination and pervasive conceptualization are themselves the phrase of the non-differentiation of the dharma-realm;
they are the phrase of the phrase that enters into no-phrase. Samudrareṇu!

If there are bodhisattvas who, according to their capacity, can receive and discern the meaning of such supreme and wondrous vajra phrases as these, I declare that such persons will certainly sit at the site of enlightenment and let out the lion’s roar.

When the Blessed One spoke these words—these phrases of the gate, phrases of the seal, and phrases of the vajra—eight thousand bodhisattvas within this assembly attained the *dhāraṇī* of the seal that enters the gates of all phenomena, as well as the samādhi of universally entering the mental dispositions of all sentient beings.

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions leaped for joy and felt great delight in their hearts. Each, by means of their own supernatural power, returned to the various Buddha-fields from which they had come; from each of those fields, they brought with them all manner of flower garlands, unguents, and powdered incense.

Within this assembly, they rained down a vast abundance of various exquisite flower garlands, incense, and other offerings, universally presenting them as an offering to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and to this True Dharma, with the aspiration that this True Dharma may long abide in the world.
Having made these offerings, all those bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison to praise the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:
“Displaying formlessness within the marks of form, The Great Sage Honored One is the single mark apart from all marks;
All marks are equal, being the markless mark— We bow our heads to you who abide in the reality-mark.”
Pervading the speech of all sentient beings, Entering their sounds with wisdom that follows along;
The gate of liberation through all sounds— I bow my head to the liberation of the equanimous mind.
The various mental activities of the world are like illusions, for the mind has nothing to perceive;
there is no practice, no equal practice, and no place of practice—I pay homage to the empty mind, clearly manifest.
Existence and non-existence are equal; extremes and non-extremes, phenomena and the discrimination of phenomena are free from discrimination.
All minds and mental factors are fundamentally quiescent; I now prostrate to the one whose mind is tranquil.
The Buddha knows the functioning of all causes and conditions; the Buddha can proclaim all causal practices.
Within the primordial limit of liberation from causes and conditions, the Buddha knows that the reality-limit is truly equal.
Now, this universal entry into the mark of equality— I observe that the body of the Sugata is no-body;
Since it cannot be distinguished as a body with marks, It manifests various sublime characteristics of differentiation.
All the Buddha-fields of the ten directions enter entirely into this Buddha-field;
yet this Buddha-field does not increase, nor do those fields move or diminish.
All minds are equal; mind is no-mind. The illusory mind is without difference or discrimination;
Thoroughly understanding the equal Bodhicitta, The World-Honored One constantly practices the Dharma of equality.
The dharma-realm merges with the realm of equality; all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and can be entered therein.
Their nature is eternally equal amidst both defilement and purity; I pay homage to the benefactor of the world.
The sun and moon may yet be made to fall to earth; The formless wind may likewise be bound;
Mount Sumeru may be blown away like dust— But the Buddha, the World-Honored One, never speaks falsely.
The language of truth is fundamentally pure; with a mind as empty as space, it is luminously radiant.
Worldly dharmas and craving do not stain the mind; like a lotus, it remains unstained while dwelling within the three realms of existence.
Hearing praise, they feel no joy; hearing slander, they feel no anger.
Immovable like Mount Sumeru, I pay homage to the one who bestows happiness upon the world.
At that time, after those assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world, it is the emergence of a treasure;
because the Buddha has appeared in the world, it is the emergence of bliss;
it is the emergence of mindfulness, wisdom, conduct, and knowledge.
It is the emergence of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and supreme wisdom;
it is the emergence of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
it is the emergence of the ultimate truth.
It is the emergence of the ultimate truth;
it is the emergence of the true Dharma;
it is the emergence of the Dharma that is to be realized.
Therein emerge the dharmas of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
therein emerges śamatha; and therein emerges vipaśyanā.
That is to say, they emerge through the six supernormal powers, the three clarities, and the eight liberations.
To state it briefly: they emerge by severing all unwholesome dharmas and gathering all wholesome dharmas.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Prajñākūṭa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it is because the view of a self-body arises that a Buddha appears in the world;”
Because ignorance and craving arise, the Buddha appears in the world;
because greed, hatred, and delusion arise, the Buddha appears in the world;

and because the four perversions, the five hindrances, the six sense bases, the seven stations of consciousness, the eight wrong paths, the nine bases of affliction, and the ten unwholesome courses of action arise, the Buddha appears in the world.
Why is this? It is for the sake of severing all unwholesome karma of all sentient beings that a Buddha appears in the world.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses neither a counteragent nor a power of superiority; it is precisely because there is nothing to be countered that a Buddha appears in the world.
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas wish to know the causes for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world, they should understand them in this way and train themselves accordingly.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is so, it is so!
Just as you have said, one should know and practice accordingly when a Buddha appears in the world.”
"Because the appearance of a Buddha in the world is due to such causes, one should know that the appearance of all phenomena in the world is likewise.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

When those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds hear this teaching on the causes for a Buddha’s appearance in the world, because they do not understand it, they wonder: "How can it be that a Buddha appears in the world in such a way?"
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!
Because a Buddha appears in the world, the minds of all bodhisattvas attain purification according to their respective capacities.”
Why is this so? Samudrareṇu,
you should know that there are four kinds of bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
First, the bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment;
second, the bodhisattva at the stage of practice.
Third, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas;
fourth, bodhisattvas in their final birth before buddhahood.
Samudramati!
Among these four types of bodhisattvas, those who have first resolved their minds attain purity of mind by contemplating the physical marks and adornments of the Buddha-Tathāgata;
those at the stage of practice attain purity of mind by contemplating the Buddha-Tathāgata’s accomplishment of all supreme and wondrous merits;
and those who are non-retrogressive attain purity of mind by contemplating the Buddha’s Dharma-body.

If one is a Bodhisattva in their final birth before Buddhahood, they do not contemplate the physical marks and adornments of the Buddha, nor do they contemplate the Buddha’s lineage or clan, nor do they contemplate the merits accomplished by the Buddha; within this, there is absolutely nothing that can be observed as a dharma.
Why is this? Because of the illumination of wisdom-observation;
because of the power of the eye of wisdom.
Because it is encompassed by wisdom;
because wisdom is without activity;
and because it is free from all conceptual proliferation.
He does not contemplate in such a manner, yet it is not that he lacks contemplation. Why is this?

"The view of existence" and "the view of non-existence" constitute two extremes; the Bodhisattva at this stage remains free from these two extremes regarding both view and non-view, and thus contemplates the Buddha.
Because one contemplates the Buddha in this manner, one likewise contemplates the body.
Having contemplated the purity of the body, one then contemplates the purity of the Buddha.
Having contemplated the purity of the Buddha, one should know that all phenomena are likewise pure.
If, within such contemplation, one is pure, this is called the contemplation of wisdom.
This is precisely what is meant by the true contemplation of the Buddha. "Sāgaramati!..."

Because of this, in the past I beheld the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara; having seen him at that time, I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) as well as the patience corresponding to non-apprehension (anupalambha-yukta-kṣānti).

Immediately, he surged upward into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees; dwelling in mid-air, he attained the undifferentiated power of the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), forever severing all views and transcending all thought, discrimination, and conceptual construction, so that his mind no longer dwells upon any objective realm.
At that time, I further attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi; therefore, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"When that Buddha was bestowing the prophecy, my faculty of hearing was without obstruction, nor was there anything apprehended by any other consciousness.

Amidst this harmonious convergence of perception, I dwelt nowhere. At that time, I had no notion of a Buddha nor the concept of 'Buddha'; I had no notion of a self nor the concept of 'self'; likewise, I had no notion of the prophecy nor the concept of 'prophecy'."
Sāgaramati! For this reason, when a bodhisattva’s three spheres are pure, they receive the prediction of attaining buddhahood.

As for the purity of the three spheres, it means there is no Buddha nor the perception of a Buddha; no self nor the perception of a self; and likewise, no prediction nor the perception of a prediction.
Sāgaramati!
Furthermore, there are three purities of the wheels.
What are these three?
That is to say: there is no grasping at a self, no grasping at sentient beings, and no grasping at phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the purity of the three spheres:
namely, no grasping at names, no grasping at forms and characteristics, and no grasping at objects of perception.
Furthermore, there are three purities of the wheels:
namely, the knowledge that the past has already ceased, the knowledge that the future has not yet arrived, and the knowledge that the present abides within the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there are three purities of the wheels:
This refers to the wisdom that the body is like a reflection, the wisdom that speech is like an echo, and the wisdom that the mind is like an illusion.
Furthermore, there are the three purities of the wheels:

the equality of the five aggregates with the aggregate of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), the equality of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) with the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the contemplation of the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*) as an empty village.
Furthermore, there are three wheels of purity:
namely, understanding emptiness, and having faith and compliance with signlessness, wishlessness, and non-seeking.
Samudramati!
If these three wheels are pure, then all phenomena are pure; therefore, bodhisattvas who possess the purity of the three wheels should cultivate skillful wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
That non-retrogressive bodhisattva is able to be fully endowed with the profound wisdom of the Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas are able to possess such knowledge of the Dharma, they will be well able to bring their merits to maturity.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:

"Samudrareṇu! You should know that a bodhisattva in this stage, by the power of their original vow, performs excellent deeds; even if that bodhisattva should find themselves in a state of distraction, they do not lose the merit of maturation due to the power of their original vow."
Sāgaramati!

There are certain people in the world who lack wisdom and cannot understand what I have taught; therefore, I shall now employ analogies so that those who hear them may gain understanding through these similes.
Sāgaramati!

It is, for example, as if there were in the world a field of sugarcane, or a field of rice, or a field of beans; once the cultivator has finished tending those fields, he opens the water channels so that the water flows and spreads everywhere through the ditches and furrows until they are completely filled.

Once these farmers have properly arranged everything and rested elsewhere, water naturally flows into each part of those fields according to its course; without requiring further exertion from the farmers, the various planted fields each reach maturity.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: although at times they may dwell in a state of dispersion, possessing skillful means, they are able to bring to maturity the continuity of roots of goodness within all sentient beings; according to all the Buddha-dharmas they teach, they are able to fully perfect every root of goodness.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva’s mind is pure and he skillfully guards the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). Whether abiding in meditative concentration or otherwise, by the power of his original vows, he is able to bring all roots of goodness to maturity, causing all sentient beings to continuously cultivate and increase all wholesome dharmas within the Buddha-dharma.
Sāgaramati!

For this reason, you should know that all bodhisattvas, according to their respective capacities, spontaneously fulfill all roots of goodness without relying on the exertion of effort, and further skillfully dedicate them toward omniscience.

Therefore, whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, all bodhisattvas—by the power of their original vows—experience harmony and serenity of body and mind amidst all roots of goodness; their mindfulness remains undistracted, and they do not fall into the Lesser Vehicle but instead advance toward the Great Vehicle.
“Sāgaramati! It is as if, for example, there were a great tree in a city, and someone were to come and cut its root; having cut it, they would depart.
While the tree is being cut, it gradually inclines downward and must eventually fall to the ground at the point where it was felled.”

The bodhisattva is also like this: throughout the long night, they cultivate wholesome dharmas, incline toward all-knowledge, gradually enter into all-knowledge, and ultimately bring all roots of goodness to full maturity.
Once they have been matured, he dedicates them all toward omniscience;
he dedicates them so that all sentient beings may share in their merit;
and he dedicates them with the vow that the noble lineage of the Triple Gem shall remain uninterrupted and unceasing.
Dedicate [merit] toward the perfection of the adornment of physical marks, being endowed with all the primary and secondary characteristics;
dedicate toward the perfection of the adornment of vocal karma, extensively expounding the non-deceptive Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
and dedicate toward the perfection of the adornment of mental karma, constantly mindful of the Buddhas and the fulfillment of meditative vows.
Yet this bodhisattva, without relying on effort and without any deliberate awakening, is able to fully mature all roots of goodness;
universally dedicating them toward omniscience, they do not fall into other vehicles.

Whether in meditative concentration or in a state of distraction, the complete cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening arises entirely from the power of dedication through the skillful means of one’s original vow. "Sāgaramati!

Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who wishes to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and first makes a formal resolve that he shall emerge from the absorption only upon hearing the sound of the ghaṇṭā-bell.

Once he has entered the absorption, the sound of the ghaṇṭā-bell does not actually enter into the state of concentration; nevertheless, that bhikṣu subsequently emerges from the absorption by means of the sound of the ghaṇṭā-bell.
The Bodhisattva is also like this; desiring to liberate all sentient beings, he gives rise to a great vow of compassion:

"I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings, universally causing them to attain liberation; I shall fully accomplish the work of enlightenment and extensively practice loving-kindness toward all beings."

Within the flow of birth and death, they direct their mind, intellect, and consciousness to universally deliver and liberate all beings; yet, although they enter meditative absorption, because of their fundamental vow of great compassion to deliver sentient beings, they never fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

"Subsequently, arising from meditative absorption, he develops right wisdom and once again accumulates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), extensively bringing sentient beings to maturity and delivering them.
O Sāgaramati!"

You should observe that the deeds performed by these bodhisattvas are all most supreme; although they enter into the samādhi of tranquility, they are able to transcend the realm of liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Volume Thirteen.
The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
Volume Fourteen.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Śramaṇa Subject Weijing et al., by imperial decree: "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!"
I shall now further clarify this meaning through an analogy.
Suppose, for instance, there were two people in the world:
one who, clad in armor as firm and solid as a diamond, enters into a mass of blazing, raging flames; [and another who does not].
"Suppose one were to take dry grass as armor and enter into a mass of blazing, raging flames.
Samudramati! What do you think?"
"Of those two people, which one was consumed by the fire,
and which one was not consumed by the fire?
Samudramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If one is clad in the adamantine armor, even if they enter into the midst of a mass of blazing, raging flames, because that firm armor can provide excellent protection, this person will not be burned by the fire.”
World-Honored One!
If one were to enter a great conflagration wearing dry grass as armor, that person would certainly be burned by it. Why is this?
"It would be impossible for those withered grasses to be protected by force within a blazing fire.
The Buddha said, "Sāgaramati!"

That his body, clad in adamantine armor, is not consumed when entering the great fire refers to the Bodhisattva, who always takes great loving-kindness and great compassion as his armor. With a firm inner mind protected by the power of adamant, he liberates sentient beings and never abandons his objects of focus or his vows. Although he constantly contemplates all phenomena as empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, and unarisen, and enters the samādhi of empty stillness, he always transcends the fixed positions of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and does not seek the attainment of their fruits.
Within that meditative concentration, although he experiences its sublime flavor, he does not relish or become attached to it, but rather emerges from that concentration;
having emerged from concentration, he purifies Buddha-fields, brings sentient beings to maturity, and perfects Buddha-wisdom.
Sāgaramati!

Those who enter a great fire clad in armor made of withered grass and are consumed by it are persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle. They give rise to fear toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and further perceive the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) as burning incessantly. Having abandoned sentient beings and distanced themselves from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they become attached to the taste of tranquil samādhi and have no capacity for receptivity.
Furthermore, it is impossible for one who has not yet attained the realization of the eighth fruit to be able to give rise to this samādhi.
Why is this? Because those of the Śrāvaka vehicle are unable to cultivate within the formations of merit, the formations of demerit, or the formations of immovability.

All Bodhisattvas are able to cultivate and bring to maturity within immeasurable practices of merit and wisdom, yet they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway; rather, they ultimately fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.
Sāgaramati!

Therefore, within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-activity, a bodhisattva should constantly conceive the thought of a great, blazing fire. Although they have thoroughly investigated these dharmas, they further give rise to wisdom and skillful conduct within them, never prematurely realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). For this reason, there are certain roots of goodness that bodhisattvas should not cultivate until they have brought them to maturity.

“Sāgaramati! When a bodhisattva brings their roots of virtue to maturity, it means they practice in accordance with reality within the profound Buddha-dharma, yet do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway; this is what is called bringing the roots of virtue to maturity.”

Why is this so? It is because those bodhisattvas, together with others, are all maturing the Mahāyāna teachings, gradually approaching, gradually entering, and gradually increasing in excellence; they do not mature them through the vehicles of other teachings.
Sāgaramati!
It is like a potter’s wheel: before it is struck by the sun's rays and has not yet matured, it is merely a clay mold and lacks the designation of "vessel" or "utensil";
only after it has subsequently matured can it receive the designation of "vessel" or "utensil."

It is the same for a bodhisattva: although they may extensively cultivate many roots of goodness, if they do not dedicate them toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they cannot obtain the name "perfection" (*pāramitā*);
however, if they do dedicate them toward omniscience, they then obtain the name "perfection."
Sāgaramati!
Furthermore, it is like fine, genuine gold: as long as it has not yet undergone craftsmanship, it cannot receive the name of an "ornament," but is merely called "gold";
once it has been processed and brought to maturity through craftsmanship, it can then receive the name of various ornaments.
It is the same for a bodhisattva: if the roots of goodness they cultivate are not dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they cannot receive the name "perfection" (*pāramitā*);
however, if they are dedicated toward omniscience, they then receive the name "perfection."
Sāgaramati!

For this reason, bodhisattvas should always rouse a vast mind to bring all wholesome qualities to maturity; once those roots of goodness have been matured, they should immediately dedicate them toward omniscience.

Because they dedicate [their merit] toward all-knowledge, bodhisattvas should practice in accordance with reality within the profound Dharma, without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas are able to perform what is difficult to do; they are well able to guard against all faults and do not give rise to defilement through their actions.”
"Bhagavān!
If bodhisattvas are endowed with skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they are then able to perform dedication (pariṇāmanā). Why is this so?"
Because the bodhisattva possesses skillful means, although he enters into dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti, he is not attached to the defects of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, or samāpatti.
Endowed with skillful means, he is able to manifest all manner of activities without falling into the view of non-action;

well-established in the nature of the equality of all phenomena, when there are sentient beings who incline toward the category of those fixed in wrong determination, the bodhisattva preaches for them the Dharma of the category of those fixed in right determination.
Furthermore, because that bodhisattva wishes to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings, he himself does not abide within the stage of right determination.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, “So it is, so it is!”
It is as you have said.
A bodhisattva should always cultivate skillful means in all circumstances. Why is this?
