Sāgaramati! Skillful means is itself the bodhi of a bodhisattva.
Without skillful means, one does not achieve bodhi.
For example, it is as if one were to place three kinds of colors within a single vessel: first, blue;
second, red; and [third, white].
Third, the golden-yellow color.
These three colors were used to dye three kinds of robes within the same vessel:
first, a woolen robe was dyed blue; [the second was dyed yellow, and the third was dyed red].
Second, cotton cloth dyed a crimson color;
third, priceless and exquisite celestial garments dyed a golden hue.

These three types of clothing, having been processed by that dyer within a single vessel, all attain exquisite colors according to their respective intentions: those requiring blue obtain blue, those requiring red obtain red, and those requiring yellow obtain yellow, yet the dyeing vessel itself never makes any distinction.
Sāgaramati!
That vessel for dyeing is itself emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
There are three kinds of people who are placed together within that single vessel:
First, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
second, those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
third, those of the Mahāyāna.

These three kinds of persons, according to their various activities and as they delight in them, each take up the form of wisdom as appropriate; yet that vessel of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is never subject to discrimination.
One should know that those who wear woolen robes are persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
those who wear cotton cloth are persons of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and those who wear priceless celestial garments are persons established in the Mahāyāna.
Sāgaramati!

Observe that all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature; they lack the nature of an agent, the nature of a self, the nature of a person, the nature of a sentient being, the nature of a life-span, and the nature of a sovereign. They arise according to desire, and having arisen, they assemble; yet they are without cognition and are devoid of conceptual discrimination.
Sāgaramati! If one can understand the arising of these phenomena, then bodhisattvas will not experience even the slightest weariness regarding any phenomenon.

If they attain such pure knowledge and vision, then among all their activities there will be neither benefit nor non-benefit; they will then be able to know, as it truly is, the nature of the equality of all phenomena.
Having thus understood the equality of all phenomena as they truly are, one never abandons the armor of great compassion. "Sāgaramati!
For example, suppose there were a worldly lapis lazuli jewel, its substance naturally brilliant, pure, and free from blemish, which had been placed amidst dust and filth for a thousand years;

After a thousand years have passed, one takes it out to treat it for use; having removed its dust and impurities and washed it until it is pure, it remains lustrous and bright, free from all blemishes and obscurations.

It is the same with the Bodhisattva: they fully understand that the intrinsic nature of the minds of sentient beings is originally pure, clear, and immaculate, yet is merely shrouded by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
Having observed this, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"The nature of the minds of sentient beings is originally pure; it is merely obscured by adventitious afflictions, yet those afflictions have no actual place of abiding."
Sentient beings give rise to false conceptualizations at random; I shall proclaim for those various classes of sentient beings the Dharma that severs afflictions.
With a mind free from indolence, I shall further increase my excellence toward sentient beings, directing my mind so that all may universally attain liberation.
He further reflected:

"These afflictions can destroy the power and strength of sentient beings, rendering them weak and inferior; these afflictions cause sentient beings to engage in false conceptualization regarding afflictions that lack reality. If one can apply deep and firm attention as it truly is and investigate according to principle, one will not be moved by those afflictions."
Once one has investigated in this manner, those afflictions no longer conjoin with him.
If one does not conjoin with the afflictions, that is indeed virtuous.
Furthermore, if I were now to conjoin with the various afflictions, how could I proclaim the Dharma for severing and eliminating afflictions to those sentient beings who are bound by them?
Therefore, at this time, I am not conjoined with the various afflictions (*kleśa*); I should teach the methods for severing and eliminating them to those sentient beings bound by afflictions.

Nevertheless, because I wish to transform and deliver sentient beings within saṃsāra so that their roots of goodness continue without interruption, I must likewise appear to be conjoined with the afflictions.
"What is meant by 'the continuity of roots of goodness conjoined with afflictions within saṃsāra'?
It refers to the insatiable and diligent pursuit of meritorious conduct.

Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva intentionally manifests birth within the three realms of existence; he vows to meet all Buddhas and pledges to deliver sentient beings without weariness, upholding the True Dharma. In all his activities, he is courageous and never retreats; he constantly generates a desire for the Dharma and never abandons the supreme practice of the pāramitās.
Sāgaramati! This is what is called the continuity of roots of goodness that are conjoined with afflictions within saṃsāra.
Within this state, although the bodhisattva is conjoined with afflictions, they are not defiled by the faults of those afflictions.
Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since you have now spoken of roots of goodness, for what reason do you speak of the various afflictions?”
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!
A bodhisattva thoroughly understands that these various afflictive phenomena are conjoined with the three realms, and that the three realms arise from within those afflictions.”

Because that bodhisattva possesses skillful means, the power of the accumulated roots of goodness merges with the three realms; this is precisely what is called the merging of all roots of goodness with afflictions.
Because the three realms are thus unified, the mind no longer gives rise to any secondary afflictions. Samudrareṇu!
It is like a great elder in the world who has but one son, whom he nurtures with compassion and pity, cherishing him with deep affection.
At that time, the boy was foolish and lacked wisdom; while dancing and playing by the side of a foul well, he suddenly fell into it due to his youthfulness.

Then his mother and his kinsmen, seeing their son fallen into the foul well, were filled with grief and sorrow. They rushed forward to look into the well, but its depth was unfathomable. In their extreme anguish, they were unable to devise a plan to enter the well; though they pained for their beloved son, they could not rescue him.

At that time, the father, having learned of this, rushed there; seeing the boy fallen into the foul well, he gazed upon him with grief and distress, pacing about in agitation. Out of deep love for his son and without feeling any weariness or desire to abandon him, he immediately devised a plan, entered the well, and skillfully rescued him so that the son might emerge.
Sāgaramati! You should know that the foul well is the triple world;
the son is all sentient beings, whom the bodhisattva regards with the thought of them being as one's only child.

The mother and kinsmen of the youth are those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; seeing all sentient beings fallen into saṃsāra, they feel distress in their hearts upon seeing this, yet they lack the skillful means to rescue them.
That great elder is the bodhisattva.

Although these bodhisattvas abide in unconditioned phenomena with minds that are stainless, pure, and pristine, they nevertheless harmonize with and cultivate practices within the three realms in order to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Sāgaramati!

This is the practice of a bodhisattva’s great compassion: having ultimately liberated themselves from all fetters and bonds, they nevertheless manifest birth within the three realms of existence. Endowed with skillful means and encompassed by supreme wisdom, their own afflictions no longer present any hindrance, enabling them to proclaim for all sentient beings the Dharma that severs the bonds of affliction.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas perform what is difficult to do; they are able, with a stainless, pure, and pristine mind, to feel no weariness or rejection toward saṃsāra.”
"Regarding the profound Dharma as it has been taught, one should examine it according to principle, yet not dwell in the unconditioned, nor seek the realization of its fruit.
The Buddha said, "Sāgaramati!"
This bodhisattva practices the right path in conjunction with the factors of dhyāna, namely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
O Sāgaramati, you should know this!
If bodhisattvas possess a stainless, pure, and pristine mind, this is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To feel no weariness toward saṃsāra, while manifesting birth and transformation to guide and deliver sentient beings, is skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
If bodhisattvas correctly investigate all phenomena as being empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, and unarisen, this is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the mind of great compassion manifesting before them, neither dwelling in the unconditioned nor seeking the realization of its fruit, this is skillful means.
"Moreover, Sāgaramati!..."
If bodhisattvas well abide in the equality of the three periods of time, they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having diverse characteristics.
If that dharma-realm is equal, then the realm of sentient beings is likewise equal.
If the realm of sentient beings is equal, then the realm of nirvāṇa is equal.
If the realm of nirvāṇa is equal, then the dharma-realm is equal.
If one can enter into this equality of the dharma-realm, that which is entered is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If, moreover, one can enter the single realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), yet fully understands the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) without realizing the realm of nirvana, thereby neither abandoning the realm of sentient beings nor dwelling in the realm of phenomena, and not grasping at the realization of the fruit—this is skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati! If giving is pure, this is wisdom;
if dedication is pure, this is skillful means."
If the purity of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration constitutes wisdom,
then the purity of dedication constitutes skillful means.
To state it briefly:
"The purification of all roots of goodness is itself wisdom;
the purification of dedication is skillful means.
Samudramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the purity of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness?
What is the purity of dedication?”
“What is the purity of wisdom?
What is the purity of skillful means?
The Buddha said:

“Sāgaramati! For a bodhisattva whose roots of virtue are purified, it is in order to be free from the views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span that they subsequently accumulate all roots of virtue.”
"Pure dedication" refers to maturing roots of goodness within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and dedicating them toward enlightenment.
"Pure wisdom" refers to the complete knowledge of the wisdom regarding the initial and final faculties of all sentient beings.
Regarding the purity of skillful means: it is to skillfully preach the Dharma to all sentient beings according to their needs.
Furthermore, Samudramati!

Regarding the purity of roots of goodness: although one manifests birth within the various realms of existence and destinies, one remains without dependence, and thereafter accumulates all roots of goodness within those realms of existence.

Regarding dedication for the sake of purity: this means being free from all mental orientations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and properly gathering all roots of goodness belonging to all vehicles, dedicating them entirely within the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Purity of wisdom means universally severing all seeds of affliction and their habitual tendencies.
Purity of skillful means refers to first engaging in the same activities as sentient beings in order to transform and deliver them, and subsequently teaching them the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
Moreover, that which is called the purity of roots of goodness refers to a bodhisattva extending his precious hand to universally bestow all inexhaustible enjoyments."

Regarding dedication for the sake of purity: this means universally gathering and incorporating all roots of goodness belonging to all sentient beings, all those in training and those beyond training, all pratyekabuddhas, all bodhisattvas, and all buddhas, into the process of dedication.
Purity of wisdom means that one upholds all that has been spoken by the Buddhas, sealing it all with the seal of dhāraṇī, so that what is upheld is never lost or corrupted.
Purity of skillful means refers to using uninterrupted eloquence and unimpeded eloquence to skillfully expound the non-deceptive Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them all to attain joy.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
Moreover, the purification of roots of goodness means that throughout successive lifetimes, one never abandons the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta)."
Purity of dedication means not forgetting the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), dedicating all roots of virtue toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Purity of wisdom means skillfully knowing that abiding in the mind of great enlightenment is the fundamental basis.
"Purity of skillful means refers to dwelling in equanimity regarding the bodhicitta and thereby teaching the Dharma of enlightenment to others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all skillful means are the bodhi of a bodhisattva; the purity of the prajñāpāramitā and the thorough penetration of all things are all bodhi. There is not even the slightest dharma that is not bodhi.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
To fully comprehend the equality of all phenomena is itself bodhi.

Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should not conceive the notion that enlightenment is extremely remote. When, among all phenomena, the objects of the six sense-fields arise as obstacles, at that time they should realize them as they truly are: these very things are enlightenment.
"If bodhisattvas understand in this way, they will attain the purity of skillful means and the purity of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
As you have said:

when a bodhisattva who is endowed with skillful means and the purity of the perfection of wisdom encounters the six sensory objects as obstacles among all phenomena, at that time they should realize, in accordance with reality, that these are themselves bodhi.
Sāgaramati! For these reasons, all bodhisattvas should understand it in this way.
*The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati*, translated by the Buddha, Scroll Fourteen.
The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Great Tang, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Guangfan; Scroll Fifteen.
The Great Master, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Wei Jing, and others, translated by imperial decree: "Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and incomparable eons ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Anantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was named Suvikurvaṇa, and his eon was named Prabhārasa."
For what reason is that Buddha-Tathāgata named Boundless Radiance?

It is because when that Blessed One first sat at the site of enlightenment, before he had realized all-knowledge and while he was still in the stage of a bodhisattva, his body emitted rays of light of various colors. These lights pervaded and illuminated all the infinite, incalculable, and beyond-numbering buddha-fields of the ten directions. Within all those buddha-fields, every single non-retrogressive bodhisattva and every bodhisattva in their final birth (ekajātipratibaddha) saw that bodhisattva sitting at the site of enlightenment; having seen him, they each scattered exquisite flowers toward that bodhisattva.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all the flowers he cast gathered together toward the body of that bodhisattva.
Each individual flower then accumulated extensively within that world of Good Transformation (Suvikrānta), rising to a height of seven human spans.
For these reasons, the names of that Buddha and the eon *Prabhārasa* were established. Samudramati!
Within that eon, fourteen koṭis of Tathāgatas appeared in the world; and that world, *Suvikurvaṇa*, was endowed with great majestic power, peace, and abundance.

The multitude of devas and humans was vast and flourishing; the land was extensive and far-reaching, comprising nine hundred and sixty quadrillion (*koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra*) great continents. Each of these continents measured eight million four hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. Within each one million *yojanas*, there were eighty-four thousand cities and towns. In each city and town, there were eighty-four thousand districts and villages. Within each city, there resided ten quadrillion people together, and in each district and village, there resided eighty million people.
The wealth and prosperity of the people in that world are already so vast; how much more so for the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas of great majesty and power!
Furthermore, that world is composed of four precious substances, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Furthermore, in that land, whatever one thinks of—food, drink, clothing, ornaments, and so forth—is spontaneously and abundantly provided.
Moreover, the people there are free from the notions of "I" and "mine."
“Sāgaramati!

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anantaprabhāsa had a lifespan of ten intermediate kalpas, and he had an assembly of thirty-six koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand śrāvakas, as well as an assembly of one thousand two hundred koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
There was a royal city named Suviśuddha, which was the birthplace of that Blessed One.
After that Buddha had departed from the royal palace, he resided separately in another city named Rativardhana.
Now, within that great city of Sukhāvatī, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Suviśuddhaviṣaya, who reigned over a trichiliocosm and possessed the seven treasures, namely:

the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the woman treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the minister-treasurer treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure—these seven treasures being the enjoyments of the king.
Sāgaramati!

That King Viśuddhaviṣaya has already resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he is fully endowed with a profound resolve and gives rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings.
The king had eighty-four *koṭi-nayuta* hundred-thousand palace ladies and handmaidens, who were upright, exquisite, and possessed the appearance of celestial maidens.
All these palace women had resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

That King Viśuddhaviṣaya invited the Bhagavān Anantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and for the duration of two intermediate kalpas, he extended his offerings. These were performed in accordance with the Dharma, pure and free from all faults, providing everything required by the way of the śramaṇa: clothing, food and drink, requisites for illness and medicine, bedding and seating, and all other provisions.

For the sake of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that king constructed a separate vihāra, pure and immaculate, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its ground was composed of lapis lazuli and precious jewels, with walls made of the seven treasures forming successive layers of enclosures. Throughout, pillars were fashioned from red sandalwood and uraśa-sandalwood, exquisitely crafted and extraordinary, equaling the palaces of the devas.
Next, ten thousand pavilions were further arranged, and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas were commanded to settle there in succession.
Samudramati!
That King Viśuddhaviṣaya reverently upheld the pure Dharma of that Buddha, received and maintained the five precepts, and diligently cultivated the holy life.
Together with his palace ladies and retinue, he served and made offerings to that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, for two intermediate kalpas.
After these two intermediate kalpas had passed, the king, accompanied by all his retinue, went to where that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Infinite Light-Radiance was residing.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, King Suviśuddhaviṣaya addressed the Tathāgata Anantaprabhāsa, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva attain non-reliance on others' faith within the Mahāyāna?
How is it that a bodhisattva, though proceeding toward the most supreme path, remains free from the mark of self?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully abide in wisdom that is both unmoving and not unmoving?
How does a bodhisattva attain the purity of expedient wisdom?
How does a bodhisattva attain long-term observation without severing the root?
How does a bodhisattva remain free from negligence even as they encounter the increasing proliferation of the six sensory objects?
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to give rise to no fear or terror amidst profound principles and meanings?
"How does a bodhisattva come to be named a 'true bodhisattva'?
Then, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Unbounded Radiance Shone Upon replied to King Pure Realm:
"Great King!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Pay close attention, and I shall now speak for you,
O Great King.
There are four kinds of dharmas; if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will attain non-reliance on others' faith within the Mahāyāna.
What are these four?
First, because it arises from resolute conviction, one has faith in the supramundane noble Dharma;
second, because of courageous non-retrogression, one diligently practices with vigor to transform and deliver sentient beings;
third, because of skillful observation, one gives rise to the wisdom of supernormal powers and performs various spiritual displays.
Fourth, because wisdom follows the knowledge of phenomena, one gives rise to the characteristic of decisive discernment regarding all phenomena.
Great King,
if a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will attain non-reliance on the faith of others within the Mahāyāna.
"Great King!
There are four dharmas which, if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will proceed toward the most excellent path without giving rise to the notion of a self.
What are these four?"
First, not clinging to the flavor of meditative concentration while the mental faculties remain harmonious and supple;
second, not clinging to one's own happiness but bestowing happiness upon others;
third, accomplishing the practice of great loving-kindness and abiding securely in great compassion.
Fourth, they attain vast faith and understanding, enabling them to give rise to the most supreme and excellent aspiration.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will proceed toward the most excellent path without giving rise to the notion of a self.
"Great King!
There are four dharmas; if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will immediately attain abiding in unshakable and non-fluctuating wisdom.
What are these four?"
First, the inner mind is free from flattery and deception;
second, the inner mind is pure and endowed with skillful means;
third, one possesses profound resolve and skillful means without regressing.
Fourth, the profound mind does not abandon what is practiced.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will immediately attain the wisdom that dwells well in immovability and non-fluctuation.
"Great King!
There are four kinds of dharmas; if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will attain the purity of skillful means and wisdom.
What are these four?"
First, although they contemplate that all phenomena are without self, they constantly use the four means of attraction to transform and deliver sentient beings.

Second, although they know that all phenomena cannot be fully expressed, they constantly use sounds and written words to expound the essentials of the Dharma for all sentient beings and to protect and uphold the True Dharma.

Third, although they contemplate the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, they always have faith and understanding in the merits of all Tathāgatas, and they cultivate the marks and signs with diligence and without weariness.
Fourth, although they contemplate all buddha-fields as empty and quiescent, they constantly adorn and purify buddha-lands with unremitting diligence.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will attain the purity of skillful means and wisdom.
"Great King!
There are four dharmas which, if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will attain the uninterrupted observation of the root for a long duration.
What are these four?"
First, they are able to skillfully observe the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), because they do not abandon or forsake the bodhicitta.
Second, they skillfully observe the Buddha’s wisdom, because their own wisdom is free from attachment.
Third, they skillfully observe the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, for they are able to preach whatever Dharma they have heard without weariness or indolence.
Fourth, they skillfully observe the dharma of Great Nirvana, yet they do not weary of or abandon the dharmas of arising and ceasing.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will attain the uninterrupted observation of the fundamental source for a long duration.
Great King!
There are four kinds of dharmas which, if bodhisattvas can fully possess them, they will remain free from negligence even as the objects of the six sense-fields increase.
What are the four?

First, as a Wheel-Turning Sage King who transforms and delivers the people, he skillfully contemplates the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena; thus, even though the objects of the six sense-fields increase, he remains free from negligence.

Second, as the Lord Śakra, he transforms the hosts of devas, skillfully observing that all conditioned phenomena are suffering; thus, even though the objects of the six sense-fields increase, they remain free from negligence.

Third, he manifests as a Māra king and transforms the hosts of Māras; skillfully observing that all phenomena are without self, he remains free from negligence even though the objects of the six sense-fields increase.

Fourth, acting as a Great Brahma King to transform the hosts of Brahmās, he skillfully contemplates the tranquility of nirvana; thus, although the objects of the six sense-fields increase, he remains free from negligence.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, then even though the objects of the six sense-fields may increase, he will remain free from negligence.
Great King!
There are four kinds of dharmas; if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they will not give rise to fear or alarm regarding profound meanings and principles.
What are these four?
First, to draw near to genuine spiritual friends;
second, to continuously and uninterruptedly reveal the profound Dharma of the Buddha’s bodhi to those spiritual friends.
Third, regarding such profound sūtras as these, one shall go even as far as many hundreds of yojanas to hear and receive them, and to discern their meaning.
Fourth, regarding the Dharma as it has been heard, one shall give rise to wisdom to investigate it, relying solely on the meaning and not on the letter.
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they will not give rise to fear or alarm regarding profound meanings and principles.
Great King!
There are four kinds of dharmas; if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, they are truly called "genuine bodhisattvas."
What are the four?
First, to practice diligence with vigor in cultivating the various pāramitās;
second, to aspire toward the mind of great compassion and diligently practice the transformation and deliverance of all sentient beings.
Third, by the power of diligence, they assiduously practice to bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment;

fourth, within immeasurable cycles of birth and death, they assiduously practice the gathering and transforming of beings without becoming weary, and are further able to accumulate the supreme practices of merit and wisdom.
"If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they shall be called a true bodhisattva.
"Sāgaramati! When that Tathāgata Anantaprabhāsa taught these four dharma-gates, ten thousand koṭis of nayutas of people within that assembly resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Eighty quadrillion (*koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasra*) bhikṣus, through the exhaustion of outflows, attained liberation of mind by not grasping at any phenomena;
the king’s crown prince, his queen, and the palace ladies all attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and King Śubhaviṣaya attained the sharp patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma.
At that moment, the king’s heart was filled with great joy, delight, and exultation; he immediately took all the exquisite objects of enjoyment belonging to the king and offered them to that Buddha.
Then, the Tathāgata Anantaprabhāsa addressed King Viśuddhaviṣaya, saying:
"Great King!
You have already renounced all that you possess as an offering to the Buddha, the Tathāgata; you should now, with pure faith, go forth from home into homelessness within my supreme Dharma."
Why is this? Great King!
Those who, with pure faith, renounce the world within the supreme Dharma of the Tathāgata possess great power and attain great renown.
"Great King, you should know that a renunciant bodhisattva attains twenty kinds of vast and excellent benefits; this is precisely the fulfillment of the unsurpassed excellence of omniscience."
What are these twenty?
First, by relinquishing all royal wealth, status, and enjoyments, one attains the great benefit of being free from "I" and "mine.
Second, having delighted in the life of renunciation, one attains the great benefit of being able to transcend afflictions.
Third, by donning the kāṣāya robe, one attains the great benefit of a mind free from defilement;
fourth, having conceived joy in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), one is able to fully accomplish the great benefit of nurturing and increasing them;
fifth, by practicing the dhūta virtues, one eliminates excessive desire and attains the great benefit of freedom from attachment.
Sixth, having purified the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), one attains the great benefit of being reborn among gods and humans;
seventh, by not abandoning the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one attains the great benefit of fulfilling the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*);
eighth, by dwelling in a secluded place, one attains the great benefit of being free from the clamor and bustle of the world.
Ninth, by having a mind free from attachment, one attains the great benefit of the joy of contemplating the Dharma;
tenth, by practicing the factors of dhyāna, one attains the great benefit of mental pliancy and composure;
eleventh, by diligently seeking extensive learning, one attains the great benefit of vast wisdom.
Twelfth, because they are free from all pride, they attain the great benefit of supreme wisdom;
thirteenth, because they have few desires and few concerns, they attain the great benefit of discerning the noble Dharma;
fourteenth, because their minds are impartial toward all sentient beings, they attain the great benefit of great compassion.
Fifteenth, by giving rise to the mind that seeks to liberate all sentient beings, one attains the great benefit of great compassion;
sixteenth, by not begrudging body or life, one attains the great benefit of upholding the True Dharma;
seventeenth, by having a mind of pliancy and tranquility, one attains the great benefit of supernormal powers.
Eighteenth, because they constantly mindfully recollect the Buddha, there is a passage here below concerning the attainment of great benefit that is missing from the Sanskrit original;
nineteenth, because they constantly investigate the profound and solid Dharma, they attain the great benefit of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
twentieth, because they accumulate all supreme merits, they swiftly accomplish the great benefit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
"Great King!
These twenty kinds of dharmas are the meritorious benefits of going forth; they are not difficult for bodhisattvas who have gone forth to obtain."
"Therefore, Great King,
you should now renounce the world with pure faith within this most supreme Dharma. "O Sāgaramati!"
At that time, the World-Honored One provided appropriate instruction for King Suviśuddhaviṣaya.

Once the king had gone forth, he immediately renounced all his possessions; having developed a sense of weary detachment even toward his royal merit, his hair and beard fell away naturally, the saffron robes appeared upon his body, and he assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu.

When that king had gone forth with pure faith within the Dharma of that Blessed One, the king’s palace ladies also followed him in going forth; the crown prince and his consort likewise went forth. Even the common people throughout the realm who were converted numbered nine hundred and ninety-nine koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands, all of whom followed in going forth and applied themselves with diligence to earnestly seek the wholesome Dharma.
Sāgaramati!
You should now behold these truthful words of all the Buddhas; they are able to give rise to pure faith, and all meritorious practices serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.

After King Suviśuddhaviṣaya had gone forth, he later went together with his retinue of renunciants to the presence of the Tathāgata Anantaprabhāsa. Upon arrival, they paid homage and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will instruct us; we shall practice with firm resolve according to the Buddha’s words, so that we may not receive food in vain within the various lands."
At that time, that Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Viśuddhaviṣaya:

"From this day forward, you shall be known by the name Bhikṣu; you have entered the assembly of bhikṣus. You should, within your own sphere, perform what is pure and conduct a profound and firm investigation of your own sphere, abiding in accordance with reality as you investigate it."
What is meant by "one's own sphere"?

It refers to the six sensory objects that come to act as obstacles. At such a time, you should realize and clearly contemplate Bodhi as it manifests before you according to reality; you should conceive of Bodhi as something profound and distant, and not conceive of it as being near.

Then, having received the instructions as taught by that Blessed One, the bhikṣu Suviśuddhaviṣaya became firm and resolute in his intention, remained free from negligence, sought liberation from the afflictions through practice in accordance with reality, and investigated his own objective sphere as it truly is.

Furthermore, what is profound and firm investigation? It is as follows: the realm of the eye is the realm of emptiness; the realm of emptiness is the realm of all sentient beings; and the realm of all sentient beings and the realm of emptiness are the realm of the Buddha.

Likewise, the realms of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the realm of emptiness; the realm of emptiness is the realm of all sentient beings; and the realm of all sentient beings and the realm of emptiness are the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the realm of the eye is the realm of signlessness; the realm of signlessness is the realm of all sentient beings; and the realm of all sentient beings and the realm of signlessness are the realm of the Buddha.

This extends even to the realm of the mind: the realm of the mind is the realm of signlessness; the realm of signlessness is the realm of all sentient beings; and the realm of all sentient beings and the realm of signlessness are the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the objective realm of the eye is the realm of wishlessness, the realm of non-action, and the realm of non-arising and non-origination; the realm of non-origination is the realm of all sentient beings; and the realm of all sentient beings, which is the realm of non-origination, is the realm of the Buddha.
Sāgaramati!
Having heard what was said, that bhikṣu Viśuddhaviṣaya entered into this Dharma and thereby attained a body and mind that were pliant, harmonious, and serviceable.

Therefore, by cultivating the four bases of spiritual power—desire, effort, mind, and wisdom—one will before long be able to give rise to the five supernormal powers; with single-minded concentration and without negligence, one attains entry into the *dhāraṇī* gate that encompasses all words and meanings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, saying:

"You should now not give rise to any doubt. As for that bhikṣu Viśuddhaviṣaya who, at that time, renounced the most supreme position of a universal monarch to leave the household life and practice the path within the Buddha-dharma—could he possibly have been anyone else?"
It is none other than you yourself.
As for those ninety-nine koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus who followed the king into the homeless life at that time, could they possibly be anyone else?
"These very bodhisattvas in this assembly who have come together to hear the Dharma according to your ocean-like intention are they.
When the World-Honored Buddha spoke these words regarding this past causal connection, eighteen thousand people within this great assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Scroll Fifteen.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
Scroll Sixteen.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Minister of State for Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Decree. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying: “Sāgaramati!
If any bodhisattvas wish to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should practice and study all that you great beings perform.
A bodhisattva should not merely cultivate swift speech and sharp eloquence; rather, they should be able to act exactly as they speak.
What is it for a bodhisattva to be unable to act according to what they have said?
Sāgaramati!
It is when a bodhisattva, despite possessing eloquence and wisdom, does not accumulate the various wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), yet makes this claim:
"Once I have attained buddhahood, I shall universally summon all sentient beings and extensively practice the gift of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to attain fulfillment in the Dharma."

However, this bodhisattva is unable to diligently practice and cultivate extensive learning, nor does he accumulate the various wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma); he deceives all sentient beings.
This is precisely what it means to be "unable to act according to one's words."
Sāgaramati! If there is a bodhisattva who speaks thus:
"Once I have attained buddhahood, I shall universally summon all sentient beings and extensively practice the gift of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to attain fulfillment in the Dharma."

At that time, that bodhisattva is able to diligently practice and cultivate extensive learning, and further accumulates all the wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment; this is precisely what it means to act according to one's words.

“Sāgaramati! Furthermore, regarding those who speak but cannot act: it is like a king or a minister in this world who issues a general summons to all the people of the realm, desiring to provide them with exquisite food so that they may all be fully satisfied, yet fails to prepare the necessary provisions, thereby deceiving all the people of the realm.”
Since these people had mistakenly received their food, they each sought it out in different places; harboring resentment and anger, they departed while reproaching [the cook].
O Sāgaramati!

The Bodhisattva is also like this: he vows that all sentient beings who have not yet crossed over shall be made to cross over; those who have not yet attained liberation shall be made to attain liberation; those who have not yet found peace shall be made to find peace; and those who have not yet reached Nirvana shall be made to reach Nirvana.

Yet, although that Bodhisattva possesses such a vow, he does not diligently cultivate extensive learning, nor does he accumulate the various wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). This is precisely what it means to be unable to practice as one speaks.

Such a bodhisattva deceives the world of devas and humans; they are censured and reviled by the noble ones and likewise spurned by them. They establish themselves in contention and cannot become masters of great wisdom, nor can they ultimately fulfill their vows.
Sāgaramati!
If you wish to give rise to the most difficult-to-attain and supreme great wisdom, you should not give way to indolence or retreat regarding that unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Therefore, you should know this!
A bodhisattva should not deceive all the worlds of gods and humans with mere words.
Furthermore, Samudramati,
when someone comes to a bodhisattva requesting a Dharma teaching, that bodhisattva should respond accordingly:
"I shall preach such a Dharma for you and transform you through such a Dharma, even to the point of sacrificing my own body without any stinginess."
"In this way, that bodhisattva does not deceive any sentient beings; you should understand the causes and conditions for this.
Furthermore, Samudramati!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a lion, king of beasts, named Abhedyakāya (Unbreakable Body). He dwelt within a mountain cave in the deep wilderness, constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness, watching over and protecting all sentient beings, and subsisting solely on grasses, leaves, flowers, and fruits."

At that time, there were two monkeys, a male and a female, dwelling together in that cave. Later, they gave birth to two sons; wishing to go elsewhere, they entrusted their children to the King of Beasts for protection and departed.
There was a king of vultures named Li-jian (Sharp Sight) who, while flying in the air, suddenly descended to the ground, seized a monkey, and whirled it about in the sky.
When the lion king saw him being seized, he approached the king of vultures and spoke this verse:
"How marvelous, O King of Vultures, you who know me! Release these two young monkeys!"
"I shall protect these two so they may be free from fear; let them find refuge with you and do not cause them harm.
At that time, the King of Vultures spoke this verse in reply to the Lion King:
"If you, O King of Beasts, can relinquish your own body, I shall relinquish these two monkey youths."
"I dwell in the air; this is my food. Without food, dwelling in the air, what would I do?
The Lion, King of Beasts, replied once more:
"I would rather give up my own body as food for you; release these two monkeys at once."
"I vow to watch over and protect you until you reach enlightenment; as a wise one, you should not speak falsely.
Having spoken these verses, the Lion, King of Beasts, with a deep and firm resolve free from falsehood, was about to sacrifice his body.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the King of Vultures marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and spoke these verses:
"To increase the lives of those in the world, One is able to sacrifice one's own body to protect others;
I now relinquish these two monkey children, So that you may dwell long and practice the Dharma."
"Samudrareṇu! You should know now that as for the Lion King Akṣayakāya at that time, do not give rise to any other view; he was none other than myself."
The male monkey was Mahākāśyapa;
the female monkey was the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrapālā;
and the two monkey cubs were none other than Rāhula and Ānanda in the present time.
The one who was seen as the King of Vultures was the bhikṣu Śubhāloka.
By this you should know:

it is better for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to sacrifice his own body than ever to abandon others and fail to act as their protector; this is precisely what constitutes fulfilling the practice of acting according to one's word.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati! What, again, is the characteristic of manifesting through practice according to what has been taught? It is as follows:
when a bodhisattva practices giving as taught, they should relinquish all that they possess exactly as it has been demonstrated; this is called 'practice.'

When a bodhisattva maintains the precepts as they have been taught, they shall accomplish all training in the precepts (*śīkṣā*) and the merits of the ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*); as thus demonstrated, this is called "capable practice."
When a bodhisattva practices patience as described, they completely eliminate all faults such as anger and resentment; as thus demonstrated, this is called "practicing it."
When a bodhisattva practices diligence as described, they shall diligently seek and cultivate all wholesome dharmas; as thus demonstrated, this is called "capable practice.
When a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration as described, they shall cultivate all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis; as thus demonstrated, this is called "capable practice."

When a bodhisattva possesses wisdom as described, they should analyze all chapters and phrases, giving rise to skillful wisdom and decisive eloquence; to manifest in accordance with this is called "capable practice."

To state it briefly: even as it is said that a bodhisattva abandons all unwholesome dharmas and accumulates all wholesome dharmas, they should indeed sever all unwholesome dharmas and diligently seek to cultivate all wholesome dharmas, just as has been demonstrated; this is called "being able to practice."
When a bodhisattva is upright as described, they shall be free from all flattery, deception, and falsehood; this is called "being able to practice.
When they act according to the described skillful means, they shall reveal the gateway of skillful means; this is called "being able to practice."
As it is said regarding diligence, one should exert effort and distance oneself from all forms of indolence and regression; this is called "capable practice.
As it is said regarding a profound and firm mind, one should abandon attachment and proceed toward the supreme path; this is called "capable practice."
As it is said regarding vows, one should bring all vows to ultimate fulfillment; this is called "being able to practice.
As it is said regarding hearing and retaining the teachings, one should practice them well according to what has been heard; this is called "being able to practice."
As it is said that one should accumulate virtuous deeds, this means that both body and mind must be free from weariness; this is called "being able to practice.
As it is said that one should abandon pride, this means that one should perfect supreme wisdom; this is called "being able to practice."
As it is said regarding the accumulation of ethical conduct, one should be without deficiency or omission in that morality; this is called "being able to practice.
As it is said regarding the stage of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one should accomplish the supreme practices of a bodhisattva; this is called "being able to practice."

As it is said regarding the stage of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one should then advance toward the stage of non-retrogression; this is called "capable practice.

As it is said regarding the stage of being in the final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), one should then advance toward sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); this is called "capable practice."
As it is said, "firmly accumulating [merit]," one shall realize the fruit of omniscience; this is called "capable practice.
As it is said, "turning the sublime wheel of Dharma," one shall ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels remains uninterrupted; this is called "capable practice."
"Samudramati!
Such dharmas as these constitute a bodhisattva’s ability to practice according to what has been taught.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these words on the dharma of practicing according to what has been taught, five thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Padmavyūha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are able to practice exactly as they teach, they have attained all the most supreme Buddha-dharmas.”
“World-Honored One!
To practice according to what the Buddha has spoken is precisely to be able to act in accordance with what was said.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Do you know how to practice the Dharma?
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I understand,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Speak now on the methods of practice as you wish to explain them.
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, for a practitioner, all phenomena are equal.

Having known this equality, one abides within the state of correctness (*samyaktva*) and, through skillful wisdom, does not take realization of the *samāpatti*; this is what constitutes the correct practice of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Śailendra said:
"World-Honored One!
I, too, would delight in explaining the Dharma of spiritual practice."
The Buddha said,
“Good son, speak as you wish.”
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To have nothing to cultivate is true cultivation.”

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being entirely unapprehendable; if there is something cultivated that is not [conceived as] cultivation, this is precisely what constitutes correct cultivation.
The Bodhisattva Guṇaprabhābhāsarāja said:
“World-Honored One!
If the mind follows the stream and consciousness undergoes transformation, how can this be called cultivation?”
If a bodhisattva’s consciousness does not dwell upon any phenomena, then there is not even the slightest phenomenon upon which it can dwell.
If there is not even the slightest phenomenon upon which it can dwell, that itself constitutes right practice.
The Bodhisattva King High Torch said:
“World-Honored One!
To have nothing to delight in is cultivation; to have nothing to weary of is cultivation.”
"Bhagavān!
Within all dharmas, the bodhisattva has neither high nor low; therefore, there is not even the slightest dharma to be delighted in or weary of. This is precisely what constitutes correct practice."
The Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is that upon which one relies, then there is that which turns; if there is nothing upon which one relies, then there is nothing that turns.”
Because the bodhisattva is without reliance and without fluctuation, they remain unshaken with respect to all phenomena; this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Courageous Mind said:
“World-Honored One!
The mind is that which acts within the world; it is that which rushes and flows through the world.”
“If a bodhisattva attains a state of no-mind regarding all minds, such that there is neither thought nor discrimination, this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
Bodhisattva Love-View said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, all that is known is entirely suffering.

If a bodhisattva attains awakening regarding all that is known, then there is neither anything to be known nor anything to be grasped; therefore, they do not enter the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception, yet they do not abandon sentient beings nor lose their great compassion—this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Gandhahastirāja said:
“World-Honored One!
Foolish ordinary beings carry heavy burdens and give rise to deep and heavy views regarding the five aggregates.”

If a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the five aggregates and attains lightness and agility, they cast off all heavy burdens; furthermore, they are able to proclaim to all foolish worldlings the method for discarding the burden of the five aggregates. Therefore, not even the slightest phenomenon gives rise to the notion of reality; knowing that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished—this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara said:
“World-Honored One!
That which is practiced correctly is true cultivation; it is not the practice of what is evil and perverse. A bodhisattva should cultivate correct skillful means.”
"What is right effort?
It is the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena, for they are equal to space; this is what constitutes right practice.
Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva possesses the wisdom of skillful means, they give birth from non-birth and arise from non-arising; even amidst arising and ceasing, they abide nowhere. This is precisely what constitutes correct practice.”
The Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭarāja said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, yet does not cast off the armor of great compassion, seeing that the fruits and benefits of diligent effort are not in vain—this is what constitutes correct practice.”
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Light said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is any trace of practice, this constitutes the work of Māra; if it is the work of Māra, it is not true cultivation.”

If there is neither practice nor dwelling, and the various Māras find no opportunity to interfere, one is then able to transcend all paths of evil Māras; this is the true cultivation of a Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Vīryotsāhin said:
“World-Honored One!
If there were even the slightest dharma that one desired to accomplish, then one’s diligent effort would be in vain, because all dharmas are such that nothing is accomplished.”
"In this regard, if there is both wisdom and that which is known, it is not without intention; this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Destroying Evil Destinies said:
"World-Honored One!"
If there is the sphere of activity consisting of conceptualizing categories, how can it be called practice?
To be without categories and without conceptualization is what constitutes practice.
That which is without categories and without conceptualization is the very nature of the mind.
"If one can thoroughly understand the self-nature of the mind, this is what constitutes true practice.
Bodhisattva Suvicintitacintin said,
"World-Honored One!"
The Bodhisattva enters into the minds of all sentient beings; having entered them, he comprehends that the minds of all sentient beings are mindless.
In this context, "mindlessness" refers to that which is entered by wisdom; this is precisely what constitutes right practice.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati said:
“World-Honored One!
Quiescence is cultivation, and non-quiescence is also cultivation.”

When a bodhisattva, regarding the objects of all mental factors—whether they be great tranquility, pervasive tranquility, or proximate tranquility—is without any fabrication concerning their increase or decrease, and because he is free from increase and decrease, he realizes them with equanimity; this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Guide said:
“World-Honored One!
For a bodhisattva to initiate roots of goodness is right practice.”
If there were anything accomplished, it would not be the arousal of roots of goodness. Why is this?
Because when a bodhisattva arouses meritorious conduct, they are simultaneously arousing wisdom conduct.
Because merit is equal, wisdom is equal; because wisdom is equal, merit is equal.
Because merit and wisdom are equal, awakening is equal; because awakening is equal, all phenomena are equal. This is what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva King of Play said:
“World-Honored One!
That all dharmas are without discrimination is what constitutes cultivation.”

If a bodhisattva, having fully realized that all phenomena are universally subsumed within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), perceives that there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is either separate or joined, this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Arthacintin said:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas rely on the meaning and do not rely on the letter.”

If a bodhisattva, through understanding the definitive meaning, is able to receive, uphold, recite, and explain the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma with wisdom, yet remains unmoved within the true meaning that is ineffable, this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati said:
“World-Honored One,
a profound and firm mind is what constitutes spiritual practice.”
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the profound mind, this is beyond verbal description or conceptual explanation; it is the supreme attainment.
One merely cultivates the true and correct path, observing that even that true path has neither going nor coming—this is precisely what constitutes correct practice.
The Bodhisattva Ultimate Stainless Contemplation said:
“World-Honored One,
just as one washes a stained garment to make it clean, what need is there to cleanse a garment that is already stainless?”
The Bodhisattva is also like this: he does not cause the mind that is inherently pure to become pure through analytical investigation according to reality.
Furthermore, if all the stains and afflictions of the mind have never arisen from the very beginning, that is itself purity.
"If one is thus purified, this itself constitutes true practice.
Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
"World-Honored One!"
A bodhisattva who is sustained by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is able to accomplish right practice with little hardship. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva’s power cannot transcend the various demonic activities (mārakarman), one should know that they are being sustained by evil associates (pāpamitra).
If one has the power to transcend all demonic activities, it should be known that they have been taken into the care of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
World-Honored One!
Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to transcend all demonic activities, they should draw near to and serve spiritual friends.
"Because a bodhisattva is sustained by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they are able to accomplish correct practice with little hardship.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
"O son of good family!"
"Do you recognize the works of Māra?
Sāgaramati replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
“I recognize the works of Māra.
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!

Speak according to your own intention, so that when the bodhisattvas have heard it, they may immediately transcend and subdue all Māras and non-Buddhists, and swiftly realize the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has commanded, I shall now speak of the deeds of Māra; I pray only that the World-Honored One will establish his majestic spiritual power [over me].”
World-Honored One!
What are called the works of Māra consist of twelve kinds.
What are these twelve?
"First, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of generosity, they give away objects that are not dear to them with a mind of joyful desire,
yet they do not feel such joyful desire when giving away objects that are dear to them."
One gives that which people do not delight in, while withholding that which people do delight in.
One gives rise to various conceptualizations regarding the objects bestowed, and one gives rise to various conceptualizations regarding the person to whom they are given.
This is the first demonic activity when a bodhisattva practices generosity. Furthermore, Blessed One,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), if he sees others who are fully endowed with the precepts, virtuous qualities, and the rules of conduct and ritual, who even regarding minor transgressions harbor great fear, who sustain themselves through a pure livelihood, and who firmly maintain their ethical discipline— such as various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas— he should then draw near to and respect them.
When one sees a person who has broken the precepts and responds with reproach, disparagement, and anger, yet before that person, one relies on one's own virtue of the precepts to slander others—
this is the second demonic obstacle for a bodhisattva while upholding the precepts.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and seeks to perfect the conduct of patience, though the body may be able to endure, the speech cannot, and anger arises in the mind."
Seeing a powerful person, one practices patience toward them; seeing a weak person, one does not practice patience toward them.
Furthermore, one displays the power of patience before a powerful person, yet manifests signs of anger before a weak person.
He thus endures in this way, and he thus does not endure in that way.
In what circumstances can one endure?
In what circumstances cannot one endure?

If, while practicing patience, one gives rise to a mind of arrogance and pride, and does not swiftly repent for instances of impatience, this is the third demonic obstacle encountered by a bodhisattva when practicing patience.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor, they arouse diligence to transform and deliver those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, as well as those of the Mahāyāna."
He continuously preached the Dharma for those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, yet conversely used the Mahāyāna teachings to transform the ignorant.

(The following section follows the sequence of text and meaning as indicated by the Sanskrit manuscript; within the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati’s discourse on the twelve kinds of demonic activities, only the first three and a half sections are present, while the final eight and a half sections are missing.)

Within the Dharma-gate of the Ten Methods for Subduing Māra spoken by the Buddha, only the final four sections remain, while the first six are missing; since these have been lost from the Sanskrit original, there is no means to supplement them.
"This is the sixth Dharma-gate for destroying māras.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati! The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unstained;
by means of this characteristic of being unstained, one transforms and delivers sentient beings who are defiled."
This is the seventh dharma-gate for destroying māras.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

All phenomena are by nature unarisen and unproduced; with this characteristic of being unarisen and unproduced, one proclaims to all sentient beings the Dharma for severing birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This is the eighth Dharma-gate for destroying māras.
Furthermore, Samantagambhīramati!
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is of a single flavor and without differentiation.

By means of the single flavor and non-differentiated characteristic, he establishes the three vehicles and preaches the Dharma for each, so that all sentient beings do not abandon their aspiration for the Mahāyāna.
This is the ninth dharma-gate for destroying māras.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!
Although the bodhisattva’s mind, thought, and consciousness have no basis or attachment, they never forget the great bodhicitta.
Although he is free from all initiations, he does not abandon the mind that seeks to liberate all sentient beings.
Although he transcends all conditioned activities, he nevertheless accomplishes the sublime practices of a bodhisattva.
This is the tenth dharma-gate for subduing Māra. Samudramati!
If bodhisattvas diligently practice these ten dharma-gates for subduing Māra, they shall transcend all demonic activities.
The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Volume Sixteen.
The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Seal as Asked by Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
Volume Seventeen.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma-gate for destroying Māra, all the palaces of Māra became pitch black and dark, and the earth shook in six ways. It was just as when the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) while still in the stage of a bodhisattva before attaining perfect awakening; at that time, he emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows, causing all the palaces of Māra to likewise become dark and gloomy, exactly as they were today, without any difference.
At that time, the hosts of evil Māras, seeing these vast and extraordinary signs of transformation, swiftly arrayed their fourfold army;

just as in the past they had gone to the site of enlightenment with such magnificent adornments, so now did they likewise lead a fourfold army, extending thirty-six yojanas in breadth and completely filling the space, arriving at the place of the World-Honored One’s Great Assembly of Precious Adornments.
Due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they were entirely unable to return to their own palaces.

Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, when the hosts of Māra arrived, some saw other buddha-fields where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was teaching and transforming sentient beings together with a multitude of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas; others saw those who had severed the fetters of existence and realized arhatship, or individuals endowed with right view.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying: "Sāgaramati!
Do you now see this assembly of evil Māras, so adorned, as they approach this gathering?"
Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, I have seen it.”
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!
These hosts of māras have come to this assembly, intending to create obstacles to my True Dharma; what, then, will you do now?”
Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One!
I shall now place this host of evil Māras within the various worlds adorned with bliss in other directions.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra in the assembly addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
"Excellent, Great Being!
Where is the world-system Sarvavyūhaprīti located?"
"What is the name of that Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma?
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
To the east, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sarvaratnavyuha.
In that land there is a Buddha, titled Tathāgata Mārajit, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides and teaches the Dharma.
For what reason is this world named "Adorned with All Joys"?
Venerable One!

It is because that world possesses all manner of joyful things, all manner of meritorious things, and all manner of adorned things; were one to proclaim those sublime and wondrous matters in detail, even speaking for an entire eon would not suffice to exhaust them.
For this reason, that world is named "Adorned with All Joys.

Furthermore, the Buddha there is titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vajradhara (The Destroyer of Māras). This means that when that Blessed One first sat at the site of enlightenment while still in the stage of a bodhisattva, before he had realized all-knowledge, his body emitted a radiance that shone everywhere upon all the māras.

Wherever that light shone, there were hundreds of koṭis of māra hosts within those māra realms, and each individual māra had a retinue of one thousand koṭis. At that time, all these māras went to where the Bodhisattva was, intending to create various obstacles for him.

Due to the majestic spiritual power of this bodhisattva, the Māras were unable to create any obstacles; immediately, each of them conceived a sense of rare wonder, took refuge in that bodhisattva, and prostrated before him, whereupon the bodhisattva preached the Dharma to them according to their needs.
Having heard the Dharma, Māra’s mind became profoundly pure, and he immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subsequently, after that Buddha had realized the fruit of the Way, he was therefore given the name Tathāgata Māradhvaja (The One Who Crushes Māra).
Furthermore, in a past life during the *Kṛta-yuga* (Adorned Eon), while that Buddha was abiding in the stage of a bodhisattva, he was named Subduer of Māras (*Māra-vinaya*).
Now, within this present Bhadrakalpa, having attained *bodhi*, he is able to cause all māras to give rise to the bodhicitta and serve him.
That Buddha teaches only the supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna for the assembly of bodhisattvas; even the names of the two vehicles no longer exist there.
Venerable One!

For this reason, I now set aside this host of māras and go to that world called Array of All Joys. Having placed them there, I shall ensure that this host of māras never again engages in the activities of Māra.
"In that buddha-field, having together with the Bodhisattva Subduer of Māras resolved upon bodhicitta, we shall fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment.

At that time, when the hosts of evil Māras heard these words, they were struck with great terror; their hair stood on end, and they sought to leave the assembly, yet by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power they could not depart. Unable to conceal their forms, their fear increased to the utmost, and they each took refuge in the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and addressed him thus: "Save us!"
World-Honored One!
Save me! Sugata!
"Do not let the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati place me within that world-system.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of Māras, saying:
"You Māras, do not give rise to fear or alarm; these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas do not conceive thoughts of harm toward sentient beings."
"You all should personally seek forgiveness and repent before the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati; he will surely provide you with excellent protection.
At that time, the hosts of Māras each joined their palms, bowed their heads to the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, and said:
"We now repent and beg for forgiveness; O Great Being, please grant us your forbearance!"
"Do not place me within the world-system Adorned with All Joys.
Just as I have acted, I shall never again go to that assembly a second time.
Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
"O Māras, you should know!
I can no longer tolerate you. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva maintains ultimate and constant patience toward all sentient beings.
You, all you Māras, should now go to that world Adorned with All Joys and observe the various adornments of that world.
"That Tathāgata Mārapramardana will not cause you, the hosts of Māras, any harm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati extended his right arm, which was radiant with golden light, and placed it upon the crown of Māra’s head to bestow empowerment, saying these words:

"If the Dharma is true, by this word of truth—that all Bodhisattvas have no stinginess nor secrecy regarding the Dharma—by virtue of this word of truth, may all these hosts of Māras obtain such supernatural powers as I possess."
After the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati had spoken these words, the hosts of Māras immediately attained mastery endowed with supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*).

At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the hosts of Māras, having vanished from this assembly, reached that world-system Adorned with All Pleasures in an instant; all this was due to the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati.

At that time, having arrived in that land, the hosts of Māras went to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Destroyer of Māra was; they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, in that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva named Mārapramardaka who, having seen this sign, addressed his Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This one here is so weak and lacking in majestic radiance; his appearance is so unusual that he is loathsome to others—from where has he come?
That Buddha replied, "O son of good family!"

To the west, beyond as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. There, the World-Honored Buddha is known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he currently resides in that Great Jewel-Adorned Bodhimanda, extensively proclaiming the True Dharma of the Mahāsannipāta.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* great bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions, exceeding all calculation, who had all gathered together to listen to and receive the true Dharma.
Within that assembly was a bodhisattva named Sāgaramati, who was well-armored in the inconceivable, great, and firm armor, and was able to inquire about such true Dharma from the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

While the Dharma was being taught, a host of Māras arrived at that assembly intending to create obstacles; thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati placed those Māras under his power and came here for the sake of transforming and liberating them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Subduer of Māras addressed the various māras, saying:
"We now, together with you all, the māras, shall jointly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? In the past, I too once belonged to the class of Māras, creating obstacles and difficulties whenever sentient beings planted roots of goodness; subsequently, within this Dharma of the Tathāgata, I gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Therefore, at this time, you demons should all swiftly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that moment, with deep and firm resolve, each of the demons gave rise to the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having thus resolved their minds, they all spoke these words:
"We have already resolved our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; we shall never again perform the deeds of Māra."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Subduer of Māra immediately commanded his Māra to sit together with him upon that lion throne adorned with various jewels, and exhorted him, saying:
"O son of good family!
"What is this True Dharma of the Great Assembly spoken by that Tathāgata Śākyamuni? Now, according to your wish, I shall expound it.

At that time, through the empowerment of the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, all the Māras immediately took their places upon lion thrones. From their mouths and all their pores, they issued a pure sound—just like the True Dharma of the Great Assembly spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—with such words and such phrases, each one proclaimed in full and without omission, with no additions or subtractions in between.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mārapramardaka, having heard such a Dharma assembly of the True Dharma from within the realm of Māra, gave rise to a sense of wonder and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I now wish to see the Sahā world and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni;
furthermore, I wish to see that Bodhisattva Sāgaramati as well as the assembly of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, the Tathāgata Demolisher of Māra in that world emitted from between his eyebrows a great radiance called "Universal Manifestation of All Phenomenal Forms. This light shone everywhere throughout the Buddha-fields to the west, numbering as many as the sands of twelve Gaṅgā rivers, extending even to the Sahā world, appearing with vast brilliance and continuous, uninterrupted splendor.

The assembly of bodhisattvas in those worlds adorned with bliss all beheld the Tathāgata Śākyamuni within the Great Jewel-Adorned Bodhimanda, seated upon a precious lion throne embellished with hundreds of thousands of varieties of colors and forms, extensively proclaiming the sublime Dharma of the Great Assembly for the great assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions.
Furthermore, he saw this Sahā world filled with vast waters, like a great ocean, and he observed that within it there was no obstruction whatsoever.

He also saw the great bodhisattvas who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions, each sitting upon a great lotus flower adorned with various jewels as they listened to and received the True Dharma; those flowers were one krośa in length and breadth.

When those great beings saw this sign, they gave rise to a heart of joy, delight, and exhilaration; they immediately took exquisite flowers and scattered them from afar as an offering toward the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the flowers that were scattered all formed a vast and exquisite floral canopy above the crown of the head of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

At that time, in this assembly of the Buddha, the entire great multitude saw this flower-canopy hovering in the air above the crown of the Buddha’s head; struck with wonder, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
